## [sc-0_investigation_report_000] Investigation Report

> **Type:** investigation_report | **Reliability:** 0.99 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 General
On January 26, 2020, at approximately 0945 Pacific Standard Time (PST), a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, registration N72EX, impacted mountainous terrain in Calabasas, California. The accident site was located at coordinates 34°08'12.4"N, 118°41'36.1"W, at an elevation of approximately 1,510 feet mean sea level (MSL). The flight was operating under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 135, as an on-demand charter flight. The aircraft was destroyed by impact forces and a post-impact fire. All nine persons on board, including the pilot and eight passengers, sustained fatal injuries. Instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) prevailed in the area at the time of the accident.

1.2 Flight History
The flight originated at John Wayne Airport (KSNA), Santa Ana, California, with a planned destination of Camarillo Airport (KCMA), Camarillo, California. The pilot departed KSNA at 0906 PST, following a preflight inspection and standard dispatch procedures. The flight plan was filed under visual flight rules (VFR) with an estimated en route time of 45 minutes. At 0922 PST, the pilot contacted Los Angeles Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC) and requested a deviation to the north due to deteriorating weather conditions along the coastal route. Radar data indicated the aircraft maintained an altitude between 1,200 and 1,500 feet MSL while tracking northwest. At 0938 PST, the aircraft's transponder altitude began to fluctuate, and the last recorded radar return was at 0943 PST at 1,100 feet MSL, approximately 2.3 nautical miles southeast of the impact site. The aircraft subsequently entered a descending right turn before terrain impact.

1.3 Regulatory Framework
The operation was conducted under 14 CFR Part 135, which governs commuter and on-demand operations. Applicable weather minimums for VFR operations in Class E airspace, as specified in 14 CFR 91.155, require a minimum visibility of 3 statute miles and a distance from clouds of 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 2,000 feet horizontal. The operator's operations specifications authorized VFR flight only when meteorological conditions met or exceeded these minimums. The flight was not operating under an instrument flight rules (IFR) clearance, and the aircraft was not equipped with a certified IFR approach system for the intended route.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Pilot-in-Command
The pilot-in-command held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate with a rotorcraft-helicopter rating, a commercial pilot certificate with airplane single-engine land and multi-engine land ratings, and a certified flight instructor (CFI) certificate for rotorcraft. The pilot possessed a type rating for the Sikorsky S-76 series. Medical certification was current under 14 CFR Part 67, with a first-class medical certificate issued on November 12, 2019, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 8,245 hours, with 1,980 hours in the S-76B. The pilot's most recent proficiency check was completed on October 18, 2019, and included a review of emergency procedures, autorotation, and instrument flight maneuvers.

2.2 Second in Command
The aircraft was certified for single-pilot operations in accordance with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) type certificate data sheet. No second in command was assigned to the flight, nor was one required under the operator's approved operations specifications. Company training records for the designated second in command position were reviewed to verify standardization across the fleet. The records indicated that all designated second in command personnel had completed recurrent crew resource management (CRM) training and VFR-into-IMC avoidance modules within the preceding 12 months. The absence of a second in command on this flight was consistent with the operator's single-pilot operational model for S-76B charter missions.

2.3 Training and Records
The pilot's training file contained documentation of recurrent ground and flight training completed on September 5, 2019, which included a review of spatial disorientation, weather decision-making, and terrain awareness. The pilot had completed a simulator-based instrument proficiency check on August 22, 2019, demonstrating proficiency in partial-panel operations and missed approach procedures. Duty time records indicated the pilot had been on duty for 3 hours and 12 minutes at the time of the accident, with a rest period of 11 hours and 45 minutes preceding the duty day. No fatigue-related anomalies were identified in the pilot's scheduling history.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Specifications
The accident aircraft was a Sikorsky S-76B, manufacturer serial number 760345, manufactured in 1988. The aircraft was registered to Island Express Helicopters, Inc., and operated under 14 CFR Part 135. Total time on the airframe was 12,452.6 hours. The aircraft was powered by two Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6B-36A turboshaft engines, each rated at 650 shaft horsepower. The maximum gross weight for the aircraft was 11,700 pounds. The calculated takeoff weight for the accident flight was 10,845 pounds, with a center of gravity located at 142.3 inches aft of the datum, within the approved envelope.

3.2 Maintenance and Airworthiness Directives
The aircraft was maintained under an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program. The most recent 100-hour inspection was completed on January 10, 2020, with no deferred maintenance items. All applicable airworthiness directives (ADs) were documented as complied with in the aircraft maintenance logbooks. Maintenance records were cross-referenced with applicable regulatory directives, including Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-51, which was issued subsequent to the accident date but reviewed for historical component tracking and regulatory compliance verification. The AD pertained to specific rotorcraft transmission inspection intervals and was not applicable to the accident aircraft's configuration at the time of the event. No outstanding maintenance discrepancies were noted in the 30 days preceding the flight.

3.3 Systems and Components
The aircraft was equipped with a standard analog flight instrument panel, including attitude indicator, heading indicator, altimeter, vertical speed indicator, and airspeed indicator. The avionics suite included a Garmin GNS 430W GPS/NAV/COM unit and a King KX 165A communication/navigation radio. The autopilot system was a Sikorsky SAS-76 stability augmentation system, which provided attitude and heading hold functions. A review of the aircraft's flight control architecture confirmed the absence of a Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), as such systems are not certified for rotorcraft applications and were not part of the original equipment manufacturer's design specifications. The aircraft was not equipped with a flight data recorder (FDR) or cockpit voice recorder (CVR), as these were not required under 14 CFR Part 135 for rotorcraft of this weight class and configuration at the time of manufacture.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Conditions
On January 26, 2020, a strong marine layer was present along the Southern California coast, driven by a high-pressure system situated over the Great Basin and a low-pressure trough offshore. The marine layer produced widespread stratus clouds, fog, and reduced visibility across the Los Angeles Basin and Ventura County. The cloud base was observed between 600 and 900 feet MSL, with visibility frequently dropping below 1 statute mile in localized areas. The terrain in the Calabasas region rises sharply from approximately 800 feet MSL in the valleys to over 2,000 feet MSL within 3 nautical miles, creating a high-risk environment for VFR flight in marginal weather.

4.2 Surface Observations and Forecasts
The nearest automated weather observing system (AWOS) at Van Nuys Airport (KVNY) reported at 0935 PST: wind 270° at 6 knots, visibility 1/2 statute mile in fog, ceiling 700 feet overcast, temperature 12°C, dew point 11°C, altimeter 30.02 inches of mercury. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) for KCMA, issued at 0500 PST, predicted visibility 1/2 to 1 statute mile in fog, ceiling 500 to 800 feet overcast, with conditions expected to persist through 1200 PST. The forecast was consistent with the observed conditions at the time of the accident.

4.3 Pilot Reports and Radar Data
Multiple pilot reports (PIREPs) were filed between 0830 and 0930 PST indicating IMC conditions along the coastal route. A Cessna 172 reported at 0855 PST: "IMC, ceiling 600 feet, visibility 1/4 mile, unable to maintain VFR, requesting IFR clearance." A Bell 407 reported at 0912 PST: "Heavy fog, terrain obscured, climbing to 2,000 feet for VFR." Radar data from the Southern California TRACON indicated the accident aircraft's ground speed averaged 115 knots during the final 10 minutes of flight. The aircraft's altitude profile showed a gradual descent from 1,500 feet MSL to 1,100 feet MSL, with a corresponding reduction in ground speed to 85 knots, consistent with a pilot attempting to maintain visual reference in deteriorating conditions.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Impact Site and Debris Field
The primary impact site was located on a steep, brush-covered hillside at 34°08'12.4"N, 118°41'36.1"W. The initial impact point was marked by a 12-foot-long gouge in the soil, oriented on a magnetic heading of 315°. The debris field extended approximately 180 feet downslope, with major components distributed in a linear pattern consistent with a high-energy, controlled-flight-into-terrain (CFIT) impact. The main rotor hub assembly was located 45 feet from the initial impact point, with all four main rotor blades fractured at the root. The tail boom was separated approximately 3 feet aft of the main cabin bulkhead, with the tail rotor assembly recovered intact 60 feet from the primary impact site.

5.2 Component Examination
Examination of the recovered components revealed no evidence of pre-impact mechanical failure, structural fatigue, or system malfunction. Both PT6B-36A engines exhibited rotational scoring on the compressor and turbine blades, consistent with impact forces. The fuel control units were intact, and fuel lines showed no signs of leakage prior to impact. The flight control linkages, including the cyclic, collective, and anti-torque pedals, were continuous and free of binding. The stability augmentation system (SAS) actuators were recovered and bench-tested; all units operated within manufacturer specifications. The GPS/NAV/COM unit was severely damaged, but memory modules were extracted and analyzed. No recorded flight path deviations or system warnings were identified prior to the final radar return.

5.3 Post-Impact Fire and Recovery
A post-impact fire consumed approximately 60% of the fuselage structure, with burn patterns indicating rapid fuel ignition following impact. The fire was extinguished by local emergency responders at 1015 PST. All nine occupants were recovered from the wreckage. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Investigator-in-Charge coordinated with the Federal Aviation Administration, local law enforcement, and the operator to secure the site and initiate evidence collection. Wreckage was transported to a secure facility for detailed examination, and all components were cataloged in accordance with NTSB evidence handling procedures.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Operator Policies and Procedures
The operator's general operations manual (GOM) required pilots to maintain VFR weather minimums at all times and to execute a diversion or return to departure if conditions deteriorated below 3 statute miles visibility or 1,000-foot ceiling. The manual included a specific section on VFR-into-IMC avoidance, emphasizing immediate 180-degree turns, altitude maintenance, and communication with air traffic control upon inadvertent entry into IMC. Dispatch procedures required a weather briefing from an FAA-approved source prior to departure, with a mandatory go/no-go decision documented in the flight release. The operator's safety management system (SMS) included quarterly risk assessments for coastal VFR operations, with historical data indicating elevated risk during winter months due to marine layer formation.

6.2 Historical Precedents and Safety Data
The NTSB has investigated multiple rotorcraft accidents involving VFR flight into IMC, with similar contributing factors including spatial disorientation, terrain proximity, and delayed decision-making. A review of NTSB accident reports from 2000 to 2019 identified 47 helicopter accidents where VFR-into-IMC was a primary or contributing factor, resulting in 112 fatalities. The Federal Aviation Administration has issued multiple safety alerts and advisory circulars addressing this hazard, including AC 90-48D, "Pilots' Role in Collision Avoidance," and AC 135-14B, "Helicopter Air Ambulance Operations." The data indicates that single-pilot VFR operations in coastal and mountainous terrain require enhanced weather monitoring, terrain awareness systems, and strict adherence to published minimums.

6.3 Regulatory Guidance and Investigative Coordination
The investigation was conducted in accordance with NTSB Part 830 regulations and coordinated with the FAA's Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) and the Aircraft Certification Service (AIR). The Investigator-in-Charge established operational, maintenance, meteorological, and human performance groups to examine all relevant data. All findings were documented in accordance with NTSB Group Chairman's Factual Report standards. The investigation did not include a determination of probable cause, as that function is reserved for the final NTSB Board Report. All data, including maintenance logs, pilot records, weather observations, and wreckage examination results, have been archived and are available for review by authorized parties. The Federal Aviation Administration continues to monitor compliance with 14 CFR Part 135 weather minimums and has initiated a review of operator training programs to address VFR-into-IMC risk mitigation.

## [sc-0_technical_analysis_001] Technical Analysis

> **Type:** technical_analysis | **Reliability:** 0.968 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data extraction procedures performed on the flight data recorder (FDR), cockpit voice recorder (CVR), and associated avionics data acquisition components recovered from the accident helicopter. The examination was conducted under the authority of the National Transportation Safety Board (Safety Board) in coordination with the Lead Investigator assigned to the aviation group. The scope of this report encompasses the physical inspection of the crash-survivable memory units (CSMUs), verification of data integrity, extraction and decoding of recorded flight parameters, and comparative analysis against manufacturer design specifications and operational limits.

The items examined were received at the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory, Washington, D.C., on February 12, 2020. The primary components subjected to analysis included:
- L-3 Communications FA2100-1020 Solid-State Flight Data Recorder (P/N 2100-1020-00, S/N 18472)
- Honeywell 980-4700-001 Cockpit Voice Recorder (P/N 980-4700-001, S/N 09284)
- ARINC 717/429 data interface module (P/N 76100-00315-102, S/N 4491)
- Forward and aft CSMU mounting brackets (Sikorsky P/N 76100-00210-101 and -102)

All examinations were conducted in accordance with NTSB Laboratory Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) 8.4.2, RTCA DO-160G environmental qualification guidelines, and manufacturer technical service bulletins. Data extraction, synchronization, and parameter validation were completed between February 14 and February 18, 2020. The findings documented herein are strictly factual and limited to the technical condition of the recorders, the integrity of the recorded data, and the operational parameters captured during the accident flight.

2. BACKGROUND

The accident aircraft was a Sikorsky S-76B twin-engine, medium-lift helicopter, serial number 760342, manufactured in 1992. The integrated avionics suite utilized a dual-channel, solid-state FDR/CVR architecture compliant with TSO-C124a and TSO-C123b certification requirements. The FDR was designed to record a minimum of 28 flight parameters via an ARINC 717 digital data bus, with sampling rates ranging from 0.25 Hz to 4 Hz depending on parameter criticality. The CSMU was engineered to withstand impact accelerations up to 3,400 g for 6.5 milliseconds, static crush loads of 5,000 lbf, and thermal exposure of 1,100 °C for 60 minutes, per RTCA DO-160G Section 16 and MIL-STD-810H Method 516.8.

The helicopter's flight control system employed a conventional mechanical-hydraulic architecture with a two-axis stability augmentation system (SAS). Unlike the MCAS (Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System) utilized in certain fixed-wing transport category aircraft, which relies on single-sensor authority and automated trim actuation, the S-76B SAS operates as a non-authoritative, pilot-override-capable damping system that modulates cyclic and collective inputs through electro-hydraulic servo valves. The FDR data acquisition unit (DAU) sampled engine torque (N1), gas generator speed (Ng), main rotor RPM (NR), collective position, pressure altitude, indicated airspeed, vertical speed, magnetic heading, pitch, roll, and GPS-derived position at 1 Hz intervals.

The accident helicopter's operational history, as documented in the airframe logbooks and reviewed by the FAA, indicated 12,480 total airframe hours and 8,920 flight cycles. The most recent heavy inspection was completed on November 14, 2019, in accordance with Sikorsky Maintenance Planning Document (MPD) Revision 14 and FAA Order 8900.1 Volume 6, Chapter 2, Section 3, which governs recurrent airworthiness directive compliance and component life-limit tracking. All mandatory service bulletins and airworthiness directives applicable to the FDR/CVR installation were documented as complied with. For comparative reference, subsequent regulatory guidance (AD 2024-02-51) addressing non-volatile memory retention thresholds and post-impact data recovery protocols was reviewed to contextualize the CSMU's endurance characteristics, though it was not in effect at the time of manufacture or operation.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

Upon receipt, the FDR and CSMU housings exhibited localized impact deformation consistent with high-energy terrain contact. The forward mounting bracket (P/N 76100-00210-101) displayed 14.2 mm of lateral crush deformation on the port side, with a 3.8 mm shear fracture at the aft bolt interface. The aft bracket (P/N 76100-00210-102) remained structurally intact, with bolt torque measurements recorded at 43.5 ft-lbs and 46.2 ft-lbs, within the Sikorsky specified range of 45 ± 5 ft-lbs. No evidence of pre-impact fatigue cracking, corrosion, or fastener loosening was observed.

The CSMU outer casing, constructed of titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V, AMS 4911), exhibited thermal discoloration consistent with post-impact fire exposure. Surface temperature mapping via infrared thermography indicated peak localized heating of 312 °C, well below the 1,100 °C design threshold. The internal memory array, housed within a stainless steel (AISI 304) thermal insulation blanket, showed no signs of delamination or solder joint failure. Metallurgical analysis of the aluminum 7075-T6 mounting brackets (ASTM B209) was performed per ASTM E8/E8M tensile testing standards. Hardness testing yielded Rockwell B values of 87–91, consistent with the T6 temper specification. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) confirmed the absence of intergranular corrosion or stress-corrosion cracking. Fracture surfaces exhibited ductile dimple rupture morphology, indicative of single-event overload rather than progressive fatigue.

Data extraction was performed using the L-3 proprietary FA2100-1020 interface module and NTSB Laboratory Decoder Software v4.8.1. The ARINC 717 data stream was synchronized using the embedded time code generator (TCG) and validated against the CVR's 30-minute loop timestamp. Parity bit error rate was calculated at 0.0003%, well within the RTCA DO-160G maximum allowable threshold of 0.01%. Frame synchronization was achieved across 100% of recorded sectors, with no missing or corrupted data blocks. The CVR's four-channel audio (captain, copilot, observer, and area microphone) was successfully recovered, with signal-to-noise ratios averaging 28 dB across all channels.

Photographic documentation of the physical examination is referenced as NTSB-2020-001-IMG-042 through NTSB-2020-001-IMG-089, including macro-photography of mounting hardware, CSMU casing deformation, and internal memory board layout. All components were cleaned, cataloged, and stored in accordance with NTSB evidence preservation protocols. No anomalies were identified in the power supply circuitry, data bus termination resistors, or solid-state memory controllers that would indicate pre-impact system degradation.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

The FDR recorded 28 parameters at 1 Hz sampling intervals, with pitch, roll, and vertical acceleration sampled at 4 Hz. Data was time-synchronized to UTC and converted to local Pacific Standard Time (PST) for operational correlation. The recorded flight profile commenced at 09:45:12 PST from John Wayne Airport (KSNA), with initial climb to 1,200 ft MSL and transition to cruise at 145 KIAS. At 09:58:33 PST, the aircraft entered instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), as evidenced by a rapid decrease in indicated airspeed from 145 KIAS to 112 KIAS over a 42-second interval, accompanied by a gradual increase in descent rate from -180 fpm to -650 fpm.

Between 09:59:14 PST and 10:01:02 PST, the FDR recorded sustained oscillatory pitch and roll attitudes, with peak deviations of +4.2°/-3.8° pitch and +6.1°/-5.4° roll. Vertical speed progressively increased to -1,240 fpm, while pressure altitude decreased from 1,850 ft MSL to 920 ft MSL. Indicated airspeed continued to decay, reaching 82 KIAS at 10:01:47 PST. Main rotor RPM (NR) remained within the normal operating envelope of 100.2% to 101.8%, with no evidence of underspeed or overspeed conditions. Collective position was stable at 68% ± 2% travel, indicating no abrupt pilot input or mechanical binding. Engine torque parameters (N1) for both Pratt & Whitney Canada PW210A engines remained synchronized at 84% ± 1.5%, with gas generator speeds (Ng) tracking within 0.8% of each other.

The CVR audio transcript, synchronized to the FDR timeline, captured pilot communications consistent with visual flight rules (VFR) navigation, including references to terrain avoidance and weather observation. No automated terrain awareness warning system (TAWS) alerts, engine parameter exceedances, or system fault annunciations were recorded. The flight path reconstruction, derived from GPS position data and inertial reference unit (IRU) outputs, indicates a gradual left turn of approximately 18° over a 3.2 NM segment, with a continuous descent profile intersecting rising terrain at 10:02:14 PST.

Comparison with Sikorsky S-76B Flight Manual limitations reveals that the recorded descent rate of -1,240 fpm exceeded the normal operational limit of 1,200 fpm but remained below the emergency descent threshold of 1,800 fpm. Airspeed decay to 82 KIAS approached the minimum controllable airspeed (Vmc) envelope for the aircraft's weight and configuration, though no stall warning or aerodynamic buffet was indicated in the recorded parameters. The absence of system warnings, combined with stable engine and rotor parameters, indicates that the aircraft remained fully controllable and mechanically sound throughout the recorded flight segment. The progressive descent and airspeed decay, coupled with oscillatory attitude deviations, are consistent with spatial disorientation in reduced visibility conditions.

All data parameters were cross-validated against the Sikorsky S-76B Performance and Limitations Manual, Revision 12, and the FAA Type Certificate Data Sheet H10NE. No discrepancies were identified between recorded values and expected sensor outputs for the given flight conditions. The data integrity index, calculated using the NTSB Laboratory's proprietary validation algorithm, returned a score of 99.73%, confirming the reliability of the extracted parameters for investigative analysis.

5. SUMMARY

The physical examination of the flight data recorder, cockpit voice recorder, and associated mounting hardware revealed no evidence of pre-impact mechanical failure, electrical degradation, or structural fatigue. The crash-survivable memory units sustained localized impact deformation and thermal exposure within certified design limits, with all internal memory arrays remaining fully functional. Metallurgical and hardness testing of the aluminum 7075-T6 mounting brackets confirmed material properties consistent with manufacturer specifications, and fracture analysis indicated single-event overload consistent with terrain impact.

Data extraction and decoding procedures yielded a complete, time-synchronized record of 28 flight parameters with a data integrity index of 99.73%. The recorded flight profile indicates sustained VFR flight into deteriorating visibility, characterized by progressive airspeed decay, increasing descent rate, and oscillatory pitch/roll attitudes. Engine torque, rotor RPM, and collective position remained within normal operating envelopes throughout the recorded segment. No system warnings, fault codes, or automated alert activations were captured. The flight parameters and audio recordings are consistent with controlled flight into terrain under instrument meteorological conditions, with no technical anomalies identified in the aircraft's avionics, powerplant, or flight control systems.

## [sc-0_witness_testimony_002] Witness Testimony

> **Type:** witness_testimony | **Reliability:** 0.671 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

INTERVIEW OF MARCUS VEGA, FLIGHT OPERATIONS COORDINATOR
Date: March 14, 2024
Time: 09:30 AM PST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Los Angeles, California
Interviewer: Lead Investigator Sarah Chen, NTSB
Witness: Marcus Vega, former Flight Operations Coordinator, Island Express Helicopters

[Recording begins]

Q: Good morning, Mr. Vega. Thank you for making the time to come in today. For the official record, please state your full name and your position at the time of the January 26, 2020 incident.

A: Yeah, good morning. It’s Marcus Vega. I was the Flight Operations Coordinator for Island Express Helicopters back then. I handled flight following, weather monitoring, crew scheduling… basically the ops desk. I’d been in that seat for about four years when the accident happened.

Q: And you were on duty that morning?

A: I was. Yeah. I got in around six-thirty, maybe a little after seven. It was a Sunday, so the schedule was lighter than a weekday, but we had a few charters lined up. The one that… well, the one that went down was logged as a standard VIP transport. I didn’t know the passenger manifest at first. Just another tail number in the system. N72EX. Sikorsky S-76B. Beautiful machine, honestly. Sikorsky Aircraft really built those things to last. Smooth, reliable.

Q: Walk me through your morning. What was the first thing you noticed about the weather or the flight plan?

A: Right. So, around eight-fifteen, I pulled up the METARs and the TAFs for the Van Nuys area. It was… it was already getting thick. Low ceilings, patchy fog rolling in off the coast. I remember thinking, “This is gonna be a go/no-go day.” The pilot, Ara, he called in for a standard pre-flight. We talked about the route, the altitudes, the usual stuff. He was confident, you know? He’d flown that corridor a hundred times. But the visibility was dropping. I told him, “Hey, if it gets below VFR minimums, don’t push it. We can delay or divert.” He said he’d keep an eye on it.

Q: What time did they depart?

A: Uh… I want to say nine-oh-two. Maybe nine-oh-five. I logged it in the flight following system. They lifted off, climbed out, and I started tracking them on the radar overlay. First ten minutes were fine. They were heading northwest, following the 101 corridor, staying under the cloud deck. But then… around nine-twenty, nine-twenty-five, the fog just… it thickened. Like a wall. I could see on the weather loop that the marine layer was pushing inland fast. I tried hailing them on the company frequency. Static. Just a lot of white noise. I remember gripping the desk, thinking, “Come on, just check in.”

Q: Did you attempt to contact ATC or any other aircraft in the area?

A: Yeah, I called SoCal Approach. They said they had him on radar but he was squawking VFR, so they weren’t providing separation. I asked if they could relay a message, but… I don’t know, it felt like everything was moving too slow. I was watching the terrain elevation on my screen. The hills around Calabasas, they rise up pretty quick. If you’re flying VFR and you lose visual reference, you’re… you’re in trouble. I kept telling myself he’d turn back. He had to. But the last transmission I got was around nine-forty. Just a quick, “Uh, we’re in the soup, turning around.” And then… nothing.

Q: You mentioned the pilot was flying VFR into deteriorating conditions. Was there a second in command on board that flight?

A: No. No, there wasn’t. It was a single-pilot operation. Standard for that type of charter. I mean, we had guys who could fly as a second in command, but for this trip, it was just Ara. He was highly experienced, but… look, spatial disorientation is real. When you lose the horizon, your inner ear lies to you. You think you’re level, you’re actually banking. I’ve read the reports since, and it’s… it’s exactly what happened. He probably didn’t even realize he was descending until it was too late.

Q: Let’s talk about maintenance and regulatory compliance. How did Island Express track airworthiness directives and manufacturer bulletins at the time?

A: We had a pretty solid system. Everything went through our maintenance tracking software. We’d get the FAA alerts, cross-reference them with the tail numbers, and if something applied, we’d ground the bird until it was done. I mean, after the whole MCAS situation with the 737s, the whole industry got… I don’t know, hyper-aware. You couldn’t just brush off a bulletin anymore. We started doing extra cross-checks, even for stuff that didn’t directly apply to our fleet. It changed the culture. And honestly, it’s only gotten stricter. I mean, look at AD 2024-02-51. That one came out a few months ago, right? It’s for rotorcraft transmission components, but it’s a good example of how the FAA and the manufacturers are tightening the loop. Back in twenty-twenty, we were compliant, but the oversight wasn’t as… granular. Now, if a Sikorsky Aircraft service letter drops, we’re on it within forty-eight hours.

Q: You mentioned the FAA. Did you have any direct communication with them that morning?

A: Not directly. I mean, we’re a Part 135 operator, so we’re under their umbrella, but the actual flight following was internal. The FAA handles the airspace, the ATC, the big picture. We handled the operational side. But after the crash, obviously, the NTSB took over. You guys were on site within hours. I remember seeing the black SUVs pull up to the hangar. It was… surreal. I gave my initial statement to a field investigator, but I guess that’s why I’m sitting here with you now, Lead Investigator.

Q: Yes. I want to go back to the final moments. What were you doing when you realized the aircraft hadn’t checked in?

A: I was pacing. I had the headset on, just listening to the dead air. I called the pilot’s cell. Straight to voicemail. I called the charter coordinator. She was panicking. I told her to stay calm, that maybe the radio was just out. But I knew. I knew. The terrain warning system… I don’t know if the S-76B had a TAWS that would’ve triggered, but even if it did, at that point, it’s a matter of seconds. I remember the clock on the wall ticking. Nine-forty-five. Nine-forty-six. I was staring at the radar, watching the blip just… stop. It didn’t fade. It just vanished. I felt sick. I actually had to sit down. My hands were shaking. I called 911, gave them the last known coordinates, and then I just… waited.

Q: How did the investigation process affect your work afterward?

A: It changed everything. The NTSB’s preliminary report came out, and it was… it was hard to read. VFR into IMC, spatial disorientation, terrain. All the things I’d been worried about. We had to overhaul our weather minimums, implement stricter go/no-go protocols, and mandate dual-pilot crews for certain conditions. The FAA came in for audits, we had to retrain everyone on risk management. It was a long year. But you know, aviation’s built on learning from the worst days. I still think about that morning. The fog, the static, the silence. It stays with you.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add for the record?

A: Just… I want to make sure it’s clear that the crew, the passengers, they didn’t do anything wrong. The weather just closed in faster than anyone expected. And the system… it’s better now. We track everything. We don’t cut corners. I hope that’s what comes out of this. That’s all.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Vega. We’ll be in touch if we have follow-up questions.

A: Yeah. Thank you. I appreciate it.

[Recording ends]

## [sc-0_regulatory_filing_003] Regulatory Filing

> **Type:** regulatory_filing | **Reliability:** 0.976 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION
FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
FLIGHT STANDARDS SERVICE
NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION SAFETY BOARD
JOINT REGULATORY COMPLIANCE AND SAFETY OVERSIGHT REPORT

DOCUMENT CONTROL: FAA-2020-0892 / NTSB-DCA20MA028-REG-01
DATE OF ISSUANCE: October 14, 2024
CLASSIFICATION: UNCLASSIFIED // REGULATORY COMPLIANCE

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This document constitutes the formal regulatory response and compliance framework addressing National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Safety Recommendations A-20-001 through A-20-004, issued in conjunction with the investigation of the January 26, 2020, aviation accident involving a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter. The occurrence is cataloged under NTSB Accident Number DCA20MA028. The subject matter pertains to the regulatory oversight of Part 135 rotorcraft operations, specifically addressing inadvertent flight into instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), terrain avoidance system mandates, and operational control deficiencies. This correspondence references Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Docket No. FAA-2020-0892, Proposed Rulemaking for 14 CFR Part 135, Subpart E, and establishes the compliance baseline for air carrier certificate holders operating under 14 CFR Part 135. All regulatory actions herein are promulgated pursuant to the authority vested in the Administrator under 49 U.S.C. § 44701 and 49 U.S.C. § 44702.

2. BACKGROUND
The Federal Aviation Administration maintains statutory oversight of commercial rotorcraft operations under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 135. The subject aircraft, a Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation S-76B, holds Type Certificate No. H10WE and was operated under an active Part 135 air carrier certificate at the time of the occurrence. The regulatory framework governing visual flight rules (VFR) operations, weather minimums, and equipment requirements is codified in 14 CFR 135.181, 14 CFR 135.183, and 14 CFR 135.185. Historically, the FAA has addressed VFR-into-IMC accident trends through Advisory Circular (AC) 135-14B, which provides guidance on inadvertent IMC recognition and recovery, and through voluntary adoption of Helicopter Terrain Awareness and Warning Systems (HTAWS). However, prior NTSB safety recommendations, including the A-19-001 series, have consistently identified systemic gaps in mandatory terrain avoidance equipment and standardized pilot training for degraded visual environments.

The certification basis for rotorcraft flight control and terrain avoidance systems is established under 14 CFR Part 27 and Part 29, with specific airworthiness standards for flight control systems delineated in 14 CFR 27.672 and 14 CFR 29.672. For comparative regulatory analysis, the certification history of the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) under 14 CFR 25.672 and 14 CFR 25.1309 provides a critical precedent for evaluating human-machine interface validation, failure mode analysis, and pilot awareness requirements in automated flight control augmentation. While MCAS is a fixed-wing transport category system, its regulatory scrutiny underscores the necessity of transparent system logic, unambiguous pilot alerting, and rigorous failure mitigation protocols. These principles directly inform current FAA policy regarding rotorcraft terrain avoidance and automated warning system integration, particularly where pilot reliance on visual references intersects with automated terrain proximity logic. The regulatory divergence between transport category augmentation systems and rotorcraft terrain awareness mandates has prompted a comprehensive review of 14 CFR 135.185 equipment requirements and associated training curricula under 14 CFR 135.215 and 14 CFR 135.243.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
Post-accident regulatory audit and certificate surveillance of Island Express Helicopters, Inc. (Certificate No. 1E3R509C) reveal that the operator maintained compliance with baseline 14 CFR Part 135 operational requirements at the time of the occurrence. However, detailed analysis of operational control records, pilot training documentation, and flight following procedures identifies material deficiencies in weather decision-making protocols and inadvertent IMC mitigation. The operator’s Minimum Equipment List (MEL), derived from the Master Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) for the S-76B, did not mandate operational terrain awareness systems, relying instead on pilot visual reference, basic navigation instrumentation, and company-specific flight following procedures. This configuration, while compliant with extant 14 CFR 135.185 provisions, proved insufficient to prevent controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) during rapid meteorological degradation.

Regulatory oversight actions conducted by the FAA Principal Operations Inspector (POI) and Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI), in accordance with FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 12, Chapter 3, confirm that the operator’s operational control program lacked real-time meteorological monitoring integration and automated IMC alerting thresholds. Furthermore, pilot recurrent training curricula did not incorporate standardized, simulator-based inadvertent IMC recovery modules aligned with AC 135-14B. The regulatory framework governing Part 135 rotorcraft operations currently permits discretionary HTAWS installation, creating an inconsistent safety baseline across the commercial rotorcraft fleet.

A critical gap identified in the regulatory architecture is the absence of mandatory, integrated terrain avoidance logic for rotorcraft operating under VFR in mountainous or rapidly changing meteorological environments. The certification standards for the Sikorsky S-76B, while fully compliant with 14 CFR Part 27 airworthiness requirements, do not mandate automated flight path monitoring or predictive terrain avoidance algorithms. Drawing upon the regulatory lessons derived from the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System certification review, the FAA recognizes that automated warning systems must incorporate unambiguous pilot alerting, fail-safe operational logic, and rigorous human factors validation to prevent mode confusion or delayed pilot response. The current regulatory posture under 14 CFR 135.185 fails to harmonize these principles with rotorcraft operational realities, necessitating immediate rulemaking action to mandate HTAWS installation, standardize inadvertent IMC training, and enhance operational control oversight.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
Pursuant to the findings detailed herein, the FAA shall initiate the following corrective actions and regulatory compliance measures:

a. Rulemaking and Equipment Mandate: The FAA shall publish a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) to amend 14 CFR 135.185, requiring the installation and operational use of FAA-approved Helicopter Terrain Awareness and Warning Systems (HTAWS) for all Part 135 rotorcraft conducting passenger-carrying operations. The rule shall establish technical performance standards aligned with TSO-C194 and mandate integration with primary flight displays to ensure unambiguous terrain proximity alerting.

b. Operator Compliance Requirements: Island Express Helicopters, and all similarly certificated Part 135 operators, shall implement an enhanced Operational Control Program in accordance with 14 CFR 135.63. The revised program shall incorporate real-time meteorological data integration, mandatory automated flight following, and defined IMC transition protocols. Operators shall submit revised Operations Specifications (OpSpecs) to the cognizant Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) within 90 days of final rule publication.

c. Training and Qualification Standards: All Part 135 rotorcraft pilots shall complete recurrent training on inadvertent IMC recognition, spatial disorientation mitigation, and instrument transition procedures. Training shall be conducted in FAA-approved flight simulation training devices (FSTDs) and shall align with AC 135-14B and FAA-S-8081-14 standards. Compliance shall be achieved within 12 months of the final rule effective date.

d. Manufacturer and Certification Coordination: The FAA Office of Aviation Safety shall coordinate with Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation to evaluate supplemental type certificate (STC) pathways for legacy S-76B fleet HTAWS integration. All modifications shall comply with 14 CFR 21.113 and 14 CFR 21.115, ensuring continued airworthiness and type design conformity. The FAA shall issue an Airworthiness Directive (AD) if necessary to mandate compliance timelines for existing fleet installations.

e. Oversight and Follow-Up Schedule: The FAA shall conduct targeted surveillance audits per FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 12, Chapter 4, Section 2, to verify operator compliance with revised OpSpecs, training records, and HTAWS installation status. Interim compliance reports shall be submitted to the FSDO at 90-day intervals. The NTSB shall monitor implementation progress and issue a follow-up safety recommendation assessment within 18 months of final rule publication. Full regulatory compliance shall be achieved within 24 months of the effective date, with non-compliant operators subject to enforcement action under 14 CFR 13.11 and 14 CFR 13.15.

This document serves as the official regulatory response and compliance directive. All referenced actions shall be executed in strict accordance with applicable Federal Aviation Regulations, FAA policy directives, and NTSB safety recommendation protocols.

HEADLINE: Nine Dead After Helicopter Crashes in Southern California Hills Amid Poor Weather

BYLINE: Marcus Thorne, The Metropolitan Herald
DATELINE: CALABASAS, Calif. —

A private helicopter carrying nine people crashed into a steep hillside in Calabasas, California, on Sunday morning, killing everyone on board. The Sikorsky S-76B went down in dense fog and low clouds, prompting a massive emergency response and sending shockwaves through the local community.

Preliminary data indicates the pilot was operating under visual flight rules, a standard that requires pilots to navigate by sight and maintain a clear view of the ground, when the aircraft entered an area of severely reduced visibility and rising terrain. The decision to continue the flight into instrument meteorological conditions—weather that requires reliance on cockpit instruments rather than outside visual references—appears to have been a critical factor in the tragedy. The crash site, located in a rugged canyon area northwest of Los Angeles, was quickly cordoned off as first responders battled difficult access and hazardous conditions to secure the wreckage and begin recovery operations.

“Our investigators are on the ground and have begun the painstaking process of documenting the scene,” said a spokesperson for the National Transportation Safety Board. “We are treating this as a major accident and will leave no stone unturned in determining the sequence of events that led to this loss of life.” The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it is cooperating fully with the NTSB, noting that the helicopter was operating under a commercial charter certificate. “The safety of the flying public remains our highest priority,” an FAA regional director stated during a press briefing. “We are reviewing all operational records, pilot qualifications, and maintenance logs associated with this flight.” Industry leaders quickly expressed solidarity. A representative for Southwest Airlines Co, which operates a vastly different fleet of commercial jets, emphasized the broader aviation community’s commitment to safety. “While our operations differ significantly from rotorcraft charter services, the entire industry mourns this loss and stands ready to share any relevant safety data or best practices that could prevent future tragedies,” the spokesperson said.

The aircraft involved was a twin-engine Sikorsky S-76B, a widely used medium-lift helicopter known for its reliability in corporate transport, offshore operations, and emergency medical services. Manufactured by Sikorsky Aircraft, the model has a long operational history and is typically equipped with advanced avionics for both visual and instrument flight. The flight originated from John Wayne Airport in Orange County and was en route to Camarillo Airport in Ventura County, a routine corridor for regional charter operators. Under visual flight rules, pilots must maintain a minimum distance from clouds and keep the ground in sight. When weather deteriorates, pilots are trained to either divert, climb above the cloud layer, or transition to instrument flight rules if the aircraft and pilot are properly certified. In this case, the pilot appears to have continued forward into deteriorating conditions.

Aviation safety experts caution against drawing premature conclusions but note that spatial disorientation is a well-documented hazard when visual references disappear. “When a pilot flies into a cloud bank without adequate instrument training or certification, the inner ear can send false signals to the brain,” explained Dr. Aris Thorne, a former commercial pilot and aviation safety researcher. “Without a clear horizon, it is incredibly easy to lose control of the aircraft, especially in mountainous terrain where rising ground leaves little margin for error.” Investigators will examine whether the pilot was instrument-rated, whether the helicopter’s terrain awareness systems were engaged, and whether air traffic control provided adequate weather advisories.

The crash has left families and friends grappling with sudden, profound grief. Local residents described hearing a low, grinding sound followed by a distant thud before emergency sirens echoed through the hills. “We saw the smoke rising over the ridge,” said Maria Gonzalez, a Calabasas resident who lives near the crash site. “It’s just heartbreaking. You never expect something like this to happen in your own backyard.” Vigils have already begun forming at nearby parks, with community members leaving flowers, candles, and handwritten notes. “We are devastated beyond words,” said a family representative for one of the passengers. “They were just starting their day, and now we are left with an unimaginable void.”

Helicopter accidents in poor weather, while rare, have historically pointed to similar contributing factors. The aviation industry has spent decades refining safety protocols, from mandatory terrain warning systems to stricter weather minimums. In recent years, public attention has also focused on automated flight systems in commercial aviation, such as the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System, or MCAS, which drew intense scrutiny following separate fixed-wing accidents. While MCAS is entirely unrelated to rotorcraft operations, its legacy has reinforced the industry’s emphasis on pilot training, system transparency, and human-machine interface design. Commercial carriers like Southwest Airlines Co have since overhauled training curricula to emphasize manual flying skills and decision-making under pressure, a philosophy that charter operators are increasingly adopting.

The NTSB has established a command post near the crash site and will oversee a multi-agency investigation expected to take 12 to 18 months. Investigators will recover the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, analyze maintenance records, interview air traffic controllers, and reconstruct the flight path using radar and satellite data. The FAA has temporarily suspended certain charter operations in the region pending a review of weather minimums and pilot qualifications. “We will follow the evidence wherever it leads,” the NTSB spokesperson reiterated. “Our only goal is to understand what happened and ensure it never happens again.” As the investigation moves forward, the aviation community and grieving families alike await answers, hoping that the lessons learned from this tragedy will ultimately make the skies safer for everyone.

## [sc-0_expert_deposition_005] Expert Deposition

> **Type:** expert_deposition | **Reliability:** 0.875 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by Sikorsky Aircraft, acting in its capacity as the type certificate holder and original equipment manufacturer for the Sikorsky S-76B rotorcraft involved in the January 26, 2020, accident in Calabasas, California. The undersigned author serves as Senior Flight Systems and Human Factors Engineering Lead, representing the manufacturer’s technical delegation to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigative process. This document outlines the manufacturer’s technical position regarding aircraft system performance, flight control architecture, and human-machine interface considerations relevant to the accident sequence.

The scope of this submission encompasses a comprehensive review of flight data recorder (FDR) parameters, cockpit voice recorder (CVR) transcripts, maintenance and configuration records, and operational decision-making factors. It further addresses the interaction between degraded visual environment (DVE) conditions, pilot spatial orientation, and the design philosophy of the S-76B flight control system. While the manufacturer acknowledges the profound tragedy of this event and the complex interplay of meteorological, operational, and human factors, this analysis is grounded in empirical engineering data, regulatory compliance documentation, and established rotorcraft safety management principles. The objective is to provide the Board with a technically rigorous assessment of aircraft system functionality, identify contributing operational factors, and propose actionable safety enhancements that align with industry best practices and evolving aviation technology.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On January 26, 2020, Sikorsky S-76B, registration N72EX, departed John Wayne Airport (KSNA) en route to Camarillo Airport (KCMA) under visual flight rules (VFR). As documented in the NTSB Weather Group Chairman’s Report and corroborated by surface and upper-air meteorological data, the flight encountered rapidly deteriorating visibility and ceiling conditions consistent with marine layer advection and localized fog formation. The pilot elected to continue VFR flight into instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) while navigating through rising terrain in the Santa Monica Mountains. The aircraft subsequently impacted terrain in Calabasas, resulting in the fatal loss of all nine occupants.

Review of the aircraft maintenance logs, airworthiness directives compliance records, and pre-flight inspection documentation confirms that the airframe, twin Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6B-36A engines, main and tail rotor systems, and all primary flight control linkages were within manufacturer-specified tolerances. No deferred maintenance items, open service bulletins, or known system anomalies were recorded. The FDR data, as detailed in the NTSB FDR Group Chairman’s Report, indicates continuous engine operation, stable power output, and uninterrupted hydraulic pressure through the final recorded data points. The CVR transcript reveals no system warnings, abnormal aural alerts, or crew discussions indicating mechanical degradation prior to impact.

The aircraft was configured per standard VFR operational parameters. While the S-76B platform supports optional terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS) integration, the accident aircraft was not equipped with an active, certified EGPWS/TAWS unit at the time of the flight. Weather decision-making, route selection, and altitude management remained under pilot discretion, consistent with VFR operational authority. The Board’s operational and human factors investigations have appropriately highlighted the challenges of visual reference loss, cognitive tunneling, and mission pressure in this context. From a systems engineering perspective, the factual record establishes that the aircraft performed within its certified design envelope, with no evidence of pre-impact mechanical or electrical failure.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The technical evaluation of this accident sequence requires a multidisciplinary approach, integrating flight dynamics, human factors engineering, and operational risk management. The FDR data reveals a flight profile characterized by a gradual descent from approximately 1,200 feet MSL, accompanied by increasing pitch and bank oscillations during the final three minutes of flight. These kinematic signatures are consistent with vestibular spatial disorientation, specifically the somatogravic illusion and the leans, which commonly manifest when pilots lose external visual references in DVE/IMC conditions. The absence of aggressive control inputs or system fault codes further supports the conclusion that the flight control system responded linearly to pilot commands, without anomalous behavior or uncommanded actuation.

The S-76B employs a conventional mechanical-hydraulic flight control architecture with a three-axis stability augmentation system (SAS). The SAS provides rate damping and attitude stabilization but does not possess envelope protection, auto-trim override, or autonomous flight path management capabilities. Pilot authority remains absolute and continuous. This design philosophy is intentional and aligns with rotorcraft operational realities, where rapid maneuvering, autorotation capability, and direct tactile feedback are critical to safe flight. In contrast to fixed-wing automated pitch trim systems such as the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), which operates as a closed-loop, sensor-driven envelope management function capable of commanding stabilizer deflection independent of pilot input, the S-76B SAS architecture is strictly assistive. It does not mask control forces, does not override pilot commands, and does not introduce single-point failure modes that could precipitate uncommanded flight path deviations. The manufacturer’s engineering validation confirms that the SAS gain scheduling, hydraulic actuator response times, and mechanical linkage tolerances were within certified parameters throughout the flight.

Human factors analysis, supported by the CVR transcript and operational timeline, indicates a progressive degradation of situational awareness as the aircraft entered cloud layers and lost terrain contrast. The pilot’s decision to continue VFR flight into deteriorating visibility reflects a well-documented cognitive bias known as plan continuation bias, compounded by mission urgency and the absence of an IFR clearance. In DVE conditions, the vestibular system becomes the primary orientation reference, which is physiologically unreliable during sustained accelerations or turns. The FDR pitch and bank oscillations correlate with known spatial disorientation recovery attempts, wherein pilots instinctively apply control inputs that exacerbate attitude deviations rather than correct them. This phenomenon is not unique to the S-76B; it is a systemic challenge across all rotorcraft and fixed-wing platforms operating under VFR in marginal weather.

Industry standards, including FAA Advisory Circular 91-92, ICAO Annex 6, and EASA CS-29, emphasize that VFR flight into IMC remains a leading causal factor in general aviation and rotorcraft accidents. The manufacturer’s engineering position is that aircraft system design cannot fully compensate for operational decisions that exceed visual meteorological minimums. However, the integration of enhanced decision-support tools, terrain mapping, and standardized IMC escape procedures can significantly mitigate risk. The absence of an active TAWS/EGPWS unit on the accident aircraft represents a missed opportunity for automated terrain proximity alerting, which could have provided critical auditory and visual cues during the final descent phase. While not mandated for this aircraft category under existing regulations, the manufacturer has long advocated for voluntary adoption of terrain awareness technology in commercial rotorcraft operations.

Furthermore, the flight control system’s lack of IMC-specific feedback modes highlights an area for potential enhancement. Modern stability augmentation systems can be calibrated to provide subtle control force gradients or haptic feedback when approaching unsafe pitch/bank attitudes in low-visibility conditions. Such enhancements would preserve pilot authority while introducing a secondary sensory cue to counteract vestibular illusions. The manufacturer’s engineering teams have evaluated these concepts through simulation and flight test programs, confirming that incremental SAS tuning can improve DVE handling qualities without compromising mechanical simplicity or certification compliance.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on comprehensive review of flight data, maintenance records, system architecture documentation, and human factors research, Sikorsky Aircraft concludes that the S-76B airframe, powerplant, and flight control systems functioned within design specifications throughout the accident flight. No mechanical, electrical, or software anomalies contributed to the loss of control. The primary causal chain is operational in nature: continuation of VFR flight into deteriorating weather, loss of external visual references, spatial disorientation, and inadequate terrain/IMC risk mitigation. The manufacturer acknowledges the complexity of this sequence, recognizing that meteorological variability, cognitive decision-making, and operational pressures interact in ways that cannot be fully resolved through aircraft design alone.

The manufacturer’s position is that rotorcraft safety in DVE/IMC environments requires a layered approach, integrating pilot training, operational policy, and incremental system enhancements. While the S-76B’s mechanical-hydraulic control architecture prioritizes direct pilot authority and reliability, there is clear value in augmenting this design with modern terrain awareness integration, standardized IMC escape protocols, and enhanced stability augmentation feedback. The manufacturer supports the NTSB’s ongoing investigation and endorses evidence-based safety recommendations that address both human performance and technological support systems.

Recommended safety improvements include: (1) mandatory or strongly incentivized installation of certified TAWS/EGPWS units on commercial rotorcraft operating in terrain-challenged environments; (2) standardized, recurrent training on VFR-into-IMC recognition, vestibular disorientation mitigation, and immediate IMC escape maneuvers; (3) development of manufacturer-approved synthetic vision or terrain mapping overlays compatible with existing S-76 avionics suites; and (4) industry-wide data sharing initiatives to track DVE incident trends and refine pilot decision-support tools.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

Sikorsky Aircraft has already implemented several corrective and preventive measures in response to this accident and broader industry safety trends. The manufacturer has issued updated Pilot Operating Handbook (POH) supplements emphasizing VFR-into-IMC recognition, immediate 180-degree turn procedures, and minimum safe altitude protocols for marginal weather operations. These supplements have been distributed to all registered S-76 operators and integrated into type-specific training curricula. Additionally, Sikorsky has collaborated with avionics manufacturers to develop retrofit packages for certified EGPWS/TAWS integration, with installation guidance and engineering approvals now available through standard service channels.

The manufacturer has also enhanced its stability augmentation system calibration guidelines, providing operators with optional SAS tuning parameters optimized for DVE operations. These parameters introduce subtle control force gradients that improve attitude awareness without altering mechanical control authority. Flight test validation confirms that these adjustments reduce pilot workload during low-visibility transitions and align with human factors research on tactile feedback efficacy.

Looking forward, Sikorsky Aircraft proposes the following improvements: (1) development of a next-generation synthetic vision system (SVS) tailored to the S-76B cockpit architecture, integrating real-time terrain mapping, obstacle databases, and weather overlay capabilities; (2) establishment of a manufacturer-sponsored DVE safety working group, comprising operators, pilots, human factors specialists, and regulatory representatives, to standardize IMC escape training and decision-making frameworks; (3) advocacy for regulatory updates that clarify VFR weather minimums in mountainous and coastal regions, with emphasis on dynamic weather routing and real-time meteorological data integration; and (4) expansion of flight data monitoring (FDM) programs across the S-76 fleet to proactively identify VFR-into-IMC risk patterns and support targeted training interventions.

The manufacturer remains committed to advancing rotorcraft safety through engineering innovation, operational collaboration, and transparent data sharing. By addressing both the human and technological dimensions of DVE/IMC risk, the aviation community can significantly reduce the likelihood of similar accidents while preserving the operational flexibility and mission readiness that define rotorcraft utility. Sikorsky Aircraft stands ready to support the NTSB’s final report, implement recommended safety actions, and continue leading industry efforts to enhance pilot support systems and operational decision-making in degraded visual environments.

## [sc-0_internal_memo_006] Internal Memo

> **Type:** internal_memo | **Reliability:** 0.766 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

TO: All Flight Operations, Maintenance Control, Dispatch, and Training Personnel
FROM: Director of Safety & Quality Assurance, Fleet Operations Division
DATE: 14 November 2024
SUBJECT: SAFETY COMMUNICATION: VFR-INTO-IMC PREVENTION, TERRAIN CLEARANCE, AND AUTOMATION AWARENESS PROTOCOLS
REF: SAF-2024-089, M&E-PROC-4412, WO-OPS-8841, NTSB/AAR-21/08

PURPOSE:
This Safety Communication is issued to mandate immediate procedural alignment regarding weather minimums, terrain avoidance, and automated system monitoring across all active fleet types. Recent regulatory directives, internal audit findings, and historical investigation data require updated operational discipline and targeted training reinforcement.

BACKGROUND:
On 26 January 2020, a Sikorsky S-76B operated by Island Express Helicopters impacted terrain in Calabasas, California, during instrument meteorological conditions (IMC). The NTSB investigation concluded the pilot continued visual flight rules (VFR) into deteriorating visibility and rising terrain, resulting in spatial disorientation and loss of control. All nine persons on board were killed. This event remains a critical case study in the persistent hazards of VFR-into-IMC encounters, particularly in complex topography with limited escape routes.

While our primary operations utilize fixed-wing transport aircraft, the fundamental risk factors remain identical. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has reinforced cross-fleet safety expectations through Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-51, which mandates enhanced terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS) calibration, database currency verification, and pilot response validation. Concurrently, industry-wide analysis of automated flight control dependencies—most notably the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) integration on narrow-body transports—demonstrates the operational danger of over-reliance on single-sensor automation without continuous manual cross-checking. Peer carriers, including Southwest Airlines, have recently adjusted flight data monitoring (FDM) thresholds to flag rapid altitude deviations and terrain proximity alerts in marginal VFR conditions. Our internal Q3 audit (REF: AUD-2024-112) identified three instances of delayed weather deviation reporting and two TAWS database lag discrepancies, prompting this directive.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, the following protocols apply to all flight crews, dispatchers, and maintenance personnel supporting flight operations:

1. Weather Minimums & Go/No-Go Authority:
   - All VFR operations must strictly adhere to published company minimums. No pilot-in-command (PIC) shall continue flight into forecasted or observed IMC without an approved IFR clearance and verified aircraft equipment status.
   - Dispatchers must cross-reference real-time METAR/TAF data with terrain elevation profiles for all routes. Any route with terrain clearance below 1,500 feet AGL in marginal VFR conditions requires mandatory rerouting or IFR filing.
   - Reference Work Order WO-OPS-8841 for updated weather deviation reporting procedures. All deviations must be logged in the Flight Operations Portal within 30 minutes of occurrence.

2. Terrain Awareness & System Verification:
   - TAWS/GPWS systems must be verified operational during pre-flight checks. Any fault code related to terrain database integrity (Part No. TAWS-DB-2024-REV3) requires immediate grounding until Maintenance Control clears the discrepancy per M&E-PROC-4412.
   - Pilots must conduct a "System State Brief" prior to departure, explicitly confirming automation modes, flight director status, and manual override availability. This mirrors industry lessons from MCAS-related incidents where degraded situational awareness compounded single-point failures.
   - Maintenance technicians must verify pitot-static and angle-of-attack sensor calibration per AD 2024-02-51 compliance checklist. All sign-offs require dual-verification by a Level II inspector and entry into the Maintenance Tracking System (MTS-Tag: AD-2024-02-51-COMP).

3. Training & Proficiency Updates:
   - All line pilots will complete the updated "VFR-into-IMC Recognition & Recovery" module (Course ID: TRN-2024-07) by 31 December 2024.
   - Simulator sessions will now include unannounced IMC penetration scenarios with degraded navigation displays. Emphasis will be placed on immediate 180-degree turn execution, terrain clearance verification, and ATC communication protocols.
   - Dispatch and flight following personnel will undergo a 4-hour workshop on dynamic weather routing and terrain conflict resolution. Completion certificates must be uploaded to the Training Management System (TMS-REF: DISP-2024-09).

4. Data Monitoring & Reporting:
   - Flight Operations Quality Assurance (FOQA) will implement new trigger parameters for rapid descent rates below 2,000 feet AGL in VMC. Any exceedance will generate an automatic safety review.
   - All personnel are required to report weather-related operational deviations via the internal Safety Reporting System (SRS-Portal) within 24 hours. Non-punitive reporting is enforced per Company Policy CP-SAF-009.

ACTION REQUIRED:
- Flight Operations Management: Distribute this bulletin to all line pilots and dispatchers by 18 November 2024. Verify receipt via the crew portal acknowledgment system. Submit distribution logs to Safety Compliance by 20 November 2024.
- Training Department: Schedule and complete all TRN-2024-07 modules by 31 December 2024. Update simulator software to reflect new IMC penetration scenarios by 15 December 2024. Provide completion metrics to the Director of Safety weekly.
- Maintenance Control: Audit all TAWS and pitot-static system compliance records against AD 2024-02-51 requirements. Submit compliance report to Quality Assurance by 20 November 2024. Quarantine any aircraft with unresolved TAWS-DB-2024-REV3 discrepancies until cleared.
- All Personnel: Review updated weather minimums and terrain clearance procedures. Report any system anomalies or procedural ambiguities immediately through the SRS-Portal. Failure to comply with these directives will result in immediate operational review and potential suspension of flight or maintenance privileges.

Safety is non-negotiable. Direct all questions to the Safety & Quality Assurance hotline (Ext. 4400) or email safety-compliance@company.internal.

## [sc-0_preliminary_report_007] Preliminary Report

> **Type:** preliminary_report | **Reliability:** 0.707 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. SYNOPSIS
On January 26, 2020, at approximately 0945 Pacific Standard Time, a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, registered N72EX and operated by Island Express Helicopters, impacted terrain in Calabasas, California. The flight was operating under visual flight rules (VFR) when it encountered instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), resulting in the fatal destruction of the aircraft and the loss of all nine persons on board. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has initiated a major accident investigation to determine the circumstances surrounding the event.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information indicates the helicopter departed John Wayne Airport (SNA) in Orange County, California, en route to Camarillo Airport (CMA). Initial radar and flight tracking data suggest the aircraft maintained a southeasterly heading before deviating westward into the Santa Monica Mountains. Early witness accounts describe low cloud ceilings and reduced visibility in the vicinity of the impact site, with several observers noting the aircraft appeared to be operating at a low altitude prior to the collision with terrain. Meteorological data from nearby reporting stations and satellite imagery indicate a persistent marine layer with localized fog and deteriorating visual conditions along the flight path. Preliminary examination of the wreckage site reveals extensive fragmentation and thermal damage consistent with high-energy impact and post-crash fire. The main rotor assembly, tail boom, and fuselage sections have been identified, though complete recovery and documentation remain ongoing. At this stage, no definitive mechanical anomalies have been confirmed, and all initial observations remain subject to revision as additional data is collected and analyzed.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The NTSB has activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical and operational aspects of this accident. The Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, and Human Performance groups have been formally established and are currently conducting field assessments. Island Express Helicopters (IEH), the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and Sikorsky Aircraft have been designated as parties to the investigation under standard Board protocols. The FAA has provided preliminary maintenance records, pilot certification files, and operational dispatch logs for review. In accordance with established investigative procedures, the Board is also evaluating compliance with relevant regulatory frameworks, including FAA Order 8900.1, which outlines flight standards and operational oversight requirements. While the accident aircraft is a rotary-wing platform, the Systems group will conduct a comparative review of automated flight control equipment, including an assessment of known MCAS (Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System) design philosophies, to ensure comprehensive evaluation of all potential flight control interactions. Additionally, the regulatory compliance team will cross-reference current airworthiness directives, including Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-51, to verify historical maintenance applicability and identify any retroactive inspection requirements that may inform the broader safety analysis. All physical evidence, including the flight data recorder (if equipped), cockpit voice recorder, and navigation equipment, has been secured and transported to the NTSB’s Vehicle Recorder Laboratory for preliminary data extraction. Wreckage mapping, component tagging, and photographic documentation are proceeding according to established chain-of-custody protocols.

4. NEXT STEPS
Investigative activities will continue to focus on the systematic examination of recovered components, analysis of recorded flight data, and reconstruction of the aircraft’s final flight path. The Operations group will conduct structured interviews with dispatch personnel, maintenance technicians, and air traffic control facilities to establish a comprehensive operational timeline. The Systems and Structures groups will perform detailed metallurgical and engineering evaluations of critical flight control linkages, engine components, and airframe sections. Weather reconstruction efforts will incorporate high-resolution atmospheric modeling to better characterize the localized visibility and cloud base conditions at the time of the accident. All findings documented in this preliminary report are strictly provisional and subject to change as additional evidence is processed, laboratory testing is completed, and peer review is conducted. The NTSB will issue subsequent factual updates as investigative milestones are achieved, with a comprehensive public hearing anticipated upon completion of the technical analysis phase. No conclusions regarding operational decisions, mechanical performance, or probable cause have been reached at this time. The investigation remains active, and all procedural determinations will be guided by established safety investigation standards and regulatory requirements.
