## [sc-0_preliminary_report_031] Preliminary Report

> **Type:** preliminary_report | **Reliability:** 0.729 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. SYNOPSIS
On January 26, 2020, at approximately 0945 Pacific Standard Time, a Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation S-76B helicopter, registered as N72EX, impacted terrain in Calabasas, California, resulting in the fatal injury of all nine persons on board. The flight was operating under visual flight rules (VFR) when it encountered instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) and subsequently deviated from its intended route. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has initiated a major accident investigation to determine the circumstances surrounding the event, with preliminary data collection currently underway.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information gathered during the initial response phase indicates that the helicopter departed John Wayne Airport (SNA) in Orange County, California, en route to Camarillo Airport (CMA) in Ventura County. Initial information indicates the aircraft was operating under a VFR flight plan. Radar data and preliminary flight tracking information suggest the aircraft maintained a southeasterly heading before executing a series of turns in the vicinity of the Santa Monica Mountains. Initial witness accounts describe low cloud cover and reduced visibility in the area at the time of the event, with several observers noting the aircraft appeared to be operating at a low altitude relative to the surrounding topography. 

Weather conditions at the time of the accident were characterized by a marine layer advecting inland, resulting in ceilings below 1,000 feet above ground level and visibility frequently reported at less than one mile. Surface observations from nearby automated weather stations corroborate the presence of dense fog and mist. Preliminary examination of the accident site revealed that the helicopter impacted a steep, brush-covered hillside at a high rate of speed, resulting in catastrophic structural failure and a post-impact fire. The National Transportation Safety Board’s on-scene team has documented the wreckage distribution, which appears concentrated within a relatively small area, consistent with a high-energy impact. Initial damage assessment indicates that the main rotor system, tail boom, and fuselage sustained severe fragmentation. No evidence of pre-impact mechanical failure or in-flight breakup has been identified at this stage, though this assessment remains subject to change as detailed component examinations are conducted.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The NTSB has formally activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical and operational aspects of this event. The Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Human Performance, and Weather groups have been established and are currently conducting preliminary data collection and analysis. Parties to the investigation include representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the helicopter operator, Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation, and the engine manufacturer. These parties are operating under strict NTSB guidelines to ensure the integrity and independence of the investigative process.

Evidence secured to date includes the wreckage, which has been stabilized and documented in situ prior to recovery operations. The flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) have been recovered and transported to the NTSB’s Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C., for preliminary readout and data extraction. Initial data retrieval efforts are ongoing, and the integrity of the recording media appears to be intact. The Systems group has initiated a review of the aircraft’s flight control architecture, including an examination of automated stability augmentation systems. As part of a broader procedural review of flight control augmentation equipment, the group will also examine technical documentation related to the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) to evaluate industry-wide design philosophies and pilot interface standards. This review is strictly comparative and does not imply the presence or relevance of such equipment on the accident airframe.

Additional evidence, including maintenance records, pilot training files, and air traffic control communications, has been secured and is currently undergoing preliminary review. The Human Performance group is coordinating with medical examiners to obtain toxicology samples and is reviewing the pilot’s recent flight history, duty time, and physiological factors. All examinations are being conducted in accordance with established NTSB protocols, and initial findings remain strictly preliminary.

4. NEXT STEPS
Planned investigative activities over the coming weeks will focus on the detailed examination of recovered components, the completion of recorder data analysis, and the reconstruction of the flight path using radar, telemetry, and witness information. The Systems and Structures groups will conduct teardown inspections of the main rotor assembly, transmission, and flight control linkages to identify any anomalies or pre-existing conditions. The Operations group will continue to analyze air traffic control transcripts, company dispatch records, and the pilot’s decision-making process regarding weather avoidance and route selection.

A public hearing is anticipated once the factual record has been sufficiently developed, though no date has been established at this time. The NTSB will issue periodic updates as significant milestones are reached, with the next formal status report expected within 30 to 45 days. All parties are reminded that preliminary information is subject to revision as additional data becomes available and as laboratory testing progresses. The investigation will proceed methodically, with all conclusions deferred until the comprehensive analysis is complete. The NTSB remains committed to a thorough, transparent, and scientifically rigorous process to determine the factors that contributed to this tragic event.

## [sc-0_investigation_report_032] Investigation Report

NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION SAFETY BOARD
GROUP CHAIRMAN’S FACTUAL REPORT
AVIATION ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION
ACCIDENT NUMBER: WPR20MA085
DATE OF ACCIDENT: JANUARY 26, 2020
AIRCRAFT: SIKORSKY S-76B, N72EX
LOCATION: CALABASAS, CALIFORNIA

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 General Information
On January 26, 2020, at approximately 09:45:00 Pacific Standard Time (PST), a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, bearing registration N72EX, impacted mountainous terrain in Calabasas, California. The accident site was located at geographic coordinates 34.1056° North latitude, 118.6853° West longitude, at an elevation of approximately 1,240 feet mean sea level (MSL). The helicopter was destroyed by impact forces and a post-impact fire. All nine persons on board, including the pilot-in-command, a second in command, and seven passengers, sustained fatal injuries. The flight was conducted under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 91, as a personal/corporate transport operation. No flight plan was filed with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) prior to departure.

1.2 Flight History
The helicopter departed John Wayne Airport (KSNA), Santa Ana, California, at 09:06:12 PST, with a planned destination of Camarillo Airport (KCMA), Camarillo, California. The flight was intended to transport passengers to a scheduled event. Following departure, the aircraft proceeded northwest along a visual flight rules (VFR) route, maintaining altitudes between 1,200 and 1,800 feet MSL. At approximately 09:20:00 PST, the pilot-in-command contacted Los Angeles Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC) to request a Special VFR clearance through Class B airspace. The clearance was granted, and the aircraft continued northwest. At 09:32:15 PST, the pilot requested a deviation to the west due to deteriorating visibility. The aircraft subsequently entered an area of instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) and began a gradual climb while tracking over rising terrain. The final recorded Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) position was captured at 09:44:58 PST, indicating an altitude of 1,610 feet MSL and a groundspeed of 142 knots. Radar contact was lost at 09:45:02 PST.

1.3 Regulatory Framework
The operation was conducted under 14 CFR Part 91, which governs general operating and flight rules. Applicable provisions included 14 CFR 91.103 (preflight action), 14 CFR 91.119 (minimum safe altitudes), and 14 CFR 91.155 (basic VFR weather minimums). The aircraft was not operating under 14 CFR Part 135 or Part 121, and therefore was not subject to commercial air carrier operational specifications or mandatory instrument flight rules (IFR) equipment requirements for the route flown. The National Transportation Safety Board initiated an investigation under 49 CFR Part 831, with the Investigator-in-Charge assuming overall coordination of the factual inquiry.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Pilot-in-Command
The pilot-in-command held an FAA Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, number 1234567, with rotorcraft-helicopter and airplane multiengine land ratings. The pilot also held a Certified Flight Instructor (CFI) certificate for rotorcraft-helicopter and a commercial pilot certificate for airplane single-engine land. The pilot’s most recent FAA first-class medical certificate was issued on August 14, 2019, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 8,200 hours, with approximately 1,250 hours in the Sikorsky S-76 series. The pilot’s most recent flight review was completed on November 12, 2019, in accordance with 14 CFR 61.56. Instrument proficiency was documented through a recent instrument competency check conducted on October 5, 2019.

2.2 Second in Command
A second in command was aboard the aircraft, holding an FAA Commercial Pilot certificate, number 7654321, with rotorcraft-helicopter and airplane single-engine land ratings. The second in command possessed a current FAA second-class medical certificate, issued on September 22, 2019. Total flight time was recorded at 1,850 hours, with 420 hours in turbine-powered helicopters. The second in command was not designated as the pilot flying for this operation, and the aircraft was certificated for single-pilot operations per the FAA-approved Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM). The second in command’s recent flight experience complied with 14 CFR 61.57, including three takeoffs and landings within the preceding 90 days. Training records indicated completion of a recurrent safety seminar on January 10, 2020, covering spatial disorientation and VFR-into-IMC avoidance.

2.3 Training and Experience Records
Review of the operator’s training database and FAA Airman Certification Records confirmed that both crewmembers met all regulatory currency requirements. The pilot-in-command had completed a manufacturer-sponsored S-76B systems course in March 2018 and a simulator-based emergency procedures evaluation in July 2019. The second in command had completed a helicopter instrument transition course in February 2019. No discrepancies were identified in the crewmembers’ logbooks or training files. Both individuals were current for night operations, though the accident occurred during daylight hours.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Specifications
The accident aircraft was a Sikorsky S-76B, serial number 760234, manufactured in 1988. The airframe was powered by two Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6B-36A turboshaft engines, each rated at 650 shaft horsepower. The helicopter was equipped with a four-blade main rotor system and a four-blade tail rotor system. At the time of the accident, the total airframe time was 14,872.5 hours. The left engine had accumulated 3,210.4 hours since overhaul, and the right engine had accumulated 2,985.1 hours since overhaul. The aircraft was registered to a private corporate entity and operated under Part 91.

3.2 Maintenance History
The most recent annual inspection was completed on December 18, 2019, at 14,810.2 airframe hours. A 100-hour inspection was performed on November 5, 2019. Maintenance records indicated compliance with all manufacturer-recommended service bulletins and FAA-mandated inspections. The last recorded discrepancy was a minor hydraulic line seepage noted on January 15, 2020, which was rectified on January 17, 2020, per maintenance manual procedures. All logbook entries were reviewed and found to be complete, legible, and properly signed by appropriately certificated mechanics.

3.3 Airworthiness Directives and Service Bulletins
A review of the aircraft maintenance records confirmed compliance with all applicable airworthiness directives (ADs) in effect at the time of the accident. Notably, AD 2024-02-51, issued by the FAA on February 12, 2024, addresses recurring fatigue inspections for main rotor blade retention hardware on S-76 series helicopters. Although this directive was promulgated post-accident, it applies to the airframe type and establishes updated inspection intervals for critical rotor components. At the time of the accident, the aircraft was in compliance with all preceding ADs, including AD 2018-15-09 and AD 2019-08-12. No outstanding ADs or deferred maintenance items were documented.

3.4 Systems and Components
The aircraft was equipped with a standard avionics suite, including dual VHF communication transceivers, a Garmin GNS 430W GPS/NAV/COM unit, a King KX 165A navigation receiver, and a Bendix/King KRA 405 radar altimeter. The helicopter was not equipped with a terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS) or a flight data recorder (FDR), as neither was required under 14 CFR Part 91 for this aircraft category. The aircraft was not equipped with a Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), and no MCAS-related hardware, software, or control logic was present or evaluated during the investigation. The autopilot system, a S-76B standard three-axis stability augmentation system, was found to be inoperative at the time of the accident, with maintenance logs indicating a deferred repair for a yaw axis servo motor. The fuel system was intact, with both main tanks containing approximately 180 gallons of Jet A fuel at the time of impact.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Weather Analysis
On January 26, 2020, a low-pressure system was situated off the coast of Southern California, generating a persistent marine layer and widespread stratus clouds across the Los Angeles Basin. A temperature inversion at approximately 1,500 feet MSL trapped moisture and particulate matter, resulting in reduced visibility and low ceilings. Surface winds were light and variable, with speeds generally below 5 knots. The synoptic pattern was consistent with typical winter coastal fog conditions, which frequently produce rapid transitions from VFR to IMC in the Santa Monica Mountains and surrounding valleys.

4.2 Surface Observations and Forecasts
Aviation routine weather reports (METAR) from nearby airports indicated deteriorating conditions. At 09:00 PST, KSNA reported visibility of 10 statute miles, ceiling 2,500 feet broken, temperature 14°C, dewpoint 12°C, altimeter 30.02 inHg. At 09:30 PST, KCMA reported visibility 3 statute miles, ceiling 800 feet overcast, temperature 13°C, dewpoint 12°C, altimeter 30.01 inHg. A terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) for KCMA, issued at 05:00 PST, predicted visibility 3 to 5 statute miles in mist, ceiling 1,000 feet broken, with temporary conditions of 1/2 statute mile visibility in fog between 08:00 and 12:00 PST. Pilot reports (PIREPs) received by Los Angeles ARTCC between 09:15 and 09:35 PST described ceilings at 600 to 900 feet AGL with visibility fluctuating between 1 and 3 statute miles in the Calabasas and Agoura Hills areas.

4.3 In-Flight Weather Data and Radar
ADS-B track data indicated the aircraft maintained a relatively constant groundspeed of 135 to 145 knots until 09:38:00 PST, at which point the groundspeed decreased to 112 knots, and the vertical rate transitioned from a slight descent to a gradual climb of approximately 300 feet per minute. The climb profile coincided with the aircraft’s entry into a localized area of reduced visibility and rising terrain. No onboard weather radar was installed, and the pilot did not request real-time weather updates from flight service or ATC after 09:32:00 PST. Satellite imagery and surface analysis confirmed the presence of a dense fog bank extending inland from the Pacific coast, with the leading edge positioned directly over the accident route.

4.4 Regulatory Weather Minimums
Under 14 CFR 91.155, basic VFR weather minimums for Class E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL require 3 statute miles visibility and a ceiling of 1,000 feet above ground level (AGL). The observed conditions at the time of the accident fell below these minimums, with visibility estimated at 1/2 to 1 statute mile and ceilings at 600 to 800 feet AGL. The transition from VFR to IMC occurred without a formal IFR clearance or instrument approach procedure. The pilot’s decision to continue visual flight into an area of known deteriorating weather was not supported by regulatory allowances for Special VFR, which require clear of clouds and 1 statute mile visibility, conditions that were not met at the time of the accident.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Impact Site and Terrain
The primary impact site was located on a steep, south-facing slope at an elevation of 1,240 feet MSL. The terrain gradient at the point of initial contact was approximately 38 degrees, with dense chaparral and scattered oak trees. The initial impact scar measured 12 feet in length and 4 feet in width, oriented on a magnetic heading of 285 degrees. The scar exhibited deep gouging into the underlying soil and bedrock, consistent with a high-energy, nose-low, left-wing-low impact attitude. No evidence of pre-impact mechanical failure, fire, or structural separation was observed in the surrounding vegetation.

5.2 Wreckage Distribution
The main wreckage was concentrated within a 45-foot by 30-foot area, with secondary debris scattered approximately 120 feet downslope. The fuselage was fragmented into three primary sections: the forward cabin, the mid-section, and the tail boom. The main rotor hub assembly was separated from the mast and located 18 feet northeast of the primary impact scar. All four main rotor blades were fractured near the root, with evidence of torsional overload and bending failure. The tail rotor assembly remained attached to the tail boom but exhibited severe impact deformation. The debris field orientation and component distribution were consistent with a controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) scenario, with no indication of in-flight breakup or mid-air collision.

5.3 Component Examination
The left and right engines were recovered and transported to the NTSB Materials Laboratory for teardown and analysis. Both engines exhibited rotational signatures consistent with power application at impact, with no evidence of compressor stall, turbine blade failure, or fuel starvation. The fuel control units, fuel pumps, and ignition systems were intact and functionally tested post-recovery. The flight control system, including the cyclic, collective, and anti-torque pedals, was examined for continuity and freedom of movement. All control linkages were severed at impact, but pre-impact binding or restriction was not identified. The stability augmentation system (SAS) servos were removed and bench-tested; the yaw axis servo exhibited an open circuit, consistent with the deferred maintenance log entry.

5.4 Structural and Systems Analysis
Metallurgical examination of the main rotor blades revealed fatigue striations originating from the root attachment bolts, consistent with normal operational loading. No manufacturing defects or corrosion were identified. The avionics stack was severely damaged by impact and post-impact fire, rendering data extraction from the GPS/NAV unit impossible. The radar altimeter was recovered with the display shattered, but internal circuitry indicated a last recorded altitude of 1,610 feet MSL, matching the final ADS-B transmission. The fuel system was examined for leaks or contamination; both main tanks were ruptured, and fuel residue was consistent with Jet A. No evidence of electrical arcing, short circuits, or pre-impact fire was found in the wiring harnesses or battery compartment.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Operator Policies and Procedures
The operator maintained a Part 91 operations manual that outlined standard operating procedures for weather assessment, route planning, and pilot decision-making. The manual referenced FAA Advisory Circular (AC) 91-78, Use of Aircraft Flight Manual Supplements, and AC 90-48C, Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance. The operator’s policy required pilots to obtain current weather briefings prior to departure and to divert or delay flights if conditions fell below VFR minimums. No formal risk assessment matrix or go/no-go checklist was mandated for Part 91 operations. The operator did not employ a dedicated flight following or dispatch service, and weather monitoring during flight was the sole responsibility of the pilot-in-command.

6.2 Historical Precedents and Safety Data
The National Transportation Safety Board has investigated numerous accidents involving VFR flight into IMC, particularly in mountainous or coastal terrain. Historical data from 2010 to 2019 indicates that spatial disorientation and loss of situational awareness are primary contributing factors in helicopter accidents occurring under similar meteorological conditions. The NTSB has previously issued safety recommendations addressing the need for enhanced pilot training in instrument meteorological conditions, mandatory installation of terrain awareness systems, and improved weather dissemination for Part 91 operators. This accident aligns with established patterns of VFR-into-IMC transitions in the Southern California region, where rapid weather changes and complex topography frequently challenge visual navigation.

6.3 Regulatory Guidance and Advisory Circulars
Applicable regulatory guidance includes 14 CFR 91.13, which prohibits careless or reckless operation, and 14 CFR 91.119, which establishes minimum safe altitudes over congested and non-congested areas. FAA AC 91-78, Use of Aircraft Flight Manual Supplements, provides guidance on operational limitations and equipment requirements. AC 00-6B, Aviation Weather, details the meteorological phenomena associated with marine layer fog and temperature inversions. The FAA’s Helicopter Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-21B) emphasizes the hazards of continued VFR flight into deteriorating weather and outlines recommended procedures for immediate 180-degree turns or controlled descents when visual references are lost. No regulatory requirement existed at the time of the accident mandating TAWS or FDR installation for Part 91 helicopters of this weight class.

6.4 Investigative Coordination and Documentation
The Investigator-in-Charge coordinated the factual investigation in accordance with NTSB Order 8020.11C, Aircraft Accident and Incident Investigation Procedures. Multiple NTSB groups, including Operations, Structures, Powerplants, Systems, and Meteorology, were established to examine specific aspects of the accident. The FAA provided technical support, maintenance records, and airman certification data. The Los Angeles County Fire Department and Sheriff’s Department secured the accident site and facilitated evidence recovery. All factual data, photographs, wreckage diagrams, and laboratory reports were compiled into the official docket. The Investigator-in-Charge ensured that all group chairman reports were reviewed for accuracy, completeness, and adherence to NTSB documentation standards prior to final submission. No probable cause determination is included in this factual report, as such findings are reserved for the final NTSB accident report.

## [sc-0_technical_analysis_033] Technical Analysis

> **Type:** technical_analysis | **Reliability:** 0.944 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis of the flight data recorder (FDR) system, primary structural components, and powerplant-related telemetry recovered from the accident helicopter. The scope of this examination encompasses the crash-survivable memory unit (CSMU), associated wiring harnesses, main rotor pitch control linkages, tail rotor drive shaft assembly, and the Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6B-36A engine fuel control unit. All examinations were conducted under the authority of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) in accordance with 49 CFR Part 831.

The physical examination and data extraction were performed between February 10 and February 28, 2020, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., and the Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation engineering facility in Stratford, Connecticut. The CSMU was recovered from the accident site on January 27, 2020, and transported under chain-of-custody protocols to the NTSB Vehicle Recorder Laboratory. Structural and powerplant components were recovered from the impact crater and surrounding debris field, cataloged under NTSB evidence tags S-76B-001 through S-76B-047, and subjected to non-destructive and destructive testing per established aerospace engineering standards.

The examination was coordinated with representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the helicopter manufacturer, and independent materials engineering consultants. Data validation procedures incorporated cross-referencing protocols aligned with FAA Flight Standards Order 8900.1, Volume 3, Chapter 18, Section 4, which governs FDR operational requirements, parameter retention, and post-accident data handling. Comparative analysis methodologies were adapted from commercial transport FDR/QAR processing frameworks, including those utilized by Southwest Airlines Co. for high-frequency parameter filtering and time-synchronization validation. All findings presented herein are strictly factual and derived from physical evidence, recorded telemetry, and standardized engineering test procedures.

2. BACKGROUND

The accident aircraft was a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, serial number 760342, registered as N72EX. The airframe was manufactured in 1992 and operated under 14 CFR Part 91. The aircraft was equipped with a dual-channel solid-state flight data recorder, L-3 Communications model FA2100-1020, certified to TSO-C124a and RTCA DO-178B/DO-254 standards. The FDR system records 88 discrete and analog parameters at a sampling rate of 1 Hz, with a continuous recording capacity of 25 hours. The CSMU is housed in a titanium alloy enclosure (AMS 4911) with integrated thermal insulation and shock isolation mounts, designed to withstand impact accelerations up to 3,400 G, static crush loads of 5,000 lbs, and post-crash fire exposure of 1,100 °C for 60 minutes per MIL-STD-810G Method 516.6 and RTCA DO-160G Section 21.

The helicopter's flight control architecture consists of a dual-axis stability augmentation system (SAS) with mechanical mixing, hydraulic actuation, and pilot override capability. The SAS provides pitch and roll damping, with trim authority limited to ±1.2°/sec. While the S-76B does not incorporate automated flight envelope protection systems, comparative control law latency analysis was performed against fixed-wing augmentation architectures, including the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), to evaluate pilot interface response times and control surface deflection characteristics under high-workload conditions. The MCAS reference was utilized strictly for control system architecture benchmarking and does not imply system commonality or installation on the accident aircraft.

The powerplant consists of two Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6B-36A turboshaft engines, each rated at 650 shp at takeoff. The fuel control units (FCU) are Hamilton Sundstrand model 3062501, serial numbers 77412 (left) and 77415 (right), calibrated to deliver fuel flow within ±2% of the manufacturer's performance curve across the N1/N2 operating envelope. The main rotor system utilizes a fully articulated hub with elastomeric bearings, titanium pitch links (P/N 76000-02012-101), and composite main rotor blades. The tail rotor drive shaft is constructed from 4340 steel, heat-treated to 180-200 ksi tensile strength per AMS 6308.

Operational history indicates the airframe accumulated 12,450 flight hours and 18,200 cycles at the time of the accident. The most recent heavy inspection was completed on November 14, 2019, in accordance with Sikorsky Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) Chapter 5, with all airworthiness directives and service bulletins current. The FDR system was last downloaded on December 3, 2019, with no recorded exceedances or fault codes. Maintenance records were cross-validated against FAA Form 337 entries and operator logbooks, with data formatting aligned to ARINC 717 standards for parameter mapping consistency.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

The CSMU housing exhibited localized deformation on the forward-left quadrant, measuring 0.125 inches maximum deflection, with no breach of the internal memory compartment. The titanium alloy casing retained structural integrity, and the thermal insulation blanket showed charring consistent with post-impact exposure to temperatures not exceeding 450 °C. The 25-pin MIL-DTL-38999 Series III connector was intact, with pin continuity verified via Fluke 8846A precision multimeter. All 16 NAND flash memory modules (Samsung K9F1G08U0D, 128 MB each) were extracted and subjected to read/write cycle testing per JEDEC JESD218A standards. Data recovery was achieved at 100% integrity, with no bit errors or sector corruption detected.

The main rotor pitch link (P/N 76000-02012-101, S/N 44821) was recovered from the debris field and subjected to metallurgical examination. Visual inspection revealed ductile overload fracture at the spherical bearing interface, with no evidence of fatigue initiation, corrosion, or manufacturing defects. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) at 500x magnification confirmed microvoid coalescence and dimpled rupture morphology, consistent with high-strain-rate tensile failure. Tensile testing per ASTM E8/E8M-21 yielded a yield strength of 115 ksi and ultimate tensile strength of 132 ksi, within the Sikorsky Aircraft engineering specification of 110-135 ksi. Hardness testing (Rockwell C) measured 34.2 HRC, aligning with the specified 32-36 HRC range. Chemical analysis via optical emission spectroscopy confirmed composition within AMS 6308 limits for 4340 steel: 0.42% C, 0.78% Mn, 0.24% Si, 0.81% Cr, 0.25% Mo, 1.82% Ni.

The tail rotor drive shaft (P/N 76000-03015-104, S/N 88214) exhibited torsional overload failure at the forward coupling flange. Fracture surface analysis revealed 45° shear lips and radial crack propagation, indicative of sudden torque application exceeding the design limit of 1,850 ft-lbs. Dynamic balancing records from the last overhaul indicated residual unbalance of 0.12 oz-in, well within the 0.5 oz-in tolerance per Sikorsky Aircraft AMM Section 63-20-00.

The left engine FCU (P/N 3062501, S/N 77412) was disassembled and flow-tested on a calibrated fuel bench at 45 PSI supply pressure, 150 °F fuel temperature, and 28 VDC actuation. At 100% N1, fuel flow measured 12.8 GPH, within ±1.5% of the OEM performance curve. The metering valve exhibited no stiction, and the governor spring tension measured 14.2 lbs, within the 13.8-14.6 lbs specification. The right FCU (S/N 77415) demonstrated identical performance characteristics. No evidence of fuel starvation, vapor lock, or control linkage binding was identified.

Wiring harness segments (P/N 76000-04022-101) were subjected to insulation resistance testing per MIL-STD-202 Method 302. All conductors measured >100 MΩ at 500 VDC, with no short circuits or open circuits detected. The FDR power supply module (P/N FA2100-PSU-02) was bench-tested at 28 VDC nominal, drawing 1.8 A, with ripple voltage <50 mV peak-to-peak.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

The recovered FDR data was decoded using L-3 FDR Readout Station software v4.2.1, with parameter mapping validated against the Sikorsky Aircraft S-76B FDR Parameter List (Document 76000-00012-001, Rev D). Time synchronization was achieved via GPS epoch alignment, with a maximum drift of ±0.05 seconds across the recording interval. Data filtering utilized a 4th-order Butterworth low-pass filter at 0.5 Hz to remove high-frequency vibration noise, consistent with parameter smoothing protocols adapted from commercial transport QAR processing frameworks, including those implemented by Southwest Airlines Co. for high-fidelity flight path reconstruction.

The recorded timeline begins at 09:45:12 PST, corresponding to engine start and FDR initialization. At 09:58:03 PST, barometric altitude indicated 2,100 ft MSL, with indicated airspeed at 128 knots and heading 245° magnetic. The aircraft entered a cloud layer, as evidenced by a rapid decrease in outside air temperature from 12 °C to 4 °C over 18 seconds, and a corresponding increase in relative humidity to 98%. The SAS remained engaged, with pitch and roll trim positions within ±0.3° of neutral.

Between 09:59:47 and 10:01:12 PST, the aircraft executed a series of heading corrections, with roll attitude oscillating between -8° and +11°. Indicated airspeed fluctuated between 110 and 135 knots, with collective position varying from 62% to 78% travel. Engine torque remained stable at 88-92%, with N1 and N2 parameters within normal operating ranges (N1: 98-101%, N2: 99-102%). No system fault codes or warning flags were recorded.

At 10:01:47 PST, the aircraft initiated a rapid descent. Barometric altitude decreased from 1,850 ft MSL to 1,200 ft MSL in 14 seconds, yielding an average descent rate of 2,785 fpm, with peak instantaneous rates exceeding 3,200 fpm. Pitch attitude oscillated between -6° and +12°, with collective position increasing to 85% travel. Engine torque transiently reached 102% for 1.8 seconds before stabilizing at 96%. The SAS remained active, but pilot control inputs exceeded the system's trim authority, resulting in manual override. GPS position data indicated a ground track deviation of 18° from the intended route, with lateral displacement increasing at 4.2 knots/sec.

At 10:02:14 PST, the final recorded parameters indicated altitude 1,050 ft MSL, airspeed 118 knots, pitch -4°, roll +9°, collective 88%, torque 94%, and heading 238°. The recording terminated abruptly at 10:02:14.32 PST, consistent with impact-induced power loss.

Comparison with normal operational parameters per the Sikorsky Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM) Section 4-12 indicates that the observed descent rate exceeded the maximum recommended limit of 1,500 fpm for instrument meteorological conditions. The collective position at 85-88% travel approached the upper mechanical stop, with corresponding torque values within transient limits. The SAS response time to pilot inputs measured 0.18 seconds, consistent with design specifications. No control system anomalies, hydraulic pressure drops, or engine performance degradations were recorded.

The data was cross-validated against radar returns from the Southern California TRACON facility, with positional correlation within ±0.3 nautical miles and altitude agreement within ±150 ft. Time-synchronization discrepancies were resolved using GPS epoch alignment, with residual error <0.1 seconds. Parameter filtering algorithms were verified against ARINC 717 decoding standards, with no data loss or interpolation artifacts identified.

5. SUMMARY

The crash-survivable memory unit sustained localized external deformation but maintained internal structural integrity, enabling complete data recovery with zero bit errors. Metallurgical examination of the main rotor pitch link and tail rotor drive shaft revealed ductile overload and torsional shear failures, respectively, consistent with high-energy terrain impact. No evidence of pre-impact fatigue, corrosion, manufacturing defects, or material degradation was identified. Chemical composition and mechanical properties of all examined components conformed to Sikorsky Aircraft engineering specifications and applicable aerospace material standards.

The Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6B-36A fuel control units demonstrated nominal performance across the tested operating envelope, with fuel flow, governor tension, and metering valve response within manufacturer tolerances. No fuel system anomalies, control linkage binding, or hydraulic pressure irregularities were detected. Wiring harness insulation resistance and FDR power supply parameters remained within design limits.

Flight data recorder telemetry confirms continuous system operation until impact, with all 88 recorded parameters functioning within calibrated ranges. The aircraft operated within normal engine and rotor system parameters until the initiation of a rapid descent at 10:01:47 PST. The stability augmentation system remained engaged, with response times and trim authority consistent with design specifications. Pilot control inputs exceeded SAS trim limits, resulting in manual override. Descent rates, collective positions, and pitch/roll attitudes exceeded normal operational envelopes for instrument meteorological conditions, as defined in the Sikorsky Aircraft Flight Manual.

All structural, powerplant, and avionics components examined exhibited failure modes consistent with post-impact overload. No pre-impact mechanical, electrical, or control system malfunctions were identified. The recorded data aligns with radar returns and environmental conditions documented in the investigation. All findings are strictly factual and derived from physical examination, standardized testing, and telemetry analysis.

## [sc-0_witness_testimony_034] Witness Testimony

> **Type:** witness_testimony | **Reliability:** 0.898 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

INTERVIEW OF DAVID R. CHEN, CHIEF FLIGHT DISPATCHER
Date: March 12, 2020
Time: 10:00 AM PST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Los Angeles, California
Interviewer: Investigator Elena Martinez, NTSB Aviation Safety Board
Witness: David R. Chen, Chief Flight Dispatcher, Island Express Helicopters

Q: Mr. Chen, thank you for coming in today. For the official record, please state your full name, your current title, and your role with the company on the morning of January 26th.

A: Yeah, sure. David Chen. I’m the Chief Flight Dispatcher—well, at the time I was acting as the primary operations coordinator for the morning shift. I handle flight following, weather briefings, crew scheduling, and dispatch release for Island Express Helicopters. I’ve been with the company for about eight years now, so I know the routes, the pilots, the whole operation pretty well.

Q: Can you walk me through your activities that morning, starting from when you first became aware of the flight?

A: Right. So, I got into the ops center around 06:30, maybe 06:40. The flight was scheduled for a 09:00 departure out of John Wayne, heading up the coast to Camarillo, then inland to the Calabasas area for a client pickup. The pilot was Ara Zobayan. He’s… he was one of our senior guys. Extremely experienced. I pulled up the standard pre-flight weather package. The marine layer was definitely pushing in, but the TAFs and the METARs were showing VFR conditions along the coastal corridor. I remember looking at the ceiling reports, and they were, uh, maybe two thousand feet, scattered. I thought it’d be fine. We operate under Part 135, so we follow the FAA Flight Standards Order guidelines pretty strictly, especially for VFR flight following. I mean, we’re not a casual Part 91 operation, so the oversight is tighter. We have hard minimums.

Q: Did you speak with the pilot before departure?

A: Yeah, we had a quick radio check around 08:45. He called in from the ramp. Sounded completely normal. He mentioned the visibility was a little hazy near the coast, but he was comfortable. I told him to keep an eye on the cloud base as he tracked north, and to call if it started closing in. He acknowledged. Standard stuff. I signed off the dispatch release.

Q: Once airborne, how were you tracking the flight?

A: We use a combination of ADS-B tracking and our internal flight following software. I had the flight on my primary monitor, updating every thirty seconds or so. The Sikorsky S-76B has a pretty robust avionics suite, so the telemetry was clean. I was watching his ground speed, altitude, heading. He was cruising around 1,500 feet MSL initially, then started climbing a bit as he approached the Santa Monica Mountains. I think it was around 09:20 when I noticed his altitude started fluctuating. Not dramatically, but… he’d drop a couple hundred feet, then climb back. I figured he was just adjusting for terrain or maybe some light chop. You know, pilots do that all the time.

Q: At what point did you become concerned?

A: Uh, around 09:30, maybe 09:32. I’m looking at the track, and he’s heading into a sector where the terrain starts rising pretty sharply. The weather reports from the nearby stations were showing the ceiling dropping. I tried to get a hold of him on the company frequency. No answer. I switched to the VHF guard, then tried the cell phone we have on file for the aircraft. It went straight to voicemail. I remember my stomach just… dropped. I called the tower at Camarillo to see if they had him on radar, and they said he was squawking VFR, no transponder code change, but he was descending. I think he was trying to maintain visual reference.

Q: Can you describe what you were seeing on your tracking display during those final minutes?

A: Yeah. The screen showed him turning left, which… that’s not the standard route. He was banking into the hills. The altitude readout was dropping. 1,200… 1,000… 800. I was calling out the numbers to myself, honestly. I remember thinking, “He’s too low for that terrain.” The last update I got was at 09:44. The altitude just… it flatlined. The GPS track stopped moving. I knew. I just knew. I immediately initiated our emergency protocol. Called 911, notified our management, started logging everything. The silence on the radio… it’s hard to describe. You just sit there staring at a frozen dot on a screen.

Q: You mentioned the Flight Standards Order earlier. How does that apply to your operations in marginal weather?

A: Right. So, under the FAA’s Flight Standards Order—specifically the guidance for Part 135 operators—we’re required to have strict VFR minimums and a clear go/no-go decision matrix. If the ceiling drops below a certain threshold, or visibility goes under three miles, you’re supposed to divert or hold. We also have a policy that if a pilot reports IMC, they’re to execute a 180-degree turn immediately and climb to a safe altitude. But… I don’t know if he realized he was in it. Sometimes the marine layer rolls in so fast, you don’t even notice until you’re completely enveloped. The Sikorsky’s instruments are good, but if you’re flying VFR and you lose visual, spatial disorientation can set in within seconds. I’ve read the reports. It’s… it’s a known hazard. We train for it, but training and reality are two different things.

Q: Were there any maintenance or equipment issues reported prior to the flight?

A: No. Absolutely not. The aircraft had just come out of a scheduled inspection. We run everything through the MCAS diagnostic system—our Maintenance Control and Avionics System—before every dispatch. It checks the engine parameters, rotor track and balance, avionics health, everything. All green. The S-76 is a solid platform. We’ve never had a single discrepancy on that tail number. I double-checked the logs myself that morning. The MCAS unit actually prints out a hard copy of the health report, and I initialed it. No faults, no warnings, nothing.

Q: How did you learn about the crash site?

A: Uh, around 10:15, maybe 10:20. The first responders started calling in. I was on the phone with our VP of Operations when the news broke on the local radio. They said it was in a steep ravine near Calabasas. I remember just… sitting there. The phone was ringing, people were asking questions, but I couldn’t really process it. I kept replaying the last telemetry update in my head. The altitude, the heading, the silence on the radio. It’s… it’s heavy.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add for the record?

A: I… I just want to make sure you understand that we followed every procedure we had. The weather was borderline, but it wasn’t below minimums when he departed. I think… I think it’s just one of those things where the conditions changed faster than anyone anticipated. The pilot was highly trained. He knew the area. But when you’re in a helicopter, and the ground disappears, and you’re relying on instruments you weren’t actively scanning… it’s a different world. I’ve been going over the Flight Standards Order again, looking at our training modules, wondering if we could’ve done something differently. Maybe more aggressive weather diversion protocols. I don’t know. I just… I hope the investigation helps prevent this from happening again. I’ll cooperate with the NTSB however I can.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Chen. We’ll be in touch if we have follow-up questions.

A: Yeah. Of course. I’ll be here.

## [sc-0_regulatory_filing_035] Regulatory Filing

> **Type:** regulatory_filing | **Reliability:** 0.972 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION
FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
FLIGHT STANDARDS SERVICE
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20591

MEMORANDUM

DATE: October 14, 2020
TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: Federal Aviation Administration, Flight Standards Service, Aircraft Certification and Operations Division
SUBJECT: REGULATORY RESPONSE AND COMPLIANCE FRAMEWORK
DOCKET NO.: FAA-2020-0892; NTSB DOCKET NO. WPR20MA085
REFERENCE: 14 CFR PART 135, SUBPART E; FAA ORDER 8900.1, VOL. 3, CH. 18

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This correspondence constitutes the Federal Aviation Administration’s formal regulatory response to NTSB Safety Recommendation A-20-014, issued in conjunction with the investigation of the January 26, 2020, aviation accident involving a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, registration N72EX, operating under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 135. The referenced accident, designated NTSB Accident Number WPR20MA085, occurred during visual flight rules (VFR) operations in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) with rising terrain in Calabasas, California. This document addresses applicable regulatory frameworks, compliance verification protocols, and mandated corrective actions pursuant to 14 CFR 135.185, 14 CFR 135.215, 14 CFR 135.154, and 14 CFR 29.1309. All referenced procedures align with the Flight Standards Information Management System (FSIMS) guidance contained in FAA Order 8900.1.

2. BACKGROUND
The regulatory oversight of rotorcraft operations under Part 135 is predicated upon strict adherence to weather minimums, pilot qualification standards, and airworthiness directives. 14 CFR 135.185 establishes baseline VFR weather minimums, while 14 CFR 135.215 governs instrument flight rules (IFR) takeoff, approach, and landing minimums. Historically, inadvertent VFR-into-IMC encounters have been identified as a persistent causal factor in rotorcraft accidents, prompting multiple NTSB safety recommendations and subsequent FAA rulemaking initiatives. The Type Certificate (TC) holder for the S-76 series, Sikorsky Aircraft, has maintained continuous compliance with 14 CFR Part 29 airworthiness standards, including structural integrity, flight control system redundancy, and equipment installation requirements. 

The regulatory framework governing automated flight control systems has undergone significant revision following recent fixed-wing certification events. While the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) was developed and certified under 14 CFR Part 25 for transport category fixed-wing aircraft, its operational history has necessitated a comprehensive cross-category review of human-machine interface (HMI) standards, pilot override transparency, and automated system monitoring. Although MCAS is not applicable to the S-76B airframe, the certification principles derived from its oversight have been integrated into broader FAA policy regarding stability augmentation systems (SAS) and autopilot architectures across all aircraft categories. 

FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 3, Chapter 18, Section 4, provides Aviation Safety Inspectors (ASIs) with standardized procedures for evaluating operator compliance with weather minimums, flight following requirements, and terrain avoidance protocols. Prior Airworthiness Directives (ADs) addressing rotorcraft flight control system anomalies and terrain awareness equipment have been issued under Docket Nos. FAA-2018-0451 and FAA-2019-0722. However, existing regulatory language permits phased compliance for Helicopter Terrain Awareness and Warning Systems (HTAWS) under 14 CFR 135.154, creating operational variances that require harmonization with contemporary risk mitigation standards.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive review of the operator’s compliance posture reveals that while the operator maintained nominal adherence to 14 CFR 135.185 weather minimums and dispatch documentation requirements, real-time meteorological data integration and pilot decision-making protocols were insufficient to prevent inadvertent IMC penetration. The operator’s Operations Specifications (OpSpecs) did not mandate continuous terrain monitoring or automated weather alerting for VFR operations in mountainous and coastal corridors. Furthermore, the aircraft’s Master Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) configuration did not require operational HTAWS, consistent with current regulatory exemptions for legacy rotorcraft fleets.

Sikorsky Aircraft, as the TC holder, has satisfied all applicable 14 CFR Part 29 airworthiness requirements for the S-76B. The aircraft’s existing SAS and autopilot systems functioned within certified parameters; however, the absence of mandatory terrain proximity alerting and automated weather deviation protocols represents a systemic regulatory gap. The FAA has initiated targeted surveillance under FAA Order 8900.1, directing Principal Operations Inspectors (POIs) to evaluate operator training curricula for inadvertent IMC recovery, spatial disorientation mitigation, and dispatch authority limitations. 

A critical oversight asymmetry has been identified between fixed-wing and rotorcraft automated system certification. While MCAS oversight reforms under 14 CFR Part 25 mandated enhanced pilot training, system annunciation, and dual-sensor validation, rotorcraft SAS architectures remain governed by 14 CFR Part 29, which does not require equivalent HMI redundancy or automated system status transparency. This disparity results in inconsistent enforcement of 14 CFR 135.215 and 14 CFR 91.175 operational standards. Additionally, FAA Order 8900.1 guidance does not currently require POIs to validate operator-specific terrain avoidance protocols during routine surveillance, resulting in fragmented compliance verification across Flight Standards District Offices (FSDOs).

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
To address identified regulatory deficiencies and ensure uniform compliance, the FAA shall implement the following corrective actions:

a. Rulemaking and Equipment Mandates: The FAA shall issue a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) to amend 14 CFR 135.154, eliminating phased compliance exemptions and mandating the installation and continuous operational use of Class A HTAWS on all turbine-powered rotorcraft conducting Part 135 operations in terrain-constrained environments. Operators shall revise their OpSpecs and MMEL configurations to reflect mandatory HTAWS operational status within 180 days of final rule publication.

b. Training and Operational Protocols: All Part 135 operators shall submit revised training programs addressing inadvertent IMC recovery, spatial disorientation mitigation, and automated weather deviation procedures within 90 days of this directive. Training curricula must incorporate simulator-based scenarios validating pilot decision-making under rapidly deteriorating meteorological conditions, consistent with 14 CFR 135.341 and 14 CFR 135.343.

c. Manufacturer Service Directives: Sikorsky Aircraft shall issue a Service Bulletin (SB) detailing recommended upgrades to existing SAS architectures to enhance pilot situational awareness, automated system status annunciation, and override transparency. The SB shall align with 14 CFR 29.1309 system safety assessment requirements and shall be distributed within 180 days. Operator compliance with SB recommendations shall be required within 12 months of issuance.

d. Regulatory Guidance Updates: The FAA shall revise FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 3, Chapter 18, Section 4, to incorporate mandatory terrain and weather surveillance checklists for POIs. The updated guidance shall require validation of operator-specific dispatch authority protocols, real-time weather monitoring integration, and HTAWS operational verification during routine surveillance. Implementation shall be completed within 120 days.

e. Compliance Verification and Follow-Up Schedule: FSDOs shall conduct targeted ramp inspections and operational audits at 6-month intervals for the first 24 months post-implementation. Compliance verification shall be documented via the Safety Assurance System (SAS) and reported to the Office of Aviation Safety. A comprehensive regulatory review of rotorcraft automated flight control system certification standards, incorporating lessons learned from fixed-wing MCAS oversight reforms, shall be completed within 36 months. The FAA shall submit formal compliance reports to the NTSB within 45 days of each audit cycle, with final rulemaking implementation status reported no later than 24 months from the date of this correspondence.

All referenced actions shall be executed in accordance with established FAA administrative procedures, with non-compliance subject to enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR 13.1 through 13.19. This memorandum constitutes the official regulatory response and shall be incorporated into the permanent docket record.

HEADLINE: Nine Killed as Helicopter Crashes in Calabasas Hills During Heavy Fog

BYLINE: Elena Rostova, The National Chronicle
DATELINE: CALABASAS, Calif. —

A private helicopter carrying nine people crashed into a steep hillside in Calabasas on Sunday morning, killing everyone on board, authorities confirmed. The Sikorsky S-76B went down in dense fog and low visibility, prompting a massive emergency response and casting a shadow over the region’s aviation community.

Preliminary flight data and weather reports indicate the pilot continued flying under visual flight rules into an area of rapidly deteriorating conditions and rising terrain. The impact occurred shortly after 9 a.m. local time, leaving no survivors and triggering an immediate outpouring of grief from families, local officials, and the broader public.

“Our investigators are on the ground securing the wreckage and collecting critical data,” said National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) lead investigator David Chen. “The focus right now is on understanding the sequence of events that led to this tragedy, particularly the decision to maintain visual flight in instrument meteorological conditions.” The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) echoed the call for caution, with a regional spokesperson stating, “We are fully cooperating with the NTSB and will review all operational and maintenance records. Safety remains our highest priority, and we will take whatever regulatory action is necessary based on the findings.”

The aircraft, manufactured by Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation, was a twin-engine S-76B commonly used for corporate transport and charter flights. It had departed from John Wayne Airport in Orange County and was en route to Camarillo when it encountered a thick marine layer that blanketed the Santa Monica Mountains. Visual flight rules, or VFR, require pilots to navigate by sight and maintain a safe distance from clouds. When visibility drops below those minimums, pilots must transition to instrument flight rules, relying on cockpit gauges and air traffic control guidance. In this case, the pilot appears to have continued visually into a weather system that obscured the terrain.

Aviation safety experts note that spatial disorientation—a condition where a pilot loses their sense of direction and altitude due to a lack of visual references—is a leading cause of fatal helicopter accidents in poor weather. “When you lose the horizon, your inner ear can deceive you,” said Dr. Marcus Lin, an aviation human factors specialist at the University of Southern California. “The transition from visual to instrument flying requires rigorous training and strict adherence to protocols. Without it, the margin for error vanishes.” Lin added that while modern rotorcraft like the S-76B are equipped with advanced avionics, they do not feature automated flight control systems like the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System, or MCAS, found on some commercial jets. “Helicopter safety relies heavily on pilot judgment and real-time weather assessment, which is why regulatory bodies continuously update training standards and maintenance directives,” he noted.

The crash has left families and friends grappling with sudden loss. “They were just heading to a routine meeting,” said Maria Gonzalez, whose brother was among the passengers. “He loved flying, but he always respected the weather. We’re heartbroken and just want answers.” Local community leaders organized a makeshift memorial near the crash site, where flowers, photographs, and handwritten notes have accumulated. “This isn’t just a statistic,” said Calabasas Mayor Alicia Torres. “These were neighbors, colleagues, and loved ones. Our community is united in mourning and in demanding transparency as the investigation unfolds.”

Helicopter operations in Southern California have long navigated complex microclimates, where coastal fog can roll inland with little warning. The region has seen several high-profile rotorcraft accidents over the past two decades, many involving similar weather-related factors. In response, the aviation industry has pushed for enhanced terrain awareness warning systems and stricter weather minimums for charter operators. Regulatory frameworks continue to evolve; for instance, recent airworthiness directives like AD 2024-02-51 have mandated updated inspection protocols for critical flight control components across multiple aircraft types, reflecting a broader industry shift toward proactive risk mitigation. Meanwhile, commercial carriers such as Southwest Airlines have publicly reinforced their commitment to conservative weather dispatch policies, with a company spokesperson noting, “We stand with the families affected by this tragedy. The entire aviation community must remain vigilant about weather-related risks and ensure that safety protocols are never compromised.”

The NTSB has established a command post near the crash site and is coordinating with local law enforcement, the FAA, and Sikorsky engineers to recover the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder. Wreckage mapping and weather reconstruction are underway, with investigators expected to release a preliminary report within 30 days. The agency has temporarily suspended similar charter operations in the immediate area pending a review of local weather monitoring procedures. As the investigation continues, officials stress that the findings will shape future training requirements, equipment standards, and regulatory oversight to prevent similar tragedies. “We owe it to the victims and their families to get this right,” Chen said. “Every piece of data matters, and we will follow the evidence wherever it leads.”

## [sc-0_expert_deposition_037] Expert Deposition

> **Type:** expert_deposition | **Reliability:** 0.942 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Rotorcraft Safety Engineering Consortium (RSEC), acting as a technical party to the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigative hearing regarding the January 26, 2020, accident involving a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter in Calabasas, California. Our delegation comprises senior human factors specialists, flight operations engineers, and aviation safety management professionals with direct experience in rotorcraft certification, operational risk assessment, and pilot training program development. The scope of this document is to provide an independent technical analysis of the contributing factors to the accident, evaluate the intersection of operational decision-making, aircraft systems capabilities, and regulatory oversight, and present evidence-based recommendations for systemic safety improvements.

Our position is grounded in a comprehensive review of the investigative docket, including flight telemetry reconstructions, meteorological data packages, pilot training records, maintenance documentation, and air traffic control communications. While the primary accident sequence is well-documented, this submission focuses on the underlying systemic vulnerabilities that permitted a visual flight rules (VFR) operation to transition into instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) without adequate mitigation. We further contextualize these findings within broader aviation safety paradigms, drawing comparative insights from commercial airline safety management practices and fixed-wing automation certification experiences to inform rotorcraft-specific risk reduction strategies.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On January 26, 2020, at approximately 09:45 Pacific Standard Time, the accident helicopter departed John Wayne Airport (SNA) en route to Camarillo Airport (CMA) under VFR. The flight was operating under Title 14 CFR Part 91, which does not mandate the same operational controls, weather minimums, or equipment requirements as Part 135 commercial operations. As the aircraft proceeded northwest through the Santa Monica Mountains, meteorological conditions deteriorated rapidly. Marine layer fog, combined with localized terrain-induced cloud formation, reduced visibility to less than one-half mile and lowered ceilings below 500 feet AGL.

Docket materials, including the Telemetry Reconstruction Report (Exhibit 12-C) and the Weather Analysis Package (Exhibit 7-A), confirm that the pilot maintained VFR flight into an area of rising terrain and diminishing visual references. Cockpit voice recorder (CVR) transcripts indicate the pilot acknowledged deteriorating conditions but elected to continue the route rather than execute a diversion or climb to a safer altitude. The flight path reconstruction demonstrates a gradual, uncommanded descent consistent with spatial disorientation, culminating in controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) at approximately 1,700 feet MSL. All nine occupants sustained fatal injuries.

The aircraft was equipped with standard S-76B avionics, including a dual-axis autopilot and basic attitude indicators, but lacked a terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS) or synthetic vision system (SVS). Maintenance records (Docket Item 19-F) indicate the aircraft was airworthy and all systems were functioning within manufacturer specifications at the time of departure. Pilot training documentation reveals recurrent VFR proficiency checks but no documented instrument meteorological condition (IMC) recovery training or formalized weather diversion decision matrix.

For contextual comparison, commercial operators such as Southwest Airlines Co have institutionalized predictive weather analytics, mandatory diversion thresholds, and robust safety management systems (SMS) that require real-time risk assessment and crew resource management protocols. The Federal Aviation Administration’s certification framework, while rigorous, historically permitted operational gaps between Part 91 and Part 135 rotorcraft operations, particularly regarding terrain awareness equipment and IMC training requirements. Furthermore, the aviation industry’s broader examination of automation dependency—most notably through the investigation of the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) on fixed-wing transport aircraft—has underscored the critical importance of transparent system design, pilot training alignment, and regulatory assumptions regarding human-machine interaction. These cross-industry lessons are directly applicable to the S-76B accident sequence.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The accident sequence is best understood through the integration of human factors, operational risk management, and aircraft systems engineering. Our analysis identifies three primary technical domains that converged to produce the fatal outcome: (1) spatial disorientation and vestibular illusion under degraded visual conditions, (2) inadequate terrain and weather awareness systems, and (3) regulatory and training gaps in VFR-to-IMC transition management.

Human Factors and Spatial Disorientation
Cockpit voice recordings and control input telemetry indicate that the pilot experienced a gradual loss of visual reference, followed by control inputs consistent with somatogravic and vestibular illusions. In the absence of external visual cues, the human vestibular system cannot reliably detect gradual pitch or bank changes, particularly during low-altitude flight over undulating terrain. Research from the FAA’s Civil Aerospace Medical Institute (CAMI) demonstrates that untrained pilots can succumb to spatial disorientation within 10 to 15 seconds of entering IMC. The S-76B’s primary flight display provided basic attitude information, but without synthetic vision or terrain overlay, the pilot lacked an intuitive, heads-up reference to counteract illusionary cues. The telemetry data shows a 12-degree nose-down pitch and a 15-degree left bank developing over a 40-second window, with corrective inputs applied too late to arrest the descent.

Systems Engineering and Terrain Awareness
The absence of a TAWS or SVS represents a critical engineering gap. Modern rotorcraft operating in mountainous or coastal environments routinely encounter rapid visibility degradation. Industry standards, including RTCA DO-315 and ICAO Annex 6, recommend terrain awareness systems for all commercial rotorcraft operations. The S-76B’s certification basis did not require such equipment under Part 91, leaving operators reliant on pilot visual scanning and sectional chart awareness. In contrast, operators like Southwest Airlines Co have integrated predictive terrain and weather modeling into their dispatch and flight deck decision support tools, enabling proactive route adjustments before conditions reach critical thresholds. The accident helicopter’s flight path reconstruction shows the aircraft entered a terrain corridor with a 1,200-foot elevation gain over 4.2 nautical miles. Without automated terrain proximity alerts, the pilot lacked objective, real-time feedback to override the cognitive bias of mission continuation.

Operational Risk Management and Training Assumptions
The pilot’s decision to continue VFR into deteriorating conditions reflects a well-documented phenomenon in aviation safety: plan continuation bias. This bias is exacerbated when operators lack formalized weather diversion protocols, real-time meteorological updates, and structured IMC recovery training. The training records submitted to the docket indicate the pilot held a commercial rotorcraft certificate with instrument rating, but recurrent training emphasized VFR navigation and standard emergency procedures rather than inadvertent IMC recovery. Human factors research consistently shows that IMC recovery requires specific, scenario-based training that conditions pilots to immediately transition to instrument references, execute a 180-degree turn, and climb to a safe altitude. The absence of such training, combined with organizational pressure to complete the mission, created a high-risk operational environment.

Comparative Certification and Automation Lessons
While the S-76B does not employ flight control augmentation systems analogous to the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System, the underlying certification philosophy warrants examination. The MCAS investigations revealed how assumptions about pilot response times, system transparency, and training adequacy can diverge from operational reality. Similarly, rotorcraft certification has historically assumed that VFR pilots will self-divert when conditions deteriorate, without mandating decision-support tools or standardized diversion protocols. This assumption fails to account for cognitive load, mission pressure, and the physiological limitations of human perception in degraded visual environments. The FAA’s regulatory framework has since evolved to emphasize performance-based safety management, yet Part 91 rotorcraft operations remain outside many of the equipment and training mandates applied to commercial carriers. Bridging this gap requires a shift from reactive compliance to proactive risk mitigation.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the technical evidence, telemetry reconstruction, and human factors analysis, the Rotorcraft Safety Engineering Consortium concludes that the January 26, 2020, accident resulted from a convergence of operational, engineering, and regulatory factors. The primary contributing factor was the pilot’s continuation of VFR flight into IMC, compounded by spatial disorientation and the absence of terrain awareness and synthetic vision systems. Secondary factors included inadequate IMC recovery training, lack of formalized weather diversion protocols, and regulatory gaps that permitted Part 91 rotorcraft operations without mandatory terrain warning equipment or standardized decision-support tools.

We acknowledge the complexity of this accident. Weather forecasting in coastal mountainous regions remains inherently challenging, and mission profiles often involve time-sensitive constraints that influence pilot decision-making. However, aviation safety must prioritize systemic resilience over individual performance expectations. The evidence demonstrates that reliance on pilot visual judgment alone is insufficient when environmental conditions degrade rapidly. The aviation industry’s broader safety evolution—exemplified by the operational safety frameworks adopted by carriers such as Southwest Airlines Co and the certification reforms prompted by fixed-wing automation incidents—confirms that proactive risk management, transparent system design, and standardized training protocols are essential to preventing CFIT and VFR-into-IMC accidents.

We recommend the following safety improvements:
- Mandate TAWS and synthetic vision systems for all rotorcraft operating in commercial or revenue-generating capacities, regardless of Part 91 or Part 135 classification.
- Require recurrent, scenario-based IMC recovery training for all commercial rotorcraft pilots, with emphasis on immediate instrument transition, terrain avoidance, and standardized diversion procedures.
- Implement predictive weather and terrain risk modeling into rotorcraft dispatch and flight planning systems, with mandatory diversion thresholds tied to real-time meteorological data.
- Strengthen FAA oversight of Part 91 rotorcraft operations by aligning equipment and training requirements with Part 135 standards for flights conducted in mountainous, coastal, or high-terrain environments.
- Establish an industry-wide safety data sharing platform to track VFR-into-IMC incidents, near-misses, and weather-related diversions, enabling continuous improvement in operational risk management.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

The Rotorcraft Safety Engineering Consortium and its member organizations have already initiated several corrective measures in response to this accident and related safety findings. These include:
- Voluntary retrofit programs for TAWS and synthetic vision integration across participating operator fleets, with over 60% of member aircraft now equipped with Class A terrain awareness systems.
- Development and deployment of an IMC Recovery Training Module, incorporating full-motion simulator scenarios, vestibular illusion education, and standardized decision matrices for inadvertent IMC encounters.
- Implementation of predictive weather monitoring partnerships with meteorological service providers, enabling real-time visibility and ceiling alerts directly to flight dispatch and cockpit displays.
- Internal SMS audits focused on plan continuation bias, weather diversion compliance, and crew resource management, with findings integrated into recurrent training curricula.

Looking forward, we propose the following industry-wide improvements:
- Collaborative rulemaking with the FAA to establish performance-based equipment and training standards for rotorcraft operating in marginal VFR conditions, with phased implementation timelines and financial incentives for early adoption.
- Standardization of automation transparency and human-machine interface design principles across rotorcraft manufacturers, ensuring that flight deck systems provide intuitive, unambiguous terrain and weather references without increasing pilot cognitive load.
- Expansion of open-reporting safety cultures modeled after commercial airline practices, encouraging voluntary incident reporting, non-punitive data analysis, and cross-organizational safety briefings.
- Continuous monitoring of VFR-into-IMC risk factors through telemetry analytics, weather pattern modeling, and human factors research, with annual safety performance reviews published for industry stakeholders.

The aviation community has repeatedly demonstrated its capacity to transform tragedy into systemic improvement. By integrating advanced terrain awareness technology, standardizing IMC recovery training, and aligning regulatory frameworks with operational realities, we can significantly reduce the risk of VFR-into-IMC accidents. The Rotorcraft Safety Engineering Consortium stands ready to support the NTSB, the FAA, and industry partners in implementing these recommendations, ensuring that future rotorcraft operations are conducted with the highest standards of safety, transparency, and operational resilience.
