## [sc-0_internal_memo_038] Internal Memo

> **Type:** internal_memo | **Reliability:** 0.688 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

TO: All Flight Operations Personnel, Maintenance Control, Training Department, SMS Coordinators, Dispatch
FROM: Director of Flight Safety & Chief Pilot, Rotorcraft Operations Division
DATE: 14 March 2024
SUBJECT: MANDATORY TRAINING UPDATE: VFR-INTO-IMC PREVENTION & TERRAIN AWARENESS PROTOCOLS
REF: SMS-2024-089, TRN-BUL-2024-014, WO-7742-ALPHA, FOP-LOG-2024-03

PURPOSE:
This bulletin establishes mandatory updates to our VFR-into-IMC mitigation procedures, terrain avoidance protocols, and crew resource management (CRM) training requirements. It addresses critical operational gaps identified during recent internal safety audits and aligns our fleet standards with current regulatory expectations. All flight, maintenance, and dispatch personnel must review, acknowledge, and implement these directives immediately.

BACKGROUND:
On 26 January 2020, a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter crashed into terrain in Calabasas, California, during instrument meteorological conditions. The aircraft continued VFR flight into an area of rapidly deteriorating visibility and rising terrain, resulting in the loss of all nine persons on board. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigation concluded that spatial disorientation, delayed decision-making, and inadequate terrain awareness were primary causal factors. The Board’s Lead Investigator specifically noted that the flight crew failed to execute a timely diversion or transition to instrument flight rules when visual references degraded.

Our Safety Management System has reviewed this event alongside recent industry-wide operational data. While our fleet operates different airframes, our primary operating corridors feature identical environmental hazards: coastal marine layers, rapid visibility reduction, and complex topography. Compliance with FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 3, Chapter 18, Section 4, mandates that Part 135 operators maintain rigorous VFR-into-IMC prevention programs, including structured weather minimums, mandatory diversion triggers, and recurrent simulator training. 

Recent regulatory updates further reinforce these requirements. Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-51 mandates updated Terrain Awareness and Warning System (TAWS) software and enhanced pitot-static system calibrations across all applicable rotorcraft. Additionally, we are integrating lessons from fixed-wing operators to strengthen our decision-making frameworks. Southwest Airlines’ recent CRM overhaul demonstrates how structured go/no-go matrices and standardized callouts reduce automation dependency and improve compliance during degraded visual conditions. Our updated curriculum will also include comparative system-reliance training, utilizing historical MCAS (Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System) event analysis to reinforce the necessity of manual flight proficiency, cross-checking automated alerts, and maintaining primary instrument scan discipline when secondary systems provide conflicting data.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, the following procedural, maintenance, and training modifications are in effect:

1. Weather Minimums & Go/No-Go Protocols
   - All VFR departures into coastal or mountainous corridors require a minimum ceiling of 1,500 feet AGL and 5 statute miles visibility.
   - If en route visibility drops below 3 SM or ceiling falls below 1,000 feet AGL, pilots must execute an immediate 180-degree turn or divert to the nearest IFR-capable alternate.
   - Dispatchers must log all pre-flight and en route weather briefings in the Flight Operations Portal (FOP) under module WX-LOG-2024. Unlogged briefings will trigger an automatic SMS audit.

2. Avionics & System Compliance
   - Maintenance Control will verify TAWS software version 4.2.1 or later on all active aircraft per Work Order WO-7742-ALPHA.
   - Pitot-static system inspections must comply with AD 2024-02-51. Technicians will reference Part Number P/N-8842-TA for replacement static ports and use calibration kit CK-9901.
   - Any aircraft with unresolved TAWS, attitude indicator, or heading system discrepancies will be grounded until cleared by the Lead Maintenance Inspector. Discrepancy tags must be logged in the Maintenance Tracking System (MTS) under code AVN-04.

3. Training & CRM Updates
   - All flight crews will complete Module TRN-IMC-04: “VFR-into-IMC Recognition & Recovery” within 30 days.
   - Simulator sessions will now include unannounced IMC entry scenarios with mandatory instrument scan verification, terrain avoidance maneuvers, and simulated radio failure protocols.
   - First Officer and Captain cross-check procedures are revised: the non-flying pilot must verbally confirm altitude, heading, and terrain clearance every 60 seconds during low-visibility operations.
   - Training will incorporate automation dependency awareness, using historical MCAS incident analysis to highlight the risks of over-reliance on single-system inputs without manual cross-verification.

4. Documentation & Reporting
   - All weather-related diversions, IMC encounters, or terrain proximity alerts must be reported via the Safety Reporting System (SRS) within 24 hours.
   - Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) parameters for “Rapid Descent in Low Visibility” and “Proximity to Rising Terrain” are now active. Exceedances will trigger automatic SMS review and mandatory instructor debrief.

ACTION REQUIRED:
- Flight Operations Management: Distribute this bulletin to all line pilots, dispatchers, and scheduling personnel by 18 March 2024. Verify receipt via the internal compliance tracker (ID: COMP-2024-0314).
- Training Department: Schedule and administer TRN-IMC-04 and updated CRM modules. Ensure all simulator instructors are briefed on the new unannounced IMC entry protocols by 25 March 2024. Submit instructor qualification logs to the Chief Pilot.
- Maintenance Control: Complete TAWS software verification and AD 2024-02-51 compliance checks on all active aircraft by 01 April 2024. Submit completion logs and calibration certificates to the Quality Assurance office.
- All Flight Crews: Acknowledge receipt of this bulletin in the FOP. Complete the mandatory online assessment (Quiz ID: VFR-IMC-2024) by 31 March 2024. Failure to complete will result in temporary flight status suspension.
- Safety Office: Monitor FDM data and SRS submissions. Compile a 60-day compliance report for the Director of Operations. Retain all training records, maintenance logs, and FDM reports for a minimum of 24 months per internal document retention policy DOC-RET-09.

This directive supersedes all prior VFR weather guidance and training bulletins issued before 01 January 2024. Questions regarding implementation should be directed to the Flight Safety Office at ext. 4402 or via email at safety.ops@rotorcraft.internal.

Compliance is mandatory. Operational safety depends on disciplined adherence to these protocols.

## [sc-0_preliminary_report_039] Preliminary Report

> **Type:** preliminary_report | **Reliability:** 0.95 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. SYNOPSIS
On January 26, 2020, at approximately 0945 Pacific Standard Time, a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, registration N72EX, impacted mountainous terrain in Calabasas, California. The aircraft was operated by Island Express Helicopters, Inc. (IEH) and was conducting a visual flight rules (VFR) charter flight when it encountered instrument meteorological conditions (IMC). Preliminary information indicates that all nine persons on board sustained fatal injuries. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has initiated an investigation to determine the circumstances surrounding the accident. This document outlines the preliminary factual data, establishes the investigative scope, and documents initial procedural decisions. All information contained herein is subject to revision as the investigation progresses.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information has been compiled from on-scene observations, air traffic control (ATC) communications, and initial witness interviews. Initial data indicates the helicopter departed John Wayne Airport (SNA) at 0906 PST, en route to Camarillo Airport (CMA). Radar and flight tracking data suggest the aircraft maintained a southeasterly track before deviating westward into the Santa Monica Mountains. Initial witness accounts describe low-hanging cloud layers, reduced visibility, and intermittent precipitation in the vicinity of the impact site. Several observers reported hearing rotorcraft noise consistent with a low-altitude transit, followed by a sudden cessation of sound and a ground impact.

Weather conditions at the time of the accident were characterized by a marine layer advecting inland, resulting in ceilings below 1,000 feet above ground level (AGL) and visibility frequently dropping below three statute miles. Automated weather observation systems from nearby reporting stations corroborate the presence of deteriorating meteorological conditions. Preliminary examination of the wreckage distribution indicates a high-energy impact with terrain, with debris scattered across a steep, wooded slope. Initial structural assessment suggests the airframe sustained catastrophic damage upon contact, with no evidence of in-flight breakup prior to ground impact.

Systems evaluation has commenced. Initial review of the flight control architecture confirms the absence of automated stability augmentation systems comparable to the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), consistent with the manufacturer’s design specifications for this rotorcraft model. Maintenance and operational records indicate the flight was conducted under single-pilot authority; no Second-in-Command (SIC) was assigned or present aboard the aircraft. The NTSB’s preliminary review of operator documentation suggests compliance with standard maintenance scheduling, though a comprehensive audit remains pending. All initial findings are considered provisional and will be refined through detailed component testing and data reconstruction.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The Lead Investigator has formally activated the following investigative groups: Operations, Structures, Systems, Human Performance, Weather, and Survival Factors. Each group has been tasked with collecting, preserving, and analyzing evidence within their respective disciplines. Island Express Helicopters has been designated as a party to the investigation, alongside representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation, and the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Party status grants access to non-public investigative materials under the supervision of NTSB personnel, with strict adherence to confidentiality protocols.

Evidence secured to date includes the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR), both of which have been transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for data extraction and analysis. Wreckage recovery operations have been coordinated with local law enforcement and fire agencies to ensure safe access to the impact site. All major airframe components, engine assemblies, and flight control linkages have been cataloged and secured for subsequent examination. Maintenance logs, pilot training records, and dispatch documentation have been obtained and are currently undergoing preliminary review.

Procedural guidance for the operational review has been aligned with FAA Order 8900.1, Flight Standards Information Management System, specifically referencing sections pertaining to VFR flight into IMC and operator risk management protocols. Cross-referencing of industry-standard operational practices has included consultation with subject matter experts from Southwest Airlines to evaluate comparative VFR/IFR transition procedures and crew resource management frameworks. Additionally, regulatory compliance reviews have been initiated to assess the applicability of recent and pending directives. Notably, Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-51 was evaluated against the aircraft’s maintenance history and airframe configuration; preliminary assessment indicates the directive does not apply to this specific model or serial number, though the review will be documented for completeness.

All investigative activities are being conducted under the oversight of the Lead Investigator, who has established a centralized evidence tracking system and mandated daily status briefings for all group chairs. The investigation remains in its formative phase, and no determinations regarding operational decisions, mechanical performance, or human factors have been finalized.

4. NEXT STEPS
Planned investigative activities over the coming weeks will focus on the systematic reconstruction of the flight path, detailed component teardowns, and comprehensive data analysis. The Systems group will conduct bench testing of recovered avionics and engine control units to identify any pre-impact anomalies. The Human Performance group will initiate structured interviews with maintenance personnel, dispatchers, and individuals familiar with the pilot’s recent flight history and training records. Weather specialists will continue to refine meteorological models using satellite imagery, radar returns, and localized atmospheric soundings to establish precise visibility and ceiling conditions along the flight route.

The Operations group will complete a thorough review of the operator’s safety management system, flight following procedures, and pilot decision-making protocols. All findings will be cross-validated against regulatory requirements and industry best practices. The Lead Investigator will convene a public hearing at a later date, should the complexity of the evidence warrant formal testimony and expert analysis. Until such time, all investigative materials will remain under NTSB control, with periodic factual updates released to the public as warranted by the progress of the inquiry.

A preliminary factual report is anticipated within 12 to 18 months, pending the completion of laboratory analyses, component testing, and party submissions. The National Transportation Safety Board emphasizes that all current information is preliminary and subject to change. No conclusions regarding probable cause, contributing factors, or operational deficiencies are presented in this document. The investigation will proceed in accordance with established NTSB protocols, with a commitment to thoroughness, objectivity, and transparency. Further updates will be issued as significant milestones are achieved and as additional data becomes available for analysis.

## [sc-0_investigation_report_040] Investigation Report

> **Type:** investigation_report | **Reliability:** 0.989 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 General
On January 26, 2020, at approximately 0945 Pacific Standard Time (PST), a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, registration N72EX, impacted mountainous terrain in Calabasas, California. The accident site was located at latitude 34°08'12.5"N, longitude 118°41'22.1"W, at an elevation of approximately 1,250 feet mean sea level (MSL). The helicopter was destroyed by impact forces and a post-impact fire. All nine persons on board, including the pilot and eight passengers, sustained fatal injuries. The accident occurred during daylight hours under instrument meteorological conditions (IMC).

1.2 Flight History
The flight was conducted as a 14 CFR Part 135 on-demand charter operation. The aircraft departed John Wayne Airport (SNA), Orange County, California, at 0906 PST, with a planned destination of Camarillo Airport (CMA), Ventura County, California. The flight plan was filed under visual flight rules (VFR) with an estimated en route time of 35 minutes. Radar data indicated the helicopter departed SNA on a northwesterly heading, climbed to approximately 1,500 feet MSL, and proceeded along the coastal corridor. At approximately 0930 PST, the aircraft deviated from the planned route, turning inland toward the Santa Monica Mountains. The final radar return was recorded at 0944:32 PST at an altitude of 1,100 feet MSL and a ground speed of 161 knots.

1.3 Regulatory Framework
The operation was conducted under the authority of 14 CFR Part 135, specifically Subpart E, which governs operating requirements for commuter and on-demand operations. Weather minimums for VFR flight in Class E airspace were governed by 14 CFR 91.155, requiring a minimum visibility of 3 statute miles and distance from clouds of 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 2,000 feet horizontal. The operator held a valid Part 135 certificate and was authorized for single-pilot operations in the S-76B under approved Operations Specifications.

1.4 Notification and Response
The Los Angeles County Fire Department received emergency notifications at 0947 PST. First responders arrived on scene at 1002 PST and established a perimeter due to hazardous terrain and active fire conditions. The National Transportation Safety Board was notified at 1015 PST. The Investigator-in-Charge was dispatched to coordinate the on-site investigation, establish group assignments, and oversee the documentation of the accident site in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Pilot-in-Command Qualifications
The pilot-in-command held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate with rotorcraft-helicopter and instrument helicopter ratings. The pilot also held a commercial pilot certificate for airplane single-engine land and multi-engine land. The pilot possessed a type rating for the Sikorsky S-76 series and was current in accordance with 14 CFR 61.57 and 135.247. Total flight time was recorded at 8,520 hours, with 1,245 hours in the S-76B. The pilot held a valid second-class medical certificate issued on November 12, 2019, with no limitations.

2.2 Training and Recent Experience
The pilot completed recurrent training and proficiency checks on October 18, 2019, in accordance with 14 CFR 135.293 and 135.297. Training records indicated satisfactory performance in instrument procedures, emergency operations, and terrain avoidance maneuvers. The pilot's 90-day flight experience prior to the accident included 142 hours of flight time, with 38 hours conducted under instrument flight rules (IFR). The pilot's most recent instrument proficiency check was completed on September 5, 2019, with no deficiencies noted.

2.3 First Officer Position and Crew Complement
The Sikorsky S-76B is certified for two-pilot operations per the manufacturer's flight manual. The operator's training program included standardized qualification requirements for the First Officer position, encompassing instrument procedures, crew resource management, and emergency checklist execution. For this specific flight, the First Officer position was not staffed. The operator's Operations Specifications authorized single-pilot operations for the S-76B under Part 135, provided the pilot met specific experience and training thresholds. Crew scheduling documentation confirmed that no First Officer was assigned to the flight manifest.

2.4 Medical and Duty Time Records
The pilot's duty time records were reviewed in accordance with 14 CFR 135.263. The pilot reported for duty at 0730 PST, with a scheduled flight time of 0900 PST. The pilot had accumulated 6.5 hours of flight time in the preceding 24 hours and 28.5 hours in the preceding 7 days, well within regulatory limits. Medical history review revealed no documented conditions that would have impaired flight performance. The pilot's rest period prior to duty commencement was 11.5 hours, compliant with 14 CFR 135.263(d).

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Specifications
The accident aircraft was a Sikorsky S-76B, serial number 760345, manufactured in 1988. The helicopter was equipped with two Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6B-36A turboshaft engines, each rated at 650 shaft horsepower. The maximum gross weight was 11,700 pounds. The aircraft was configured for eight passenger seats and one pilot seat. Total airframe time at the time of the accident was 11,247.3 hours. The engines had accumulated 2,105.4 hours and 1,988.2 hours since overhaul, respectively.

3.2 Maintenance History and Records
The aircraft was maintained under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program approved by the FAA. The most recent 100-hour inspection was completed on January 10, 2020, at 11,198.5 airframe hours. Maintenance log entries indicated no deferred items or outstanding discrepancies. Engine oil analysis reports from December 2019 showed normal wear metal concentrations. The main rotor blades were inspected for delamination and erosion on January 15, 2020, with no anomalies documented. All maintenance actions were performed in accordance with 14 CFR Part 43 and the manufacturer's maintenance manual.

3.3 Airworthiness Directives and Service Bulletins
A review of the aircraft maintenance records confirmed compliance with all applicable FAA Airworthiness Directives (ADs) as of the accident date. Compliance status with FAA Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-51, issued for the Sikorsky S-76 series, was verified through logbook review and maintenance tracking software. The directive pertained to inspection and replacement criteria for specific flight control linkage components. The operator's maintenance control center documented that the required inspection was completed on December 22, 2019, and all corrective actions were within compliance windows. No outstanding service bulletins were identified that would have affected flight safety.

3.4 Systems and Avionics Configuration
The aircraft was equipped with a Garmin GNS 430W GPS/NAV/COM system, a King KX 165A NAV/COM, and a Bendix/King KAP 140 autopilot. The terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS) was not installed, as it was not mandated for Part 135 rotorcraft operations at the time. The flight control system utilized conventional mechanical linkages with hydraulic boost. The Systems Group reviewed flight control augmentation architectures, including comparative documentation of the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), to evaluate control authority parameters and pilot interface design philosophies applicable to rotorcraft flight control systems. No evidence of flight control system malfunction was identified during preliminary examination.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Weather Overview
A strong low-pressure system was situated off the California coast, generating a marine layer that extended inland across the Los Angeles Basin. The synoptic pattern produced widespread stratus clouds, fog, and reduced visibility. Surface pressure gradients indicated onshore flow with wind speeds of 8 to 12 knots from the west-southwest. The freezing level was recorded at approximately 11,500 feet MSL.

4.2 Surface Observations and Terminal Forecasts
The 0953 PST METAR from Van Nuys Airport (KVNY) reported wind 270° at 9 knots, visibility 1/2 statute mile in fog, ceiling 200 feet overcast, temperature 14°C, dewpoint 13°C, and altimeter 30.02 inches of mercury. The 0953 PST METAR from Camarillo Airport (KCMA) reported wind 280° at 7 knots, visibility 1 statute mile in mist, ceiling 300 feet broken, temperature 13°C, dewpoint 12°C, and altimeter 30.01 inches of mercury. The Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) for KVNY, issued at 0530 PST, predicted visibility 1/2 to 1 statute mile in fog with ceilings 200 to 400 feet through 1200 PST.

4.3 Pilot Weather Reports and Commercial Operator Data
Multiple pilot weather reports (PIREPs) were recorded in the Los Angeles area between 0900 and 0945 PST. Commercial operators, including Southwest Airlines, reported instrument meteorological conditions along the coastal corridor, with cloud bases between 300 and 500 feet AGL and visibility less than 1 statute mile. A Southwest Airlines flight operating at 3,000 feet MSL reported moderate turbulence and continuous cloud cover. The PIREPs were disseminated via the Automated Flight Service Station (AFSS) and were available to the pilot prior to departure.

4.4 Visibility and Ceiling Analysis
Satellite imagery and surface observation data indicated a rapid deterioration of weather conditions along the planned route. The marine layer thickness was estimated at 1,200 to 1,500 feet, with visibility decreasing to less than 1/4 statute mile in localized areas. The terrain elevation in the accident vicinity ranged from 1,000 to 2,100 feet MSL, creating a high risk of controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) under VFR. The pilot's decision to continue VFR flight into an area of reduced visibility and rising terrain was inconsistent with 14 CFR 135.215, which requires operators to establish and adhere to weather minimums and alternate routing procedures.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Impact Site and Debris Distribution
The primary impact site was located on a steep, brush-covered hillside with a slope angle of approximately 35 degrees. The initial impact point was marked by a crater measuring 1.2 meters in diameter and 0.4 meters in depth, with soil displacement consistent with a high-energy, nose-low, right-wing-low impact attitude. The debris field extended approximately 85 meters downslope, oriented along a magnetic heading of 142°. Major structural components, including the main rotor hub, tail boom, and engine nacelles, were fragmented and distributed within a 40-meter radius of the primary impact point.

5.2 Structural and Component Examination
The airframe exhibited catastrophic structural failure consistent with impact forces exceeding design load limits. The fuselage was fragmented into multiple sections, with fire damage concentrated in the aft cabin and engine compartment areas. The main rotor blades were separated at the root fittings, with fracture surfaces exhibiting ductile tearing characteristics. The tail rotor assembly was recovered intact, with no evidence of pre-impact mechanical failure. The landing gear was retracted at impact, consistent with normal cruise configuration.

5.3 Flight Control and Rotor System Analysis
The flight control system components, including the cyclic, collective, and anti-torque pedals, were examined for continuity and binding. All control linkages were severed at impact, with no evidence of pre-existing wear, corrosion, or mechanical restriction. The hydraulic boost actuators were recovered and bench-tested; both units demonstrated normal pressure response and stroke travel. The main transmission was disassembled and inspected. Gear teeth exhibited impact-related spalling, with no evidence of fatigue cracking or lubrication failure. The engine fuel control units were intact, with no signs of contamination or malfunction.

5.4 Avionics and Data Recorder Findings
The aircraft was not equipped with a flight data recorder (FDR) or cockpit voice recorder (CVR), as these systems are not required for Part 135 rotorcraft operations under 14 CFR 135.152. The Garmin GNS 430W navigation unit was recovered and subjected to data extraction. The unit's internal memory was damaged by impact and thermal exposure, rendering flight path data unrecoverable. The autopilot control panel was examined; all switches were in the off position at impact. The transponder was recovered with the code selector set to 1200, consistent with VFR operations.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Operator Policies and Operational Specifications
Island Express Helicopters maintained an approved Operations Specifications manual under 14 CFR 135.21, which outlined weather minimums, route planning procedures, and pilot qualification requirements. The operator's policy required pilots to obtain current weather briefings prior to departure and to divert or delay flights if conditions fell below established VFR minimums. The manual referenced 14 CFR 135.215, which mandates that operators establish procedures for flight in deteriorating weather, including the use of alternate airports and IFR clearance when necessary. Internal audit records from November 2019 indicated compliance with all regulatory requirements, with no outstanding corrective actions.

6.2 Historical Precedents and Safety Data
The NTSB has investigated multiple rotorcraft accidents involving VFR flight into IMC, with similar contributing factors including spatial disorientation, terrain proximity, and inadequate weather assessment. Historical data from 2000 to 2019 indicates that VFR-into-IMC accidents account for approximately 18% of fatal rotorcraft accidents in the United States. The NTSB has issued multiple safety recommendations addressing pilot training, weather decision-making, and the installation of terrain awareness systems in rotorcraft. The operator's safety management system (SMS) documentation was reviewed and found to include standard risk assessment protocols, though no specific mitigation strategies for coastal marine layer operations were documented.

6.3 Regulatory Guidance and Advisory Circulars
The FAA Advisory Circular AC 91-79A, "Mitigating the Risks of a Runway Overrun Upon Landing," and AC 135-14, "Pilot Guide: Small Aircraft Ground Handling," were referenced in the operator's training curriculum. More relevant to this investigation, AC 90-48D, "Pilots' Role in Collision Avoidance," and AC 120-12A, "Private Carriage Versus Common Carriage of Persons or Property," provide guidance on weather assessment and operational decision-making. The FAA's Helicopter Safety Advisory Conference (HSAC) has published best practices for VFR operations in coastal environments, emphasizing the use of real-time weather data and conservative altitude planning. The operator's training program incorporated elements of these guidelines, though specific scenario-based training for rapid weather deterioration was not documented.

6.4 Investigator-in-Charge Directives and Group Coordination
The Investigator-in-Charge established a multi-disciplinary investigative structure, assigning groups to operations, maintenance, meteorology, wreckage, and human performance. Site documentation was conducted using photogrammetry, laser scanning, and GPS mapping to establish precise impact coordinates and debris distribution patterns. All recovered components were cataloged, tagged, and transported to a secure examination facility. The Investigator-in-Charge coordinated with local law enforcement, fire authorities, and the FAA to ensure compliance with 14 CFR Part 830 notification and preservation requirements. Group chairmen submitted preliminary factual reports within 30 days of the accident, with all data cross-referenced against maintenance logs, weather records, and operator documentation. The investigation remains ongoing, with additional analysis of flight control system parameters and pilot decision-making factors pending completion.

## [sc-0_technical_analysis_041] Technical Analysis

> **Type:** technical_analysis | **Reliability:** 0.886 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. INTRODUCTION
This Specialist’s Factual Report documents the examination, data extraction, and analytical evaluation of the flight data recorder (FDR) and associated structural components recovered from the accident site involving a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, registration N72EX, on January 26, 2020, in Calabasas, California. The scope of this examination encompasses the crash-survivable memory unit (CSMU), associated data acquisition modules, mounting hardware, wiring harnesses, and selected primary airframe structural interfaces. The examination was conducted under the direction of the Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) and in coordination with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) evidence custodians. All items were received at the NTSB Materials Laboratory, Washington, D.C., on February 10, 2020, with subsequent data readout and validation performed at the L-3 Communications facility in Camden, New Jersey, from February 12 through February 28, 2020. The examination adhered to NTSB Group Chairman directives, SAE AS8034, and RTCA DO-160G environmental testing protocols. All test equipment utilized during this evaluation, including the Agilent 3458A digital multimeter, Tektronix DPO70000SX oscilloscope, and FEI Quanta 650 FEG scanning electron microscope, maintained current calibration certificates traceable to NIST standards.

2. BACKGROUND
The Sikorsky S-76B is a twin-engine, medium-lift utility helicopter certified under 14 CFR Part 29, Amendment 29-24. The aircraft is equipped with a L-3 Communications FA2100-1020 solid-state flight data recorder (P/N 2100-1020-00, S/N 00045821), installed per Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) SR00878NY. The FDR is designed to record a minimum of 25 flight parameters at a sampling rate of 1 Hz, with select high-frequency parameters sampled at 4 Hz, in compliance with 14 CFR § 135.152 and TSO-C124a. The CSMU is housed within a titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V, per AMS 4928) crash-protected enclosure, rated to withstand impact decelerations up to 3,400 g for 6.5 milliseconds, fire exposure at 1,100°C for 60 minutes, and hydrostatic pressure to 20,000 ft MSL equivalent.

The accident aircraft accumulated 12,450.3 total airframe hours and 8,920.1 cycles at the time of the event. Maintenance records indicate compliance with Sikorsky Maintenance Manual (SMM) 76B-AMM-001, Revision 42, with the most recent heavy inspection completed on November 14, 2019. The flight control architecture consists of a conventional mechanical-hydraulic system with a dual-axis Stability Augmentation System (SAS) providing rate damping and attitude hold functions. Per IIC directive, a comparative review of flight control augmentation architectures was conducted, including the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), to establish baseline handling quality expectations for stability-augmented rotorcraft versus fixed-wing fly-by-wire implementations. The S-76B does not incorporate MCAS or any equivalent pitch-trim automation; all control inputs are mechanically transmitted via push-pull tubes and hydraulic actuators.

Structural evaluation criteria referenced during this examination incorporated inspection thresholds and material acceptance standards aligned with Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-51, which establishes post-accident structural integrity verification protocols for legacy rotorcraft airframes. The FAA provided supplemental engineering data, including original equipment manufacturer (OEM) stress analysis reports and fatigue life calculations for the main rotor mast interface and tail boom attachment lugs. The FDR mounting structure interfaces with the aft cabin bulkhead via four AN3-10A steel bolts torqued to 180–200 in-lbs, with load distribution calculated per MIL-HDBK-5J for combined shear and tensile loading.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS
Physical examination of the recovered FDR assembly was conducted in accordance with ASTM E3 and E407 metallographic preparation standards. The external aluminum alloy 7075-T6 housing (per AMS 4045) exhibited localized plastic deformation consistent with high-energy terrain impact. Maximum measured deformation was 14.2 mm lateral and 8.7 mm vertical relative to the original mounting plane. The CSMU remained fully intact, with no visible compromise to the hermetic seal or internal circuit boards. The MIL-DTL-38999 Series III electrical connectors (P/N D38999/20FJ35SN) displayed thermal discoloration on the outer shell, with surface temperatures estimated at 180–220°C based on oxide layer coloration. No evidence of electrical arcing, pin migration, or dielectric breakdown was observed.

Data extraction was performed using the L-3 proprietary readout interface, following SAE AS8034 procedures. The solid-state memory array (NAND flash, 256 MB capacity) was imaged at the bit level. Cyclic redundancy check (CRC) validation confirmed a bit error rate of <0.001%, well within the TSO-C124a threshold of 0.01%. All 28 recorded parameters were successfully decoded and mapped to their respective engineering units. Time synchronization with the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) was verified using the 400 Hz synchronization tone marker, yielding a temporal alignment accuracy of ±0.05 seconds.

Metallurgical analysis of the FDR mounting bracket and adjacent airframe hardpoints was conducted using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). The bracket material, Ti-6Al-4V, exhibited a fully ductile overload fracture morphology with no evidence of fatigue striations, stress corrosion cracking, or intergranular failure. Chemical composition analysis yielded: Al 6.12%, V 4.05%, Fe 0.18%, O 0.14%, C 0.02%, N 0.01%, all within AMS 4928 specification limits. Tensile testing of representative coupon samples (per ASTM E8) indicated an ultimate tensile strength of 138.5 ksi and a yield strength of 128.2 ksi, consistent with heat-treated Ti-6Al-4V in the annealed condition. Fracture surface topography revealed microvoid coalescence with dimple spacing averaging 12–18 μm, characteristic of rapid tensile failure under dynamic loading.

The associated wiring harness (MIL-W-22759/34, 22 AWG, PTFE-insulated) showed localized charring on the outer jacket, with conductor continuity verified at 0.02 Ω maximum deviation across all 14 signal pairs. Insulation resistance testing per MIL-STD-202G Method 302 yielded values >500 MΩ at 500 VDC, confirming dielectric integrity. Photographic documentation of all examined components is cataloged under NTSB reference numbers 2020-001-001 through 2020-001-045. Environmental stress screening of the CSMU was performed per RTCA DO-160G Section 4, Category A, confirming operational functionality across a temperature range of -54°C to +70°C and vibration profiles up to 15 g RMS.

4. DATA ANALYSIS
The recovered FDR data encompasses 1,842 seconds of continuous recording, beginning at 09:45:12 Pacific Standard Time (PST) and terminating at 10:15:54 PST. Parameter validation was performed against OEM calibration curves and sensor transfer functions. All recorded values fell within the specified operational ranges of the respective transducers. Linearity checks for the barometric altimeter (P/N 10-60100-1) and inertial reference unit (P/N 066-01050-0001) confirmed deviations of <0.5% full scale, well within the ±1.0% tolerance specified in the Sikorsky Avionics Installation Manual.

Initial cruise conditions at 09:45:12 indicated a barometric altitude of 1,200 ft MSL, indicated airspeed of 145 knots, and a stabilized pitch attitude of +1.2° nose-up. Rotor RPM (NR) was maintained at 100.2% ±0.3%, with engine torque values oscillating between 85% and 92% of maximum continuous rating. The Stability Augmentation System (SAS) was engaged, with rate damping gains operating within nominal parameters. No flight control system faults or warning flags were recorded.

Between 09:47:30 and 09:52:15, the aircraft exhibited a gradual descent to 850 ft MSL, accompanied by increasing pitch and roll oscillations. Pitch attitude deviations reached ±4.2°, exceeding the standard stabilized flight envelope of ±2.0°. Roll excursions peaked at 18.5° left bank, with corresponding lateral acceleration spikes of +0.6g and -0.3g. Vertical acceleration data recorded transient peaks of +1.8g and -0.4g, consistent with atmospheric turbulence and pilot control inputs. Collective position increased by 12% over an 8-second interval, correlating with a 15-knot reduction in indicated airspeed.

In the final 15 seconds of recorded data (10:15:39–10:15:54), the aircraft experienced a rapid descent rate exceeding 1,800 ft/min, with pitch attitude transitioning to -12.5° nose-down. Rotor RPM remained stable at 99.8%, and engine torque values stayed within 88–91% limits, indicating no powerplant degradation or fuel flow interruption. The FDR recorded no system warnings, fault codes, or parameter dropouts. Data integrity remained uncompromised throughout the event sequence.

Comparative analysis with normal operational parameters, as defined in the S-76B Flight Manual (P/N 76B-FM-001, Rev 18), confirms that the observed flight control inputs and attitude deviations fall outside standard handling qualities envelopes. The absence of automated trim or pitch augmentation systems, such as those found in fixed-wing platforms utilizing a Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System, necessitates continuous manual control input to maintain stabilized flight in instrument meteorological conditions. All recorded parameters were cross-referenced with radar altimetry and terrain elevation data, confirming a progressive loss of terrain clearance. GPS-derived position data, synchronized via the 1 PPS timing signal, placed the aircraft at 34.1124° N, 118.6891° W at the final data point, with a ground track of 248° magnetic.

5. SUMMARY
The examination of the L-3 Communications FA2100-1020 flight data recorder and associated structural components yielded the following technical findings:
- The crash-survivable memory unit sustained no structural compromise or data corruption, with a validated bit error rate of <0.001%.
- Physical examination of the FDR housing and mounting hardware revealed impact deformation consistent with high-energy terrain contact, with no evidence of pre-impact mechanical failure or fatigue cracking.
- Metallurgical and chemical analysis of the Ti-6Al-4V mounting bracket confirmed material properties within AMS 4928 specifications, exhibiting ductile overload fracture morphology.
- Electrical harness continuity and insulation resistance testing confirmed signal path integrity, with no evidence of arcing, short circuits, or dielectric breakdown.
- Flight data analysis indicates a progressive deviation from stabilized flight parameters, characterized by increasing pitch and roll oscillations, elevated vertical acceleration, and sustained collective input in the final 15 seconds of recording.
- All recorded parameters remained within sensor calibration limits, with no system warnings, fault flags, or powerplant anomalies detected.
- The S-76B flight control architecture relies on conventional mechanical-hydraulic actuation with stability augmentation, without automated pitch-trim or maneuvering augmentation systems.
- Data extraction, validation, and structural evaluation were conducted in accordance with SAE AS8034, TSO-C124a, ASTM E3/E407, and applicable FAA engineering standards.
These findings are strictly factual and document the physical condition, data integrity, and recorded flight parameters of the examined components. No operational, environmental, or human factors are addressed within this report.

## [sc-0_witness_testimony_042] Witness Testimony

> **Type:** witness_testimony | **Reliability:** 0.744 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

INTERVIEW OF DAVID R. CHEN, FORMER OPERATIONS COORDINATOR / MAINTENANCE LIAISON, ISLAND EXPRESS HELICOPTERS
Date: November 12, 2024
Time: 10:15 AM PST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Los Angeles, California
Interviewer: NTSB Investigator J. Miller

Q: Mr. Chen, thank you for making the time to speak with us today. For the record, could you please state your full name and your position with Island Express Helicopters at the time of the January 26, 2020 accident?

A: Yeah, sure. David R. Chen. I was the Senior Operations Coordinator, and I also handled maintenance liaison duties for the fleet. So, basically, I sat between dispatch, the line pilots, and the hangar crew. I’d been with the company for about six years by that point.

Q: Can you walk me through your morning on January 26th? What was your first indication that something was wrong?

A: Right. So, I got into the ops center around 06:30, maybe 06:40. The weather was… it was already iffy. We had that heavy marine layer pushing inland, fog rolling over the Santa Monica Mountains. I remember checking the METARs for Burbank and Van Nuys, and the ceilings were dropping fast. The flight was scheduled for a 09:00 departure, I think. It was a private charter, VIP transport. The pilot was… I don’t want to say his name, but he was one of our senior guys. Very experienced, good track record. We did the pre-flight coordination, weight and balance, fuel load, all that. Standard stuff.
Around 09:15, maybe 09:20, they pushed off. I was monitoring the flight following on our internal tracking system. At first, it was fine. They were tracking along the 101 corridor, heading northwest. But then, around 09:30, 09:35, the weather started closing in. I remember looking at the radar overlay on my screen and seeing this big green-to-yellow blob just sitting right over the Calabasas area. I tried to get on the company frequency, but… it was just static. Or maybe they were already in the soup. I don’t know. I called dispatch, asked if they had comms. They said negative.

Q: What were you hearing or seeing on the comms or tracking systems as the situation developed?

A: Honestly? Not much. Just… dead air. And then, maybe ten minutes later, I get a call from a local resident. Or maybe it was a ground observer who called the main line. They said they heard a loud, low-frequency thump, like a… like a heavy object hitting the hillside. Not an explosion, just a… a crunch. I remember my stomach just dropped. I pulled up the terrain profile on our flight planning software, and I saw the elevation spiking right where the last known position was. We were looking at, what, 1,200 feet MSL? And the ceiling was probably 400, maybe 300 feet. It’s just… math doesn’t work out.
I mean, we had procedures. We followed FAA Order 8900.1 guidelines for VFR flight following and weather minimums. But when you’re in a helicopter, especially a Sikorsky S-76B, the automation can give you a false sense of security. The autopilot holds altitude, the GPS tracks the route, but it doesn’t see the mountain. You know? It’s not like the MCAS stuff on the 737s where the system actively pushes the nose down based on sensor data. This was just… human factors. Spatial disorientation. The pilot probably thought he could pop out on top, but the layer was too thick, and the terrain was rising faster than he could climb.

Q: You mentioned the S-76B’s systems. Can you elaborate on the aircraft’s configuration and how it relates to the conditions that day?

A: Yeah, sure. The S-76B is a solid machine. Sikorsky built it for offshore and corporate work, so it’s got good basic avionics. We had a Garmin GNS 430, I think, and a two-axis autopilot. It’s not a full glass cockpit like the newer models. The pilot had to manually manage the approach if he lost visual reference. And that’s the thing—when you’re in IMC, your inner ear lies to you. You feel like you’re climbing when you’re actually descending. I’ve flown enough to know that. I mean, I’m not a line pilot, but I’ve got my private ticket, and I’ve done instrument training. You learn real quick that if you don’t trust the gauges, you’re done.
We had maintenance logs, obviously. The aircraft was current. No squawks. We were compliant with all the ADs at the time. I mean, looking back now, with things like AD 2024-02-51 coming out years later, it’s clear the industry’s been pushing for better terrain awareness and stricter VFR-into-IMC protocols. But back in 2020? We were operating under the rules we had. The company had a safety management system, but… it’s hard to enforce a “turn back” when the client’s schedule is tight and the pilot’s got that “get-there-itis.” Not that I’m blaming him. I’m just saying… it’s a systemic thing.

Q: What happened after you received the ground observer’s call?

A: I immediately called 911. Gave them the last known coordinates, the aircraft type, the number of souls on board. I think it was nine. I remember my hands were shaking. I was staring at the tracking screen, watching the little icon just… freeze. Then I heard sirens in the distance, but that was probably just normal traffic on the 101. The fog was so thick you couldn’t see past the fence line at the heliport. I walked outside, just to clear my head, and the air was cold, damp. Smelled like wet eucalyptus and jet fuel from the ramp. I just stood there for a minute, listening. Nothing. Just the wind.
By 10:15, maybe 10:30, the news started breaking. I went back inside, pulled up the NOTAMs, checked the weather again. It was still below VFR minimums. I remember thinking, “He should’ve diverted to Camarillo. Or just landed in a field.” But you don’t know what’s in the cockpit. You don’t know if the altimeter was set right, if the pitot was iced, if… I don’t know. I’m just guessing now.

Q: Were there any specific maintenance or operational directives you were following that day that might be relevant to the investigation?

A: We followed the standard ops manual. We referenced FAA Order 8900.1 for flight following procedures, specifically the sections on VFR weather minimums and pilot decision-making. We had a policy that if the ceiling dropped below 1,000 feet or visibility under three miles, you either divert or hold. But the weather was moving so fast. One minute it’s 1,500, next it’s 600. And the terrain… it’s not flat out there. It’s rolling hills, canyons. You get boxed in.
I’ll be honest, I’m not a regulatory expert. I know enough to keep the logs straight and make sure the aircraft are airworthy. But when it comes to the actual flight ops, that’s on the pilot and the chief pilot. We did our part. The aircraft was maintained per the manufacturer’s recommendations. Sikorsky’s service bulletins were all incorporated. We even had a third-party audit a few months prior. Everything checked out. It’s just… sometimes the rules don’t account for human nature. You push a little too far, you think you can beat the weather, and then… it’s over.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add about that day or the company’s operations?

A: Just that… it stays with you. I still think about it. The silence on the radio, the way the tracking screen just stopped updating. I’ve since moved on to a different role, but I still follow the NTSB reports. I mean, even with newer directives like AD 2024-02-51, it’s a reminder that we can’t just rely on paperwork. You need a culture where pilots feel safe saying “no.” Where dispatch doesn’t pressure them. Where the weather is respected, not negotiated with.
I don’t know if that answers your question, but… that’s what I remember.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Chen. We’ll follow up if we need clarification.

A: Yeah, of course. I’m here to help. Just… do right by them. That’s all I ask.

## [sc-0_regulatory_filing_043] Regulatory Filing

> **Type:** regulatory_filing | **Reliability:** 0.962 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
FLIGHT STANDARDS SERVICE
REGULATORY COMPLIANCE AND SAFETY OVERSIGHT REPORT
DOCKET NO. FAA-2021-0892
NTSB ACCIDENT NUMBER: WPR20MA040
DATE OF OCCURRENCE: JANUARY 26, 2020
PREPARED BY: OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY, REGULATORY ASSESSMENT DIVISION
DISTRIBUTION: NTSB OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY, FAA FLIGHT STANDARDS DISTRICT OFFICE (FSDO) 12, OPERATOR COMPLIANCE FILE

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This document constitutes the formal regulatory compliance assessment and corrective action framework in response to NTSB Safety Recommendations A-21-014 through A-21-018, issued following the fatal terrain collision involving a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter (Registration N72EX) operated by Island Express Helicopters under 14 CFR Part 135. The referenced accident occurred on January 26, 2020, in Calabasas, California, during instrument meteorological conditions (IMC). The investigation determined that the pilot-in-command continued visual flight rules (VFR) operations into an area of deteriorating visibility and rising terrain, resulting in controlled flight into terrain (CFIT). This report addresses applicable regulatory provisions under 14 CFR Part 135, Subpart E, and evaluates the airworthiness, operational control, and training compliance posture of the operator and manufacturer. All references herein are cross-referenced with FAA Docket No. FAA-2021-0892 and NTSB Accident Number WPR20MA040.

2. BACKGROUND
The regulatory framework governing Part 135 rotorcraft operations establishes baseline requirements for weather minimums, flight locating, and operational control. Specifically, 14 CFR § 135.215 and § 135.225 prescribe VFR weather minimums for fixed-wing and rotorcraft operations, respectively, mandating minimum visibility and cloud clearance parameters. 14 CFR § 135.181 requires operators to maintain flight locating procedures sufficient to determine the position and status of each aircraft. Furthermore, 14 CFR § 135.154 mandates terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS) installation for Part 135 fixed-wing aircraft, but explicitly excludes rotorcraft from this requirement, creating a documented regulatory asymmetry.

Historically, the National Transportation Safety Board has issued multiple safety recommendations addressing VFR-into-IMC encounters, spatial disorientation, and terrain avoidance deficiencies in rotorcraft operations. Prior recommendations, including NTSB A-19-001 and A-19-003, emphasized the need for mandatory helicopter terrain awareness and warning systems (HTAWS), enhanced weather decision-making protocols, and standardized operational control center (OCC) intervention authorities. The Federal Aviation Administration has historically addressed these concerns through Advisory Circular 135-14B and voluntary compliance programs; however, the absence of codified regulatory mandates has resulted in inconsistent fleet-wide implementation.

The certification and operational oversight paradigms established following the review of the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) have further informed this assessment. While MCAS is a fixed-wing flight control augmentation system, the regulatory scrutiny applied to its certification, pilot training requirements, and system transparency has established new FAA oversight precedents regarding automated dependency, human-machine interface design, and the necessity of explicit pilot authority in automated system management. These regulatory principles are directly applicable to rotorcraft flight management systems, navigation augmentation, and terrain avoidance automation, particularly in high-workload VFR-to-IMC transition scenarios.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive review of Island Express Helicopters’ operational records, training curricula, and maintenance documentation indicates that the Operator maintained a valid Part 135 certificate and complied with baseline airworthiness directives and scheduled maintenance requirements. However, the investigation identified systemic deficiencies in operational control authority, real-time weather monitoring, and pilot decision-making protocols. The pilot-in-command elected to continue VFR flight into deteriorating meteorological conditions, contravening 14 CFR § 135.225 and the Operator’s approved Operations Specifications. The OCC lacked the procedural authority and real-time data integration necessary to mandate flight diversion or termination, resulting in an unmitigated progression into IMC.

Regulatory oversight actions conducted by the responsible FSDO revealed historical compliance with recordkeeping, crew scheduling, and maintenance tracking. Nevertheless, the audit identified critical gaps in the Operator’s risk management framework, specifically regarding inadvertent IMC recognition, spatial disorientation mitigation, and terrain avoidance automation. The Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions for navigation and weather radar systems permitted dispatch with degraded capabilities under specific conditions, which may have inadvertently normalized operational risk acceptance.

The regulatory framework exhibits a documented deficiency in mandatory terrain avoidance requirements for Part 135 rotorcraft. Unlike fixed-wing operations governed by 14 CFR § 135.154, rotorcraft operators are not required to install HTAWS, resulting in fleet-wide variability in terrain avoidance capabilities. Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation’s original equipment configuration for the S-76B did not include integrated HTAWS as a standard requirement under the applicable Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS). Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) installations remain optional, and the manufacturer’s service bulletins regarding terrain avoidance upgrades have not been universally adopted across the operator fleet.

Furthermore, the regulatory analysis identifies a training paradigm gap. Current Part 135 pilot training requirements under 14 CFR § 135.335 and § 135.337 do not mandate standardized, simulator-based inadvertent IMC recovery training or automated system dependency management. Drawing upon the regulatory lessons established during the MCAS certification review, the FAA recognizes that over-reliance on basic flight instrumentation without adequate terrain and weather avoidance automation, coupled with insufficient training for automated system limitations, creates unacceptable operational risk. The absence of explicit pilot authority protocols for weather avoidance and terrain clearance in high-density airspace further compounds this vulnerability.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
To address the identified regulatory gaps and ensure compliance with established safety standards, the following corrective actions and compliance timelines are mandated:

a. Mandatory HTAWS Installation: All Part 135 rotorcraft operating in Class B, C, D, or E airspace, or within 50 nautical miles of designated mountainous terrain, shall be equipped with an FAA-approved Helicopter Terrain Awareness and Warning System meeting TSO-C194 standards. Operators must submit installation plans to the responsible FSDO within 90 days of this directive. Full compliance shall be achieved within 18 months.

b. Operational Control Center Enhancement: Operators shall revise their Operations Specifications to establish mandatory OCC intervention protocols. Real-time weather data uplinks, flight tracking telemetry, and explicit OCC authority to mandate flight diversion or termination shall be integrated into standard operating procedures. Compliance verification shall be completed within 12 months.

c. Pilot Training Curriculum Revision: Training programs shall be updated to include standardized, simulator-based inadvertent IMC recognition and recovery training, spatial disorientation mitigation, and automated system dependency management. Training modules shall explicitly address human-machine interface limitations and pilot authority in automated navigation environments, consistent with post-MCAS regulatory guidance. Initial and recurrent training compliance shall be achieved within 12 months.

d. MMEL Dispatch Provision Review: The FAA shall initiate a rulemaking action to revise MMEL dispatch provisions for Part 135 rotorcraft, restricting dispatch with degraded weather radar or terrain avoidance capabilities in high-risk operational environments. A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) shall be published within 6 months.

e. Follow-Up Inspection and Review Schedule: The responsible FSDO shall conduct quarterly compliance reporting reviews, biannual ramp inspections, and annual operational audits. Operators shall submit documented evidence of HTAWS installation, training program revisions, and OCC protocol implementation to the FAA Flight Standards Service. Non-compliance shall result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR § 13.11 and § 13.19.

This regulatory compliance framework is issued under the authority of 49 U.S.C. § 44701 and 14 CFR Part 135. All referenced entities, including Island Express Helicopters, Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation, and applicable equipment certification bodies, shall coordinate with the FAA Flight Standards Service to ensure timely implementation. Failure to comply with the stipulated timelines shall result in immediate operational restrictions and potential certificate suspension.

AUTHORIZED BY:
FLIGHT STANDARDS SERVICE, REGULATORY ASSESSMENT DIVISION
FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
DOCKET NO. FAA-2021-0892

HEADLINE: Nine Dead After Helicopter Crashes in Calabasas Hills Amid Dense Fog

BYLINE: Marcus Chen, The Pacific Chronicle
DATELINE: CALABASAS, Calif. —

Nine people perished Sunday morning when a charter helicopter slammed into a steep hillside in Calabasas, California, as thick fog blanketed the region. The aircraft, operated by Island Express, was en route to a local sports facility when it went down in treacherous weather conditions, leaving no survivors.

Preliminary data indicates the pilot continued flying under visual flight rules into an area of rapidly deteriorating visibility and rising terrain, a scenario that often leads to fatal spatial disorientation. The crash has triggered an immediate federal probe and sent shockwaves through the local community, prompting emergency crews to work through the night to secure the rugged crash site and begin recovery operations.

“Our hearts are broken for the families and friends of those on board,” said a spokesperson for Island Express, the charter operator. “We are cooperating fully with investigators and providing all available maintenance and flight records.” The National Transportation Safety Board, commonly referred to as the Safety Board, dispatched a rapid-response team to the scene. “We are treating this as a major accident investigation,” said the agency’s Investigator-in-Charge during a Sunday evening briefing. “Our priority is determining the exact sequence of events and the factors that contributed to this tragedy.” The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) confirmed it is reviewing the operator’s certification and the pilot’s recent flight logs. “We stand ready to support the investigation and will take any necessary regulatory action based on the findings,” an FAA representative stated.

The aircraft involved was a Sikorsky S-76B, a twin-engine helicopter widely used for corporate transport and emergency medical services. Manufactured by Sikorsky Aircraft, the model has a long operational history and is known for its reliability and performance. The flight originated in Orange County and was bound for the Calabasas area, a route frequently flown by charter services catering to high-profile clients. Under standard aviation protocols, pilots operating under visual flight rules (VFR) must maintain clear sight of the ground and horizon. When weather conditions drop below minimum visibility thresholds—known as instrument meteorological conditions (IMC)—pilots are required to either divert, land, or transition to instrument flight rules, which rely on cockpit navigation systems rather than outside visual references.

Aviation safety experts note that continuing VFR flight into IMC remains one of the leading causes of fatal helicopter accidents. “When a pilot loses visual reference in fog or low clouds, the inner ear can send false signals to the brain, creating a dangerous illusion of level flight while the aircraft is actually descending or banking,” explained Dr. Elena Rostova, an aviation human factors specialist at a major research university. “It’s a well-documented phenomenon, but it’s incredibly difficult to overcome without proper instrument training and strict adherence to weather minimums.” While the investigation focuses on pilot decision-making and weather data, industry analysts are also examining broader regulatory frameworks. Some experts have drawn comparisons to recent fixed-wing safety initiatives, noting that while systems like the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) were designed to address specific aerodynamic handling issues in commercial jets, helicopter safety relies more heavily on pilot training, terrain awareness, and strict weather compliance. The FAA has recently updated several airworthiness directives, including AD 2024-02-51, which mandates enhanced weather monitoring equipment for certain commercial rotorcraft, signaling a push toward stricter operational standards across the industry.

The identities of the passengers have not been fully released, but local officials confirmed the group included a prominent sports figure, family members, and the pilot. Grief has already begun to ripple through the community. “They were everything to us,” said a relative of one of the passengers, speaking through tears outside a makeshift memorial near the crash site. “We just want answers, and we want to know they didn’t suffer.” Vigils have been organized across Southern California, with fans, neighbors, and local leaders gathering to honor the victims and leave flowers, jerseys, and handwritten notes.

The Sikorsky S-76 series has maintained a strong safety record over decades of service, though helicopter operations in mountainous, coastal regions like Southern California have historically faced weather-related challenges. The Safety Board has previously investigated several VFR-into-IMC incidents involving charter helicopters, often citing inadequate weather briefings, operational pressure to complete flights, and gaps in instrument proficiency. Commercial carriers like Southwest Airlines have long implemented strict weather diversion policies and advanced terrain warning systems, practices that helicopter operators are increasingly adopting as the industry modernizes and regulatory scrutiny intensifies.

Recovery teams are working to retrieve the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, which will provide critical insights into the final minutes of the flight. The NTSB expects to release a preliminary report within 30 days, with a full investigation likely taking 12 to 18 months. Until then, the aviation community and grieving families await answers, hoping the tragedy will lead to meaningful changes in how charter flights navigate unpredictable weather and protect those who trust them with their lives.

## [sc-0_expert_deposition_045] Expert Deposition

> **Type:** expert_deposition | **Reliability:** 0.713 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Operator Safety & Engineering Division, acting as a designated party to the investigation under the authority of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB). Our role in this proceeding is to provide an independent, evidence-based technical assessment of the operational, human factors, and systems-related elements that contributed to the January 26, 2020, accident involving a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter in Calabasas, California. The scope of this document encompasses a detailed review of flight data, meteorological conditions, pilot decision-making pathways, and the broader safety management framework governing commercial rotorcraft operations. 

As subject-matter experts in aviation human factors, operational risk management, and rotorcraft systems engineering, we submit this analysis to assist the Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) and the Board in synthesizing the complex interplay of environmental, technological, and procedural variables that culminated in this tragedy. Our position is grounded in docketed evidence, peer-reviewed human factors research, and comparative industry safety data. While we recognize the profound loss of life and the inherent difficulty of reconstructing real-time cognitive processes under extreme stress, this submission advocates for a systemic, rather than singular, understanding of the accident sequence. We further emphasize that the lessons derived from this event must inform proactive regulatory alignment, technological modernization, and operator-level safety management practices across the rotorcraft sector.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

The accident flight departed John Wayne Airport (KSNA) at approximately 09:06 PST on January 26, 2020, bound for Camarillo Airport (KCMA). The aircraft, a Sikorsky S-76B (N72EX), was operating under Title 14 CFR Part 91. At approximately 09:40 PST, the helicopter entered a region of deteriorating visibility and rising terrain in the Santa Monica Mountains. Radar and flight data recorder (FDR) telemetry, as documented in Docket Exhibit 12B, indicate a gradual descent from approximately 1,200 feet MSL to terrain impact at 09:45 PST. The pilot had been operating under visual flight rules (VFR) and elected to continue into instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) without executing a published diversion or executing a 180-degree escape maneuver.

Weather data from the National Weather Service and onboard meteorological observations confirm a rapid deterioration in ceiling and visibility, with cloud bases dropping below 500 feet AGL and visibility reduced to less than one mile in localized fog and low stratus. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) air traffic control transcripts (Docket Exhibit 8A) reveal that the pilot requested and received a special VFR clearance but did not receive real-time terrain or weather avoidance guidance. The aircraft was not equipped with a Helicopter Terrain Awareness and Warning System (HTAWS), which, while not mandated for Part 91 operations at the time, represents a critical gap in situational awareness technology for mountainous, low-visibility environments.

Maintenance records (Docket Exhibit 15C) confirm the airframe and powerplants were in compliance with all applicable airworthiness directives and manufacturer service bulletins. The pilot held a commercial certificate with instrument rating and logged over 8,000 total flight hours, including extensive rotorcraft experience. However, training records indicate limited recent practice in simulated IMC escape procedures and no documented recurrent training on spatial disorientation mitigation in high-workload, low-visibility scenarios.

The IIC’s preliminary findings, as outlined in the Board’s public docket, correctly identify the continuation of VFR flight into IMC as the primary operational trigger. Our analysis expands upon this by examining the cognitive degradation pathways, the absence of integrated terrain alerting, and the operational risk management deficiencies that permitted the flight to proceed into a known high-risk corridor under marginal weather conditions.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The accident sequence is best understood through a multi-layered technical framework that integrates human factors, avionics architecture, and operational risk modeling. The FDR data reveals a consistent, uncorrected descent profile with minimal control inputs during the final three minutes of flight. Pitch and roll attitudes remained within nominal limits until approximately 15 seconds prior to impact, at which point a rapid nose-down pitch and left bank were recorded. This kinematic signature is highly consistent with vestibular-induced spatial disorientation, specifically the somatogravic illusion, wherein linear acceleration in low-visibility conditions creates a false perception of nose-up attitude, prompting compensatory forward control inputs.

Human factors research consistently demonstrates that VFR-into-IMC transitions degrade pilot situational awareness within 18 to 30 seconds of visual reference loss. Without immediate cross-checking of primary flight instruments, the vestibular system dominates spatial perception. The pilot’s decision to continue rather than divert or execute an instrument escape maneuver reflects a well-documented cognitive bias known as plan continuation error, exacerbated by operational pressure, passenger expectations, and inadequate risk assessment protocols. The absence of a formalized go/no-go matrix for marginal weather, combined with limited recurrent IMC training, created a permissive environment for this error cascade.

From an engineering perspective, the S-76B’s avionics suite, while robust for its era, lacks integrated terrain mapping and predictive alerting capabilities. Modern HTAWS systems utilize digital elevation models, GPS positioning, and aircraft performance envelopes to generate timely, unambiguous warnings. The absence of such a system in this aircraft meant the pilot relied entirely on visual terrain references and sectional chart interpretation, both of which are rendered ineffective in IMC. Comparative analysis with industry standards, including RTCA DO-315A and EASA CS-29, confirms that terrain awareness technology is no longer optional for safe operations in complex topography.

It is instructive to contrast this rotorcraft accident with fixed-wing automation dependency cases, such as those involving the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS). While MCAS is entirely inapplicable to the S-76B’s flight control architecture, the underlying human factors principle remains relevant: over-reliance on automated or procedural safeguards without adequate pilot training and system transparency can create latent vulnerabilities. In rotorcraft operations, where automation is intentionally limited to preserve pilot authority and tactile feedback, the burden of situational awareness falls squarely on the flight crew. This underscores the necessity of rigorous IMC transition training, standardized escape procedures, and technological augmentation that supports, rather than replaces, pilot decision-making.

Regulatory frameworks have historically lagged behind technological capability. The FAA’s Order 8900.1, Volume 3, Chapter 18, provides guidance for inspectors evaluating operator weather minimums and risk mitigation strategies. However, the manual’s prescriptive nature often fails to account for dynamic, localized weather phenomena and the cognitive load imposed on single-pilot operations. Recent regulatory actions, such as Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-51, demonstrate a shift toward proactive, data-driven airworthiness mandates. While this directive addresses a different platform, its underlying philosophy—anticipating failure modes before they manifest in operational environments—should be applied to rotorcraft terrain awareness and weather avoidance systems.

Operational risk management practices across the aviation industry offer valuable benchmarks. Southwest Airlines Co, for example, has implemented predictive risk analytics and dynamic flight planning tools that integrate real-time meteorological data, terrain profiles, and historical incident trends. While helicopter operations differ significantly in mission profile and airspace utilization, the core SMS principles—hazard identification, risk assessment, and continuous monitoring—are universally applicable. The operator in this accident lacked a mature, data-driven SMS capable of flagging high-risk route segments under marginal weather conditions. Implementing predictive risk modeling, coupled with mandatory HTAWS and standardized IMC escape training, would have materially altered the outcome.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on a comprehensive review of docketed evidence, flight data, meteorological records, and human factors research, our position is that the January 26, 2020, accident resulted from a convergence of operational, cognitive, and technological deficiencies. The primary contributing factor was the pilot’s decision to continue VFR flight into deteriorating IMC, compounded by spatial disorientation and the absence of terrain awareness technology. Secondary factors include inadequate recurrent training on IMC escape procedures, insufficient operational risk assessment protocols, and a regulatory environment that permitted Part 91 operators to fly complex terrain routes without mandatory HTAWS or predictive weather integration.

We acknowledge the inherent complexity of real-time decision-making under pressure. Pilots are routinely tasked with balancing mission objectives, passenger expectations, and dynamic environmental variables. However, the aviation safety ecosystem must evolve to support these decisions with robust technological safeguards, standardized training curricula, and proactive risk management frameworks. The continuation of VFR flight into IMC remains one of the most persistent and lethal hazards in rotorcraft operations. Addressing it requires a systemic approach that integrates engineering, human factors, and regulatory alignment.

We recommend the following safety improvements:
- Mandatory installation of HTAWS or equivalent terrain awareness systems for all commercial and high-risk Part 91 rotorcraft operations.
- Standardized, recurrent IMC escape training with emphasis on vestibular disorientation mitigation, instrument cross-checking, and automated escape maneuver execution.
- Implementation of predictive risk modeling and dynamic weather routing tools integrated into flight planning and dispatch systems.
- Regulatory updates to FAA Order 8900.1 to require operators to maintain documented, data-driven weather risk matrices for all route segments, with mandatory diversion protocols when thresholds are exceeded.
- Industry-wide data sharing initiatives to track VFR-into-IMC near-misses and develop targeted training interventions.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In response to the findings of this investigation and in alignment with the Board’s safety recommendations, our organization has implemented several immediate and long-term corrective actions. Fleet-wide avionics upgrades have been initiated, with HTAWS installation completed on 85% of our rotorcraft fleet and full compliance scheduled within 18 months. We have revised our Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) to mandate a hard diversion threshold when visibility drops below 3 statute miles or ceiling falls below 1,000 feet AGL in mountainous terrain, regardless of special VFR clearance status.

Training programs have been overhauled to include quarterly simulator-based IMC escape scenarios, with a focus on spatial disorientation recognition, instrument scan discipline, and automated recovery techniques. All pilots now undergo biannual human factors briefings covering cognitive bias, plan continuation error, and stress-induced decision degradation. Additionally, we have integrated a predictive risk analytics platform that evaluates route-specific weather, terrain, and historical incident data prior to flight release, providing dispatchers and pilots with real-time risk scoring and alternative routing options.

Looking forward, we propose the following industry-wide improvements:
- Collaboration with Sikorsky and other manufacturers to develop next-generation rotorcraft-specific terrain alerting systems that account for low-altitude flight profiles, autorotation envelopes, and dynamic obstacle mapping.
- Advocacy for regulatory harmonization that aligns Part 91 and Part 135 terrain awareness requirements, eliminating operational disparities that compromise safety.
- Establishment of a national rotorcraft safety data exchange, modeled after fixed-wing industry initiatives, to enable real-time sharing of weather-related near-misses, training effectiveness metrics, and technology performance data.
- Integration of AI-assisted weather forecasting and microclimate modeling into flight planning systems, reducing reliance on static METAR/TAF data in rapidly changing environments.

We recognize that no single intervention can eliminate the risks inherent to aviation. However, by combining technological modernization, rigorous human factors training, and proactive safety management, the industry can significantly reduce the likelihood of VFR-into-IMC accidents. We stand ready to collaborate with the NTSB, the FAA, manufacturers, and fellow operators to implement these recommendations and advance rotorcraft safety to the highest achievable standard.
