## [sc-0_internal_memo_054] Internal Memo

> **Type:** internal_memo | **Reliability:** 0.771 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

TO: Flight Operations Directorate, Maintenance Control, Training Standards Division
FROM: Chief Safety Officer / Aviation Safety Management System (SMS) Office
DATE: 14 February 2020
SUBJECT: SAFETY COMMUNICATION: VFR-INTO-IMC MITIGATION, TERRAIN AWARENESS, AND AUTOMATION MONITORING PROTOCOLS
REF: SMS-2020-014, OPS-BUL-2019-088, MNT-WO-2020-0412

PURPOSE:
This bulletin establishes immediate operational, maintenance, and training directives to mitigate VFR-into-IMC risk, reinforce terrain avoidance protocols, and standardize automation monitoring across all company aircraft. Compliance is mandatory for all flight crews, dispatch personnel, and maintenance technicians effective immediately.

BACKGROUND:
On 26 January 2020, a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter impacted terrain in Calabasas, California, during instrument meteorological conditions. All nine persons on board were fatally injured. Preliminary data indicates the flight continued under visual flight rules into deteriorating visibility while navigating rising terrain, resulting in spatial disorientation and loss of control. The NTSB has opened a formal investigation, and early telemetry confirms a rapid descent profile consistent with uncontrolled flight into terrain (CFIT).

Our internal risk assessments have identified similar operational vulnerabilities across our mixed fleet, particularly in rotorcraft and light twin-engine operations where marginal weather and terrain proximity are routine. The National Transportation Safety Board’s preliminary findings align with historical SMS data showing that delayed transition to instrument references remains a leading causal factor in CFIT events. Additionally, the Lead Investigator has emphasized the critical role of pilot-system interaction during degraded visual environments.

While the S-76B accident involves manual flight control degradation, our organization must also address parallel risks associated with automated flight control equipment. Recent fleet-wide reviews of the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) architecture and pilot response protocols have highlighted systemic gaps in automation monitoring and manual override proficiency. The Principal Investigator’s cross-fleet analysis confirms that overreliance on augmentation logic, combined with inadequate manual flight currency, compounds spatial disorientation risk during unexpected environmental transitions.

DETAILS:
The following directives are effective immediately and supersede conflicting guidance in OPS-BUL-2019-088 and MNT-WO-2020-0412.

1. Weather Minimums and Decision Gates
   - All VFR operations must adhere to revised minimums per SMS-2020-014, Section 4.2.
   - Dispatch and flight crews will implement a hard “go/no-go” decision gate at 10 NM from known terrain features when visibility drops below 3 SM or ceiling falls below 1,500 ft AGL.
   - If IMC is encountered or anticipated, crews must execute an immediate 180-degree turn or divert to the nearest approved alternate. Continued flight into deteriorating conditions is strictly prohibited.

2. Terrain Awareness and Warning System (TAWS) Verification
   - Maintenance Control will issue Work Order MNT-WO-2020-0589 to verify TAWS/EGPWS database currency and sensor calibration on all aircraft.
   - Technicians must inspect P/N 7741-C terrain database modules and confirm software revision matches the latest FAA-approved cycle (Cycle 2020-02).
   - Any discrepancy requires immediate grounding until corrective action is logged in the maintenance tracking system.

3. Automation Monitoring and Manual Flight Proficiency
   - Flight crews will complete a mandatory review of augmentation equipment behavior, with specific emphasis on MCAS response characteristics and manual trim override procedures.
   - The assigned investigator’s preliminary report notes that delayed recognition of system-induced pitch changes directly contributed to loss of control in multiple recent events.
   - All pilots must demonstrate proficiency in manual flight recovery from unexpected pitch/roll deviations during the next recurrent training cycle.

4. Training and Simulator Requirements
   - Training Standards Division will integrate a new VFR-into-IMC scenario into all Level D simulator sessions by 15 March 2020.
   - Scenarios will include rapid visibility degradation, rising terrain proximity, and simulated augmentation system anomalies.
   - Instructors will evaluate crew decision-making, instrument cross-check discipline, and manual control recovery techniques.

5. Maintenance and Airworthiness Directives
   - All aircraft equipped with flight control augmentation software must undergo a functional check per MNT-PROC-2020-031.
   - Technicians will verify sensor alignment, trim actuator response, and warning system annunciation.
   - Results must be documented in the aircraft logbook and uploaded to the central maintenance database within 48 hours of completion.

ACTION REQUIRED:
1. Flight Operations Directorate: Update all flight planning software with revised weather decision gates and terrain proximity alerts by 21 February 2020. Distribute updated quick-reference cards to all flight crews.
2. Maintenance Control: Execute Work Order MNT-WO-2020-0589 across the entire fleet. Complete all TAWS database verifications and augmentation system functional checks by 28 February 2020. Report completion status to the SMS Office via Form SMS-2020-014A.
3. Training Standards Division: Revise simulator syllabi to include the new VFR-into-IMC and automation anomaly modules. Schedule all active pilots for completion by 31 March 2020. Submit training compliance roster to the Chief Safety Officer by 5 April 2020.
4. All Personnel: Acknowledge receipt of this bulletin via the internal safety portal within 72 hours. Failure to acknowledge will result in temporary suspension of flight or maintenance duties until compliance is verified.

The Board continues to gather data, and our organization will adjust procedures as additional findings are released. Until then, strict adherence to these directives is required to maintain operational safety and regulatory compliance. Direct all technical questions to the SMS Office or your respective department lead.

## [sc-0_preliminary_report_055] Preliminary Report

> **Type:** preliminary_report | **Reliability:** 0.915 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. SYNOPSIS
On January 26, 2020, at approximately 0945 Pacific Standard Time, a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter operated by Island Express impacted mountainous terrain in Calabasas, California, resulting in the fatal injury of all nine persons on board. Initial information indicates the flight was operating under visual flight rules when it encountered instrument meteorological conditions and continued into an area of reduced visibility and rising terrain. This preliminary document outlines early-stage factual data, establishes the investigative scope, and records procedural decisions implemented by the National Transportation Safety Board; all information contained herein is subject to revision as the investigation progresses.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information gathered from the accident site, air traffic control recordings, and operator dispatch logs indicates the rotorcraft departed John Wayne Airport (SNA) en route to Camarillo Airport (CMA). Radar track data suggests the aircraft maintained a generally southeasterly course before executing a westward deviation into the Santa Monica Mountains. Initial witness accounts collected by first responders and local law enforcement describe low cloud ceilings, dense fog, and intermittent rotorcraft noise, with several observers noting a sudden cessation of engine and rotor sounds consistent with a rapid descent. Weather observations from nearby automated surface observing systems and pilot reports compiled during the initial response phase indicate deteriorating visibility and cloud bases at or below 1,000 feet above ground level along the flight corridor.

Preliminary examination of the wreckage distribution and impact signatures revealed a high-energy, terrain-impact event with localized post-impact fire. The main rotor system, fuselage, and empennage were substantially fragmented across a steep, heavily vegetated slope. Initial recovery operations secured the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR), both of which sustained varying degrees of thermal and impact damage. Data extraction and readout procedures are currently underway at the Board’s Vehicle Recorders Laboratory, with initial memory module imaging indicating partial data retention. Maintenance records provided by the operator suggest the aircraft was current on required inspections and service bulletins at the time of the accident. The investigation team is reviewing compliance with applicable Federal Aviation Administration maintenance directives, including a historical applicability assessment of Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-51, to establish a complete maintenance and modification baseline for the airframe. Additionally, the operational status, training records, and assigned duties of the second in command (SIC) are being evaluated against standard crew resource management protocols. All preliminary observations remain subject to change pending comprehensive laboratory analysis and cross-referencing with additional data sources.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The NTSB has activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical, operational, and human performance aspects of this accident. The Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Human Performance, and Weather groups have been formally established and deployed to the field. Parties to the investigation include representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration, Sikorsky Aircraft, the operator, and relevant pilot and maintenance organizations. Each party has been assigned specific technical responsibilities under the direct supervision of the respective NTSB group chair, with all activities governed by established party agreements and chain-of-custody protocols.

Evidence secured to date includes the flight recorders, select wreckage components, maintenance logs, pilot training files, and air traffic control communications. The Systems group is conducting a detailed review of the helicopter’s avionics suite, navigation equipment, and flight control architecture. As part of a comprehensive systems evaluation, investigators are cataloging all installed augmentation equipment and verifying that no MCAS (Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System) or similar automated pitch-trim architectures were present on this rotorcraft type, ensuring accurate system mapping for subsequent performance analysis. The Operations group is cross-referencing flight planning documents, dispatch records, and company guidance against FAA Order 8900.1 to assess standard operational practices, risk assessment frameworks, and decision-making protocols applicable to VFR flight in marginal weather. All physical evidence has been photographed, tagged, and transported to secure storage facilities pending detailed metallurgical, structural, and systems examinations. Preliminary data indicates that no immediate mechanical anomalies have been identified, though this assessment remains strictly provisional.

4. NEXT STEPS
Planned investigative activities over the coming weeks include the completion of flight recorder data readouts, detailed structural and metallurgical examinations of recovered components, and comprehensive interviews with operational personnel, air traffic controllers, and meteorological service staff. The Human Performance group will conduct a thorough review of crew duty times, fatigue factors, medical histories, and training curricula to better understand operational decision-making under evolving weather conditions. The Weather group will reconstruct the meteorological environment along the flight path using satellite imagery, ground-based radar, and numerical weather prediction models to characterize the visibility, cloud ceiling, and wind shear conditions encountered during the flight.

The investigation will also include a systematic review of the operator’s safety management practices, dispatch procedures, and compliance with regulatory guidance. All findings will be integrated into a comprehensive factual report, which will undergo internal peer review and party comment prior to finalization. The Board will issue periodic public updates as significant milestones are reached, with a preliminary factual report anticipated within 12 to 18 months. It is emphasized that all current assessments are preliminary, and no conclusions regarding operational decisions, equipment performance, or probable cause have been established. The investigation remains ongoing, and all data will be evaluated with rigorous objectivity, with final determinations reserved for the conclusion of the full investigative process.

## [sc-0_investigation_report_056] Investigation Report

> **Type:** investigation_report | **Reliability:** 0.985 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On January 26, 2020, at approximately 09:45 Pacific Standard Time (PST), a helicopter impacted mountainous terrain in the vicinity of Calabasas, California. The accident site was located at coordinates 34°08'12.5"N, 118°41'38.2"W, at an elevation of approximately 1,200 feet mean sea level (MSL). The impact occurred within a steep, brush-covered canyon characterized by a 35-degree upslope gradient. Local time at the accident site corresponded to 17:45 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). The terrain surrounding the impact area consisted of chaparral, oak woodland, and exposed rock formations, with elevations rising to 1,700 feet MSL within a 0.5-nautical-mile radius of the primary wreckage distribution.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, bearing United States registration number N72EX. The aircraft was manufactured by Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation and was operated under the commercial certificate of Island Express Helicopters, Inc. (IEH). The operator maintained its principal base of operations at John Wayne Airport (KSNA), Orange County, California. The aircraft was registered to a corporate entity affiliated with the operator and was utilized for on-demand passenger transportation services.

1.3 Nature of the Flight
The flight was conducted under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 135, operating as an on-demand charter flight. The flight plan indicated a point-to-point itinerary originating from John Wayne Airport (KSNA) with a destination of Camarillo Airport (KCMA), Ventura County, California. The flight was not conducted under instrument flight rules (IFR) and was filed and executed as a visual flight rules (VFR) operation. The aircraft was not equipped with, nor was it required to be equipped with, an approved flight data recorder or cockpit voice recorder per 14 CFR 135.152. The flight departed KSNA at 09:06 PST and was en route to KCMA at the time of the accident.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Pilot Qualifications and Certifications
The pilot-in-command held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate with a rotorcraft-helicopter rating, issued on March 14, 2016. The pilot also held a commercial pilot certificate with airplane single-engine and multi-engine land ratings, and a flight instructor certificate for rotorcraft-helicopter. The pilot possessed a type rating for the Sikorsky S-76 series. Medical certification was maintained through a first-class airman medical certificate, issued on November 12, 2019, with no limitations or waivers. The pilot held an instrument rating for helicopters, which was current and valid at the time of the accident. Total flight time recorded in the pilot's logbook was approximately 8,200 hours, with 1,250 hours accumulated in the S-76B.

2.2 Recent Flight Experience and Training Records
Review of the operator's training records indicated that the pilot completed recurrent training and proficiency checks in accordance with 14 CFR 135.293 and 135.297. The most recent line check was conducted on October 18, 2019, and was recorded as satisfactory. The pilot's recent flight experience included 45.2 hours of flight time within the preceding 90 days, with 12.8 hours logged in the S-76B. The pilot's instrument currency was maintained through simulated instrument flight and actual instrument conditions encountered during prior operations. Training records documented completion of a VFR flight into instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) awareness module during the 2019 recurrent training cycle. The module emphasized terrain avoidance, weather minimums, and decision-making protocols for continued VFR flight in deteriorating visibility. No discrepancies or corrective actions were noted in the pilot's training file.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Aircraft Data
The accident aircraft was a Sikorsky S-76B, serial number 760345, manufactured in 1992. The airframe was equipped with two Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6B-36A turboshaft engines, each rated at 650 shaft horsepower. The aircraft's maximum gross weight was 11,700 pounds. At the time of the accident, the aircraft's total time in service was 14,872.4 hours. The airframe had accumulated 1,245.6 hours since its last major overhaul. The aircraft was configured for a standard passenger layout with seating for eight passengers and two crew members. The aircraft was not equipped with a terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS) or a flight data monitoring system, as neither was mandated for Part 135 rotorcraft operations under the applicable regulatory framework at the time.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
Maintenance records were reviewed for compliance with 14 CFR Part 43 and Part 135.411. The aircraft was maintained on a continuous airworthiness maintenance program approved by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The most recent 100-hour inspection was completed on December 14, 2019, with no deferred maintenance items recorded. All applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) were documented as complied with, including AD 2018-12-05 regarding main rotor blade tracking and AD 2019-04-11 regarding engine fuel control unit calibration. The aircraft's logbooks indicated routine component replacements consistent with manufacturer-recommended service life limits. No open maintenance write-ups were present at the time of the accident flight.

3.3 Relevant Systems and Components
The aircraft was equipped with a dual-channel autopilot system, a radar altimeter, and a standard VHF navigation/communication suite. The flight control system utilized conventional mechanical linkages with hydraulic boost for primary control axes. The aircraft was not equipped with a Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System; however, the system was referenced in applicable FAA Order 8900.1 guidance regarding flight control augmentation system training and operational limitations for rotorcraft and fixed-wing aircraft. The radar altimeter was calibrated and functional per maintenance records, with a last calibration date of November 2, 2019. The aircraft's pitot-static system was inspected and leak-checked on December 14, 2019, with no anomalies reported. The engine fire detection and extinguishing systems were tested and recorded as operational during the most recent scheduled maintenance event.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Weather Conditions
On January 26, 2020, a low-pressure system was situated over the eastern Pacific Ocean, with a trailing cold front moving eastward across Southern California. The synoptic pattern produced widespread low ceilings, reduced visibility, and light precipitation across the coastal and inland mountain regions. Surface pressure at the time of the accident was recorded at 1012.3 millibars. Wind direction was variable from 240 to 280 degrees at 5 to 10 knots, with gusts to 15 knots reported at higher elevations. The atmospheric lapse rate indicated stable conditions with a temperature inversion layer present between 1,000 and 1,500 feet MSL.

4.2 METAR/TAF Data and Pilot Reports
The nearest automated weather observing station, located at Van Nuys Airport (KVNY), reported the following METAR at 09:53 PST: 261753Z 27006KT 1/2SM FG BKN003 OVC008 12/10 A2992 RMK AO2 SLP132 T01220100. The observation indicated a ceiling of 300 feet broken, 800 feet overcast, visibility of 0.5 statute miles in fog, temperature 12°C, dew point 10°C, and altimeter setting 29.92 inches of mercury. A terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) issued for KVNY at 05:00 PST predicted continued low ceilings and visibility through 12:00 PST, with gradual improvement expected after 15:00 PST. Pilot reports (PIREPs) received between 09:00 and 09:30 PST indicated widespread IMC conditions along the coastal mountain corridors, with multiple aircraft reporting visibility below 1 statute mile and cloud bases at or below 500 feet AGL.

4.3 Visibility and Ceiling Analysis
Radar-derived precipitation data and satellite imagery confirmed the presence of stratiform cloud cover extending from the Pacific coastline inland to the Santa Monica Mountains. The cloud base was observed to descend progressively from west to east, with the lowest ceilings recorded in the Calabasas and Agoura Hills regions. Visibility within the cloud layer was estimated at less than 0.25 statute miles, with horizontal visibility restricted by fog and low stratus. The terrain elevation in the accident area ranged from 1,000 to 1,700 feet MSL, placing the aircraft within or below the cloud base during the final segment of the flight. The pilot's last recorded radio transmission at 09:42 PST indicated a request for traffic advisories and a statement of maintaining VFR conditions.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Impact Site and Wreckage Distribution
The primary impact site was located on a steep, north-facing slope at an elevation of 1,200 feet MSL. The initial ground contact was characterized by a 15-foot-long scar oriented on a magnetic heading of 045 degrees, with a 12-degree upward slope angle. The wreckage distribution extended approximately 120 feet downslope, with major components scattered across a 40-foot by 60-foot area. The main rotor blades were fragmented and exhibited chordwise tearing consistent with high-energy impact. The tail boom was separated approximately 3 feet aft of the main cabin bulkhead and was located 45 feet from the primary impact crater. The fuselage structure was severely compromised, with the cabin floor deformed upward by approximately 18 inches. No evidence of pre-impact fire was observed.

5.2 Component Examination Findings
Examination of the recovered components was conducted in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols. The main transmission was removed and disassembled for metallurgical analysis. Gear teeth exhibited normal wear patterns with no evidence of fatigue cracking or catastrophic failure. The engine fuel control units were inspected and found to be in the full-power position at the time of impact. The pitot tube was recovered with minor deformation but no blockage. The static ports were intact and free of debris. The radar altimeter antenna was fractured, with internal circuitry showing impact-related damage. The flight control linkages were examined and found to be continuous, with no evidence of binding or separation prior to impact. The hydraulic reservoirs were intact, with fluid levels consistent with normal operational parameters.

5.3 Flight Data and Cockpit Voice Recorder Analysis
The aircraft was not equipped with a flight data recorder or cockpit voice recorder. Radar data from the Southern California TRACON facility was utilized to reconstruct the flight path. The radar track indicated the aircraft departed KSNA at 09:06 PST, climbed to 1,200 feet MSL, and proceeded northwest along the coastal corridor. At 09:32 PST, the aircraft began a gradual descent to 800 feet MSL while maintaining a ground speed of approximately 145 knots. Between 09:38 and 09:42 PST, the aircraft executed a series of right turns, with ground speed decreasing to 110 knots. The final radar return at 09:44:32 PST indicated an altitude of 650 feet MSL, a ground speed of 95 knots, and a magnetic heading of 035 degrees. The track terminated at the impact site. No transponder altitude discrepancies were noted.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Procedures
Island Express Helicopters maintained an operations manual approved by the FAA in accordance with 14 CFR 135.21. The manual contained specific guidance regarding VFR weather minimums, terrain avoidance, and decision-making protocols for continued flight in deteriorating conditions. Section 4.2.1 of the manual stipulated that pilots must maintain visual reference to the surface and avoid flight into areas where visibility is less than 3 statute miles or ceilings are below 1,000 feet AGL. The manual also required pilots to initiate a diversion or execute a 180-degree turn if visual conditions could not be maintained. Company policy mandated the use of company-approved weather briefing services prior to departure. Records indicated that the pilot obtained a standard weather briefing at 08:45 PST, which included the forecasted low ceilings and reduced visibility along the intended route.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents
A review of NTSB and FAA databases identified multiple historical incidents involving rotorcraft operating under VFR in deteriorating meteorological conditions. Between 2010 and 2019, 14 Part 135 helicopter accidents were documented where the pilot continued VFR flight into IMC, resulting in controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) or loss of control. Common contributing factors included spatial disorientation, inadequate weather assessment, and delayed decision-making. The FAA issued Safety Alert for Operators (SAFO) 18004 in 2018, emphasizing the risks of VFR flight into IMC and recommending enhanced training for terrain awareness and weather avoidance. The operator's internal safety management system (SMS) documented two voluntary reports in 2019 regarding marginal VFR conditions encountered during coastal operations. Both reports were reviewed and closed with recommendations for enhanced weather monitoring.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Guidance
The operation was conducted under 14 CFR Part 135, which governs on-demand commercial air transportation. Applicable regulations included 14 CFR 135.181, which requires operators to establish and maintain weather minimums for VFR operations, and 14 CFR 135.215, which mandates that pilots maintain visual reference to the surface and avoid flight into known or forecast IMC. 14 CFR 91.155 establishes basic VFR weather minimums, including 3 statute miles visibility and 1,000-foot ceiling for operations in Class E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL. FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 3, Chapter 18, Section 4, provides guidance for principal operations inspectors regarding the evaluation of operator weather policies and pilot decision-making in marginal conditions. The order emphasizes the importance of operator training programs that address VFR flight into IMC, terrain avoidance, and the use of available weather resources. The aircraft manufacturer, Sikorsky, published flight manual supplements and operational bulletins addressing low-visibility operations, which were incorporated into the operator's training curriculum. All referenced regulatory and guidance documents were current and applicable at the time of the accident.

## [sc-0_technical_analysis_057] Technical Analysis

> **Type:** technical_analysis | **Reliability:** 0.898 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis of the flight data recording system, associated avionics, and primary structural load-path components recovered from the Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, registration N72EX, following the January 26, 2020, terrain impact event in Calabasas, California. The scope of this examination encompasses the solid-state flight data recorder (FDR), cockpit voice recorder (CVR), main rotor mast assembly, tail rotor drive shaft, engine control units, and associated wiring harnesses. The objective is to establish the operational status of the recording systems at the time of the event, validate the integrity of recorded parameters, and characterize the mechanical and material response of recovered components to impact loading.

The examination was conducted under the authority of the NTSB at the NTSB Materials Laboratory and the Flight Recorder Readout Facility in Washington, D.C., between February 10, 2020, and April 15, 2020. All procedures were performed in accordance with NTSB Investigator's Manual Chapter 12, RTCA DO-160G environmental testing protocols, and manufacturer maintenance documentation. The Lead Investigator directed the chain-of-custody protocols, ensuring all recovered items were logged, photographed, and secured prior to laboratory disassembly. This report presents factual findings derived from physical inspection, non-destructive evaluation, metallurgical analysis, and digital data extraction. No operational conclusions or probable cause determinations are included herein.

2. BACKGROUND

The Sikorsky S-76B is a twin-engine, medium-lift utility helicopter certified under 14 CFR Part 29, Transport Category Rotorcraft. The aircraft is equipped with a crash-survivable solid-state flight data recorder (P/N 2100-0001-01, S/N 18472) and a cockpit voice recorder (P/N 2100-0002-03, S/N 18473), both installed per Supplemental Type Certificate SR00892LA and compliant with TSO-C124a and TSO-C123a, respectively. The FDR is designed to record 25 mandatory parameters at a 1 Hz sampling rate, utilizing an ARINC 717 digital data bus interface. The crash survivable memory unit (CSMU) is rated to withstand impact accelerations up to 3,400 Gs, static crush loads of 5,000 lbs, fire exposure of 1,100°C for 60 minutes, and hydrostatic pressure equivalent to 5,000 ft of seawater, per RTCA DO-160G Section 21 and MIL-STD-810H Method 516.8.

The flight control architecture of the S-76B consists of a fully mechanical-hydraulic system with dual hydraulic boost actuators, a stability augmentation system (SAS), and a three-axis autopilot. Unlike fixed-wing transport aircraft that may incorporate automated pitch-trim augmentation systems such as MCAS, the S-76B relies on direct pilot input through collective, cyclic, and anti-torque pedals, with SAS providing rate damping and attitude hold functions only. The system does not feature automated control surface authority or envelope protection logic. Certification basis for the flight control system includes 14 CFR §29.671, §29.673, and §29.675, with hydraulic system pressure maintained at 3,000 ± 50 PSI during normal operation.

The specific aircraft examined had accumulated 14,892.4 total flight hours and 18,447.3 cycles since manufacture. The FDR and CVR were last removed for bench testing and firmware verification on November 12, 2019, per Sikorsky S-76B Maintenance Manual Chapter 22-00-00, with no discrepancies noted. The aircraft was configured for single-pilot instrument flight rules (IFR) operations. The second in command seat was occupied during the flight but was not equipped with primary flight controls or independent instrument displays, consistent with the approved minimum equipment list and operational configuration.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

The CSMU was recovered from the impact site with localized deformation to the forward mounting bracket and minor abrasion scoring on the titanium alloy outer housing. Maximum housing deflection measured 2.3 mm at the lower-left quadrant, consistent with a 45° oblique terrain strike. The internal memory module assembly was extracted under clean-room conditions. Thermochromic indicators affixed to the memory board substrate indicated peak thermal exposure of 142°C, well below the 1,100°C design threshold. No evidence of thermal degradation, delamination, or solder joint failure was observed.

Data extraction was performed using the manufacturer's proprietary readout interface (P/N 2100-0005-00, Rev. 4.2). The ARINC 717 data stream was decoded and validated per RTCA DO-254 and DO-178C Level C software assurance standards. All 25 recorded parameters exhibited continuous, gap-free data streams from 09:42:11 PST to 09:49:02 PST. Parity checks, cyclic redundancy codes (CRC), and frame synchronization markers were verified with zero bit errors. The CVR audio channels (Captain, First Officer/Observer, Cockpit Area Microphone, and Radio) were recovered with 98.7% intelligibility. Background noise floor measured -42 dBV, with transient impact transients peaking at +18 dBV at 09:49:02.04.

Physical examination of the main rotor mast (P/N 7600-1234-01, S/N 44821) revealed complete separation at the lower flange interface. Fracture surface analysis was conducted per ASTM E3 and ASTM E8 standards. Optical microscopy and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) at 500x magnification revealed ductile overload characteristics, including microvoid coalescence and shear lip formation. No fatigue striations, corrosion pitting, or stress corrosion cracking were identified. Chemical composition analysis via optical emission spectroscopy confirmed compliance with AMS 4340 steel specifications: Carbon 0.38%, Manganese 0.72%, Chromium 0.81%, Molybdenum 0.21%, Nickel 1.82%. Tensile testing of adjacent coupon material yielded an ultimate tensile strength of 142,000 PSI and yield strength of 128,000 PSI, within the 135,000–155,000 PSI specification band.

The tail rotor drive shaft (P/N 7600-5567-02, S/N 33109) exhibited torsional overload failure at the forward universal joint. Fracture torque was calculated at 1,840 ft-lbs, exceeding the design limit of 1,200 ft-lbs by 53.3%. The failure mode is consistent with sudden rotor deceleration and inertial loading during ground impact. Wiring harness inspection (P/N 7600-8891-04) revealed localized chafing at station 142.5, but continuity testing per MIL-STD-202 Method 300 confirmed no pre-impact open or short circuits. Insulation resistance measured >500 MΩ at 500 VDC.

All recovered components were documented via high-resolution macro photography (Exhibits 12A through 12F) and 3D laser scanning for dimensional reconstruction. The Federal Aviation Administration provided maintenance records, airworthiness directives compliance logs, and type certificate data sheets, all of which were cross-referenced against physical findings. No discrepancies between recorded maintenance actions and component condition were identified.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

The FDR data stream was time-synchronized with FAA secondary surveillance radar returns, GPS track logs, and USGS 1/3 arc-second digital elevation models. Parameter calibration was verified against manufacturer linearity tables, with all transducers operating within ±1.5% of full-scale deflection. The following timeline reconstruction is derived exclusively from recorded parameters:

09:45:12 PST: Aircraft in level cruise at 1,200 ft MSL, 145 KIAS, heading 285° magnetic. Collective position 46.2%, cyclic longitudinal 4.1° forward, pedal position 52.3%. Engine torque 1,120 ft-lbs, N1 98.4%, N2 100.1%, main rotor RPM 100.2%.

09:47:33 PST: Aircraft entered a cloud layer. Barometric altitude remained stable at 1,180 ft MSL, but indicated airspeed decreased to 132 KIAS. Vertical speed fluctuated between +150 and -200 fpm. Pilot control inputs increased in frequency, with cyclic longitudinal deflection reaching 11.4° forward and collective rising to 51.8%.

09:48:01 PST: Sustained descent initiated. Vertical speed reached -1,200 fpm. Collective position increased to 58.4%, indicating pilot attempt to arrest descent. Cyclic forward deflection peaked at 16.7°. Engine torque increased to 1,340 ft-lbs, N1 101.2%, N2 100.8%. Main rotor RPM remained within 99.8–100.4% band.

09:48:45 PST: Terrain awareness warning system (TAWS) activated. Recorded audio confirms aural "TERRAIN, PULL UP" alert. Vertical speed increased to -1,650 fpm. Collective position reached 64.1%, approaching the 68% mechanical stop. Cyclic forward deflection measured 19.3°.

09:48:52 PST: Maximum recorded descent rate of -1,850 fpm. Collective position 66.8%. Cyclic forward 20.1°. Engine torque 1,410 ft-lbs. N1 102.1%. Rotor RPM 99.6%.

09:49:02 PST: Data stream terminates. Final recorded parameters indicate abrupt cessation of all motion parameters, consistent with high-energy terrain impact.

Comparison with normal operational parameters per the Sikorsky S-76B Rotorcraft Flight Manual (AFM) indicates that the observed descent rate of -1,850 fpm exceeds the recommended maximum of -1,500 fpm for instrument meteorological conditions. Collective position at 66.8% remains within the 0–72% operational envelope, though approaching the upper limit where hydraulic assist efficiency degrades. Cyclic forward deflection of 20.1° is within the 22° mechanical limit. No parameter exceeded redline values prior to impact. Engine performance remained within certified limits, with no evidence of compressor stall, fuel flow interruption, or FADEC fault codes.

CVR audio analysis corroborates the FDR timeline. The pilot's verbal callouts indicate spatial disorientation and reliance on instrument references. The second in command provided altitude and heading callouts at 09:47:58 and 09:48:31, with no recorded control inputs or override commands. Radio communications with Los Angeles Center ceased at 09:47:12 PST. The cockpit area microphone recorded increasing wind noise and rotor blade slap, consistent with low-altitude, high-descent-rate flight in turbulent air.

Data validation was performed through cross-referencing with independent sources. FAA ASR-9 radar data confirmed altitude and ground track within ±150 ft and ±0.3 NM of FDR-derived values. GPS position logs matched within 12 meters. Terrain elevation at the impact coordinate (34.1082° N, 118.6891° W) is 1,042 ft MSL, consistent with the final recorded barometric altitude of 1,038 ft MSL. All data sources converge on a continuous, uninterrupted flight path with no system anomalies, sensor dropouts, or recording failures.

5. SUMMARY

The examination of the Sikorsky S-76B flight data recording system, associated avionics, and primary structural components yielded the following factual findings:

1. The solid-state FDR and CVR were recovered intact, with the CSMU housing exhibiting minor impact deformation consistent with a 45° oblique terrain strike. Memory module thermal exposure remained below 150°C, and all 25 recorded parameters were successfully extracted with zero data corruption or bit errors.

2. Metallurgical and mechanical analysis of the main rotor mast and tail rotor drive shaft revealed ductile overload failure modes with no evidence of pre-existing fatigue, corrosion, or material non-conformance. Chemical composition and tensile properties met AMS 4340 and manufacturer specifications.

3. FDR data indicates continuous, uninterrupted recording from 09:45:12 to 09:49:02 PST. All engine, rotor, and flight control parameters remained within certified operational limits until the final 12 seconds of flight. Descent rate peaked at -1,850 fpm, exceeding AFM recommendations but remaining within structural design margins. Collective and cyclic positions approached but did not exceed mechanical limits.

4. No pre-impact electrical faults, hydraulic pressure losses, or FADEC anomalies were identified. Wiring harness continuity and insulation resistance met MIL-STD-202 requirements. The flight control system architecture, which relies on mechanical-hydraulic actuation with SAS augmentation, functioned as designed throughout the recorded flight segment.

5. CVR audio and FDR parameter correlation confirm pilot control inputs consistent with attempts to arrest descent in reduced visibility conditions. The second in command provided situational awareness callouts but did not interface with primary flight controls. TAWS activation occurred 17 seconds prior to impact, with no recorded system malfunctions or warning inhibitions.

6. Cross-validation with FAA radar data, GPS logs, and terrain elevation models confirms data accuracy within ±1.5% of full-scale deflection for all critical parameters. The recording systems operated in full compliance with TSO-C124a, TSO-C123a, and RTCA DO-160G environmental standards.

All findings are strictly factual and derived from physical examination, laboratory testing, and digital data analysis. No operational conclusions, system deficiencies, or probable cause determinations are presented in this report.

## [sc-0_witness_testimony_058] Witness Testimony

> **Type:** witness_testimony | **Reliability:** 0.856 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

INTERVIEW OF DAVID R. HENDERSON, PRIVATE PILOT / AVIATION CONSULTANT
Date: February 14, 2020
Time: 09:30 AM PST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Los Angeles, California
Interviewer: Lead Investigator, Safety Board

Q: Mr. Henderson, thank you for coming in today. For the record, please state your full name, your current occupation, and your relationship to the events of January 26, 2020.

A: Sure. David R. Henderson. I’m a private pilot, hold an A&P mechanic ticket, and I do part-time consulting for a few local flight schools. As for the twenty-sixth... I wasn’t on the aircraft, obviously. I was operating out of a small FBO near Van Nuys that morning, doing some pre-flight work on a client’s Cessna 172. I was monitoring the local frequency, and I was in the general airspace corridor when the weather started closing in. I heard the radio traffic, saw the cloud layer drop, and then... well, you know what happened.

Q: Walk me through your morning, starting from when you arrived at the facility. Give me approximate times if you can.

A: Yeah, I got there around, uh, seven-forty-five. Maybe eight o’clock. It was still dark out, but the sky was clear. I remember checking the METARs on my phone, and the visibility was good, ceilings were high. I started pre-flighting the 172, doing the usual walk-around, checking oil, fuel sumps. Around eight-thirty, I noticed the marine layer was pushing in from the coast faster than the morning briefings had predicted. I called up the FAA automated weather system again, and it was already showing scattered at two thousand, but the trend was downward. I figured I’d wait it out, maybe push my flight to ten. I was just sitting in the pilot’s lounge, sipping coffee, listening to the tower and approach frequencies on a handheld scanner.

Q: At what point did you first become aware of the helicopter involved in the accident?

A: I think it was... let me think. Around nine-ten, maybe nine-fifteen. I heard a pilot check in with SoCal Approach, requesting VFR flight following. He gave his call sign, altitude, heading. I didn’t catch the exact tail number, but the voice sounded calm, professional. He was heading northwest, toward the Santa Monica Mountains. I remember thinking, “That’s a tight corridor today.” The clouds were already sitting at about fifteen hundred feet in the valley, and the terrain starts climbing pretty aggressively past there. I kept listening. He reported passing over the 101, maintaining VFR. Then, maybe ten minutes later, he asked for a deviation to the south. Said the visibility was dropping. I could hear it in his voice, you know? That slight hesitation. Not panic, just... recalculating.

Q: Did you have any visual contact with the aircraft?

A: Briefly. I stepped outside to check the wind sock, and I looked up. I saw a dark shape against the gray, maybe three or four miles out. It was a twin-engine helicopter, looked like an S-76. I could hear the rotor wash, that distinct, heavy thumping sound. It was flying low, maybe a thousand feet AGL, and it was already dipping into the cloud base. I watched it for maybe twenty seconds before it just... vanished. Not like it fell out of the sky. It just got swallowed. One minute you see the silhouette, the next it’s just white. The air felt heavy, damp. You could feel the pressure change in your ears. I went back inside, turned up the scanner volume, and waited for him to report back. He never did.

Q: You mentioned the terrain. How familiar are you with that specific area, and what are the typical hazards?

A: I’ve flown it dozens of times. It’s a classic trap. You’re flying VFR, following the highway, and the mountains rise up on your left. The cloud ceiling drops, and suddenly you’re boxed in. You can’t climb because you’re in the clouds, you can’t turn back because the traffic and the terrain are behind you, and you can’t descend because the ground’s right there. It’s called a spatial disorientation corridor for a reason. I don’t know if the pilot had a second in command with him, or if he was flying solo, but in those conditions, you really need two sets of eyes. One on the instruments, one outside. If you’re alone, and you lose visual reference, your inner ear starts lying to you. It’s brutal.

Q: Were you aware of any mechanical or system anomalies reported prior to or during the flight?

A: No. Nothing on the frequency. I know people online started speculating about automation failures, like that MCAS system on the 737 MAXs, but... no, that’s not applicable here. The S-76 doesn’t have a Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System. It’s a conventional helicopter. The flight controls are direct, mechanical linkages with hydraulic assist. The pilot’s hands are on the cyclic and collective. If anything, it’s the opposite of an automation problem. It’s a human factors problem. The pilot made a decision to continue into deteriorating weather, probably thinking he could punch through or find a gap. It happens. I’ve seen it.

Q: How did you learn about the crash, and what was your immediate reaction?

A: I heard it on the news around eleven-thirty. My phone started blowing up with texts from other pilots. I turned on the TV, saw the breaking news banner, and... I just sat there. I knew the area. I knew the weather. I knew exactly what had happened. I called the FAA safety hotline to report what I’d heard on the frequency, gave them the approximate time, the call sign I’d caught, the heading. They logged it. Later that afternoon, I saw the Safety Board was taking over. I’m glad they are. You need that kind of independent, methodical review. It’s not like flying for a major carrier like Southwest Airlines, where you’ve got corporate dispatchers, real-time weather radar, strict SOPs, and a whole operations center watching your back. This was a private charter. Different risk profile. Different oversight.

Q: You mentioned the pilot’s decision to continue VFR. In your professional opinion, what factors might have contributed to that choice?

A: Pressure. Always pressure. Not necessarily from the passengers, though that’s a factor. It’s the internal pressure. You’ve got a schedule, you’ve got a client, you’ve got a reputation. You tell yourself, “I’ve flown this route a hundred times. I know where the gaps are. I’ll just get a little closer, see if it clears.” And then you’re in it. The transition from VFR to IMC is insidious. It’s not a wall. It’s a curtain. You don’t realize you’ve crossed it until your instruments are the only thing keeping you alive, and if you’re not trained for it, or if you’re not current, your brain starts fighting the gauges. I don’t know the pilot’s background, but I know the FAA requires specific instrument currency for IFR, and if he was flying VFR, he was operating under visual rules. That means he was responsible for seeing and avoiding. When you can’t see, you’re in trouble.

Q: Is there anything else you observed, heard, or felt that you think might be relevant to the investigation?

A: Just... the silence after he went in. The frequency went dead. No mayday, no distress call. That tells me it happened fast. Or he was so focused on trying to regain visual reference that he didn’t have the bandwidth to transmit. I’ve been in that situation before, in a simulator, and your hands are full. You’re scanning, you’re adjusting, you’re trying to keep the ball centered, and the ground proximity warning is screaming in your head. I don’t know if the S-76 had a terrain awareness system active, but even if it did, it’s just a tool. It doesn’t fly the aircraft. The pilot does. I guess... I just hope the Board looks at the whole picture. The weather, the terrain, the operational culture, the training standards. It’s never just one thing. It’s a chain. And on that morning, every link broke.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Henderson. We’ll be in touch if we need any clarification.

A: Yeah, of course. I’m here to help. I’ve got my scanner logs, my weather printouts, everything. Just let me know. I hope you find what you’re looking for.

## [sc-0_regulatory_filing_059] Regulatory Filing

> **Type:** regulatory_filing | **Reliability:** 0.913 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
   - Regulatory Reference: 14 CFR Part 135.181, 14 CFR Part 135.215, 14 CFR Part 135.159, 14 CFR Part 91.155, 14 CFR Part 91.177; FAA Docket No. FAA-2020-0892
   - NTSB Safety Recommendations: A-20-001 through A-20-004
   - NTSB Accident Number: WPR20MA040
   - Date of Occurrence: January 26, 2020
   - Subject: Regulatory Compliance Review, Corrective Action Directives, and Rulemaking Initiation Regarding VFR Flight into Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC) and Terrain Awareness for Commercial Rotorcraft Operations

2. BACKGROUND
   The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) formally acknowledges receipt of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) preliminary findings and subsequent safety recommendations arising from the January 26, 2020, controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) accident involving a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, registration N72EX, operated by Island Express Helicopters, Inc. The aircraft was conducting a commercial passenger flight under visual flight rules (VFR) when it encountered rapidly deteriorating meteorological conditions, resulting in pilot spatial disorientation and subsequent impact with rising terrain in Calabasas, California. All nine persons on board sustained fatal injuries.

   Commercial rotorcraft operations are regulated under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 135, Operating Requirements: Commuter and On Demand Operations. Specifically, 14 CFR § 135.181 prohibits VFR operations unless the flight can be conducted with continuous visual reference to the surface and in strict compliance with prescribed weather minimums. 14 CFR § 135.215 mandates that operators establish and maintain procedures for flight following, weather monitoring, and pilot decision-making regarding VFR/IMC transitions. The airworthiness certification of the Sikorsky S-76B is established under Type Certificate No. H10WE, with supplemental type certificates (STCs) governing avionics modifications and minimum equipment list (MMEL) provisions dictating operational allowances for inoperative equipment.

   Historically, the NTSB has issued multiple safety recommendations addressing VFR flight into IMC and the absence of mandatory terrain awareness and warning systems (TAWS) for rotorcraft. Notably, NTSB Safety Recommendations A-19-001 and A-19-002 urged the FAA to mandate helicopter terrain awareness and warning systems (HTAWS) for Part 135 operations and to enhance pilot training regarding inadvertent IMC encounters. While the FAA has issued Advisory Circular (AC) 135-14B and AC 90-105A to provide operational guidance, regulatory mandates remain advisory in nature. Concurrently, the FAA’s broader regulatory review of automated flight control augmentation systems—exemplified by the certification, operational oversight, and subsequent design modifications of the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) on fixed-wing transport category aircraft—has prompted a comprehensive reassessment of human-machine interface standards, pilot monitoring requirements, and system failure mode analysis across all aircraft categories. Although MCAS is not installed on the S-76B rotorcraft platform, the regulatory principles governing automated system transparency, pilot authority, and failure mitigation are directly applicable to rotorcraft flight control and navigation augmentation systems. This cross-platform regulatory evaluation informs the current compliance framework and subsequent rulemaking initiatives.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
   A comprehensive audit of Island Express Helicopters, Inc. operational records, training curricula, and maintenance documentation reveals partial compliance with existing 14 CFR Part 135 requirements. The operator maintained a valid Part 135 certificate and adhered to prescribed maintenance intervals per the manufacturer’s maintenance manual and applicable airworthiness directives. However, the investigation identified critical deficiencies in operational risk management, specifically regarding weather decision-making protocols, real-time meteorological data integration, and pilot training for inadvertent IMC encounters.

   Regulatory oversight actions initiated by the FAA’s Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) included a targeted surveillance audit under 14 CFR § 135.215 and § 135.159. The audit determined that while the operator’s operations specifications (OpSpecs) permitted VFR flight, the internal safety management system (SMS) lacked robust mechanisms for automated weather alerting and pilot go/no-go decision support. Furthermore, the operator’s training program did not adequately address spatial disorientation mitigation, instrument cross-check procedures, or the use of available navigation aids during rapid meteorological degradation. The aircraft’s installed avionics suite, while compliant with the approved MMEL, did not include a certified HTAWS, which remains optional under current regulatory frameworks for Part 135 rotorcraft.

   A systemic gap in the regulatory framework has been identified: the absence of a mandatory requirement for HTAWS installation on commercial rotorcraft, coupled with insufficient regulatory emphasis on VFR/IMC transition training and weather minimum enforcement. The current regulatory structure relies heavily on operator discretion and advisory guidance, which has proven inadequate in preventing CFIT accidents under deteriorating meteorological conditions. Additionally, while the FAA’s certification standards for flight control augmentation systems (e.g., 14 CFR Part 27.671, 27.1309) ensure baseline airworthiness, the integration of automated decision-support tools and pilot interface design requires enhanced regulatory scrutiny. The lessons derived from fixed-wing automated system oversight, including the MCAS certification review and subsequent operational directives, underscore the necessity of transparent system behavior, redundant pilot monitoring, and explicit failure mode training. These principles must be systematically adapted to rotorcraft operations to mitigate automation dependency and enhance pilot situational awareness during adverse weather encounters.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
   In response to the identified deficiencies and in alignment with NTSB Safety Recommendations A-20-001 through A-20-004, the FAA hereby issues the following corrective actions and compliance directives:

   1. Mandatory HTAWS Installation: All Part 135 rotorcraft operators shall install and maintain a TSO-C194 or TSO-C195 compliant Helicopter Terrain Awareness and Warning System (HTAWS) on all aircraft used in commercial passenger operations. Compliance shall be achieved within 180 days of the effective date of this directive. Operators must submit installation verification reports, updated weight and balance documentation, and revised MMEL provisions to the responsible FSDO.

   2. Enhanced VFR/IMC Transition Training: Operators shall revise their FAA-approved training programs to include mandatory simulator or flight training device (FTD) modules addressing inadvertent IMC encounters, spatial disorientation recognition, and immediate recovery procedures. Training curricula must be submitted for FAA approval within 90 days, with full implementation and recurrent training integration required within 120 days.

   3. Weather Decision-Making and SMS Integration: Part 135 operators shall implement a standardized weather risk assessment protocol integrated into their Safety Management System (SMS). This protocol shall mandate real-time meteorological data access, automated weather alert thresholds, and documented pilot-in-command authority to divert or terminate flights when conditions approach VFR minimums. Compliance shall be verified during the next scheduled surveillance audit.

   4. Regulatory Framework Review and Rulemaking: The FAA’s Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) and Flight Standards Service (AFS) shall initiate a rulemaking action under Docket No. FAA-2020-0892 to amend 14 CFR Part 135, specifically §§ 135.181, 135.215, and 135.159, to codify mandatory HTAWS requirements, standardized VFR/IMC training, and enhanced weather monitoring protocols. A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) shall be published within 12 months, with public comment periods and economic impact analyses conducted in accordance with the Administrative Procedure Act.

   5. Follow-Up Inspection Schedule: The responsible FSDO shall conduct targeted compliance inspections at 90-day, 180-day, and 365-day intervals following the issuance of this directive. Inspections shall verify HTAWS installation, training program implementation, SMS integration, and operational adherence to revised weather protocols. Non-compliance shall result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR Part 13, including potential suspension or revocation of operating certificates and imposition of civil penalties.

   The FAA remains committed to advancing aviation safety through rigorous regulatory oversight, evidence-based rulemaking, and collaborative engagement with industry stakeholders. All affected operators shall acknowledge receipt of this directive and submit a preliminary compliance plan to the designated FSDO within 30 calendar days.

   Issued under the authority of the Administrator, Federal Aviation Administration, in coordination with the National Transportation Safety Board.
   Docket No. FAA-2020-0892 | Reference: NTSB/WPR20MA040
   Effective Date: [Date of Issuance]
   Distribution: Part 135 Rotorcraft Operators, Flight Standards District Offices, Aircraft Certification Service, NTSB Office of Aviation Safety

HEADLINE: Nine Dead After Helicopter Crashes in California Hills Amid Poor Weather

BYLINE: [Reporter Name], [News Outlet]
DATELINE: CALABASAS, Calif. —

A Sikorsky S-76B helicopter crashed into a steep, brush-covered hillside in Calabasas on Sunday, killing all nine people aboard. The aircraft went down in dense fog and low clouds in the Santa Monica Mountains, prompting a massive emergency response and leaving a community in mourning.

Preliminary information indicates the pilot continued flying under visual flight rules into an area of rapidly deteriorating visibility and rising terrain. In aviation terminology, this is known as continued VFR flight into instrument meteorological conditions, or IMC, a scenario where pilots lose sight of the horizon and ground references while navigating through clouds or heavy fog. The impact triggered a localized brush fire and left no survivors, devastating families and sending immediate shockwaves through the regional aviation sector.

Federal and state authorities have mobilized to secure the crash site and begin a comprehensive inquiry. "We are treating this as a tragic loss of life and a serious aviation event," said the Lead Investigator assigned to the case. "Our priority right now is determining the exact sequence of events that led to this crash, and we will follow the evidence wherever it takes us."

The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it is providing full logistical and technical support to the investigation. "The agency is cooperating closely with federal investigators and reviewing all operational protocols associated with the flight," an FAA spokesperson said in a written statement. "Safety remains our highest priority, and we will share findings as they become available."

The operator of the aircraft, a private charter service, released a brief statement expressing profound grief. "Our hearts are broken for the families, friends, and loved ones affected by this tragedy," a company spokesperson said. "We are providing every resource we can to support them and are fully cooperating with authorities as they work to understand what happened."

The Sikorsky S-76B is a twin-engine, medium-lift helicopter widely recognized for its reliability and commonly used for corporate transport, emergency medical services, and VIP travel. Manufactured by Sikorsky Aircraft, the rotorcraft is equipped with advanced avionics and dual-engine redundancy. The flight was en route from Orange County to Camarillo, carrying a mix of passengers and crew members. The operator has maintained a strong safety record in recent years, with no prior major incidents reported to federal regulators.

Aviation safety experts note that spatial disorientation remains one of the most dangerous threats to helicopter pilots operating in marginal weather. "When a pilot loses visual reference to the horizon, the inner ear can send false signals to the brain, making it feel as though the aircraft is level when it is actually banking or descending," explained Dr. Marcus Chen, an aviation safety researcher at a major West Coast university. "Without an immediate transition to instrument flying, the risk of controlled flight into terrain increases dramatically."

Chen emphasized that rotorcraft operations differ significantly from commercial fixed-wing aviation in how they manage flight envelope protections. "Unlike modern airliners that rely on automated systems like the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System, or MCAS, to adjust control surfaces and prevent stalls, helicopters in low-visibility conditions depend almost entirely on pilot training, situational awareness, and strict adherence to weather minimums," he said. "When those minimums are breached, the margin for error shrinks rapidly."

For the families of those aboard, the crash has left an unfillable void. Relatives gathered at a local community center on Monday, sharing photographs and memories of the victims. "He was a devoted father who always made time for his kids, no matter how busy his schedule was," said one family member, who asked not to be named. "We just want answers, and we want to honor their memory in a way that reflects how much they meant to us."

Another relative described the passengers as close friends heading to a youth sports event. "They were excited, laughing, and looking forward to the day," the relative said. "It’s unimaginable that a routine flight could end like this. We are leaning on each other right now."

Helicopter accidents in poor weather have historically prompted regulatory reviews and operational changes across the industry. The Federal Aviation Administration’s Flight Standards Service Manual, widely known as Order 8900.1, outlines strict guidelines for operators conducting flights in marginal conditions, including mandatory weather briefings, minimum visibility requirements, and pilot decision-making protocols. Despite these safeguards, the unique challenges of low-altitude rotorcraft navigation in mountainous terrain remain a persistent safety concern, particularly when weather shifts faster than forecast models predict.

The NTSB continues to analyze flight data, weather radar imagery, maintenance records, and wreckage distribution. Investigators are also reviewing air traffic control communications and pilot training logs. "We are methodically working through every piece of evidence," the Lead Investigator noted. "The families deserve a thorough, transparent process, and we will not rush to conclusions."

A preliminary report is expected within weeks, while a final determination of probable cause typically takes 12 to 18 months. Until then, the aviation community and grieving families wait for answers, hoping the investigation will yield lessons that prevent future tragedies.

## [sc-0_expert_deposition_061] Expert Deposition

> **Type:** expert_deposition | **Reliability:** 0.825 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. INTRODUCTION
This submission is presented by Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation (SAC), acting in its capacity as the type certificate holder and original equipment manufacturer for the Sikorsky S-76B rotorcraft involved in the January 26, 2020, accident. As a designated party to the investigation, SAC has contributed subject-matter expertise in rotorcraft systems engineering, flight control architecture, avionics integration, and human-machine interface design. The scope of this document encompasses a technical evaluation of the aircraft’s operational performance, an analysis of the environmental and human factors documented in the investigative docket, and a review of maintenance and regulatory compliance frameworks. Our objective is to present a fact-based engineering perspective that clarifies the capabilities and limitations of the S-76B platform, contextualizes the accident sequence within established aviation safety principles, and outlines actionable recommendations to mitigate similar occurrences in the future.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND
The accident sequence, as reconstructed from primary radar telemetry, air traffic control communications, and the Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) transcript, indicates that the aircraft departed John Wayne Airport under visual meteorological conditions (VMC) and proceeded along a coastal route toward Camarillo. As the flight progressed into the Santa Monica Mountains corridor, meteorological data confirms a rapid deterioration in ceiling and visibility, with localized marine layer fog and low stratus reducing forward visibility to less than one statute mile. The pilot elected to continue under visual flight rules (VFR) into instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), ultimately resulting in controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) at approximately 1,700 feet MSL.

Docket materials, including Exhibit 12B (Weather Reconstruction Report) and Exhibit 18C (Operator Training Records), establish that the aircraft was airworthy at the time of departure. Maintenance logs reviewed by the Safety Board confirm compliance with all applicable inspection intervals, and no deferred maintenance items were identified that would have degraded flight control responsiveness, engine performance, or structural integrity. The operator, Island Express Helicopters (IEH), conducted the flight under Title 14 CFR Part 135, with the pilot holding appropriate ratings and recent experience. However, the docket also reveals that the aircraft was not equipped with a mandatory Helicopter Terrain Awareness and Warning System (HTAWS), a configuration that was permissible under the regulatory framework in effect at the time.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has since issued Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-51, which addresses enhanced inspection protocols for critical flight control linkages and avionics mounting structures across several rotorcraft models. While this directive was promulgated after the accident, its underlying engineering rationale aligns with industry-wide efforts to standardize maintenance rigor and ensure continued airworthiness in high-utilization commercial operations. The factual record, therefore, supports a clear delineation between aircraft system integrity and the operational decision-making environment that preceded the impact.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS
From an engineering and human factors perspective, the accident sequence is consistent with the well-documented phenomenon of VFR-into-IMC, wherein a pilot’s visual reference to the horizon and terrain is progressively degraded, leading to spatial disorientation and loss of situational awareness. The S-76B flight control system, a conventional mechanical-hydraulic architecture with dual-axis stability augmentation, performed within certified parameters throughout the flight. Telemetry and post-accident component testing confirm that the main rotor, tail rotor, and engine control systems exhibited no anomalies. The aircraft’s response to control inputs remained predictable, and there is no evidence of system degradation, control surface binding, or autopilot malfunction.

The absence of a terrain awareness system, however, represents a critical gap in the operational safety net. Modern rotorcraft operations in mountainous or coastal environments increasingly rely on integrated avionics suites that provide predictive terrain mapping, synthetic vision, and automated alerting. The S-76B platform, as originally certified, was not mandated to include such systems, and retrofitting was left to operator discretion. Industry standards, including RTCA DO-315 and FAA Advisory Circular 135-14, have long recognized the value of HTAWS in mitigating CFIT risk. The Safety Board’s own historical data indicates that terrain awareness systems reduce CFIT probability by over 70% in low-visibility environments.

Human factors analysis further illuminates the cognitive challenges inherent in degraded visual environments. The CVR transcript reveals a progressive increase in pilot workload, characterized by verbalized uncertainty regarding cloud base altitude and terrain clearance. This aligns with established research on somatogravic and vestibular illusions, which can induce a false perception of level flight or climb when visual cues are absent. The transition from VMC to IMC in mountainous terrain compresses decision-making timelines, often overwhelming working memory and triggering cognitive tunneling. In such scenarios, automation dependency and interface transparency become critical. While the S-76B’s stability augmentation system provides basic attitude hold and heading stabilization, it does not include automated terrain avoidance or predictive weather fusion. This design philosophy reflects the era of certification, where pilot authority and manual control were prioritized over automated intervention.

It is instructive to compare this operational context with broader aviation automation paradigms, such as the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) implemented on fixed-wing transport aircraft. While fundamentally different in architecture and application, both systems underscore the importance of clear human-machine interface design, unambiguous alerting, and pilot authority retention during degraded conditions. The MCAS case study, extensively reviewed by the Safety Board and regulatory bodies, demonstrates that automation must be transparent, easily disengaged, and supported by comprehensive training. In rotorcraft operations, where low-altitude flight and rapid environmental changes are routine, these principles are equally applicable. The S-76B’s flight control architecture does not suffer from the same automation authority conflicts, but the accident highlights the need for enhanced decision-support tools that provide pilots with actionable, real-time environmental awareness.

Maintenance and regulatory compliance also warrant technical consideration. The recent issuance of AD 2024-02-51 by the FAA reflects a proactive approach to addressing latent wear and fatigue in critical flight control assemblies. While the accident aircraft’s maintenance records indicate full compliance with prior directives, the implementation of enhanced inspection intervals and non-destructive testing protocols will further reduce the probability of undetected degradation. From a systems engineering standpoint, the integration of predictive maintenance analytics, vibration monitoring, and digital twin modeling can complement traditional inspection regimes, ensuring that airworthiness is maintained throughout the aircraft’s operational lifecycle.

4. CONCLUSIONS
Based on a comprehensive review of the docket materials, engineering data, and operational context, Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation concludes that the primary causal factors in this accident are operational and human factors in nature, rather than attributable to aircraft system failure or design deficiency. The S-76B performed as designed, with all flight control, propulsion, and structural systems operating within certified limits. The accident sequence was initiated by the pilot’s decision to continue VFR flight into deteriorating weather, compounded by spatial disorientation, terrain proximity, and the absence of mandatory terrain awareness technology.

We acknowledge the complexity of this event, which involves intersecting variables including meteorological forecasting limitations, operator training standards, regulatory requirements, and the inherent challenges of low-altitude flight in mountainous terrain. However, the technical evidence does not support a conclusion that the aircraft’s design, maintenance, or certification standards contributed to the loss of control or impact. Instead, the data underscores the critical need for enhanced decision-support systems, standardized IMC transition training, and regulatory alignment with modern safety technologies.

To mitigate future occurrences, we recommend the following safety improvements: (1) mandatory installation of HTAWS or equivalent terrain awareness systems for all Part 135 rotorcraft operating in terrain-challenged environments; (2) standardized simulator-based training modules focused on VFR-into-IMC recognition, spatial disorientation recovery, and automated system management; (3) integration of real-time weather and terrain fusion into primary flight displays, with predictive alerting thresholds calibrated for low-altitude operations; and (4) industry-wide data sharing initiatives to track near-miss events and refine operational risk models.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS
In the years following the accident, Sikorsky has implemented several proactive measures to enhance operational safety and support the rotorcraft community. We have issued Service Bulletin S76B-2021-04, which provides updated guidance on weather decision-making, IMC transition procedures, and recommended avionics upgrades. The Pilot Operating Handbook (POH) has been revised to include expanded human factors training references, emphasizing cognitive workload management and terrain clearance protocols. Additionally, we have collaborated with the FAA and industry stakeholders to develop standardized retrofit kits for HTAWS and synthetic vision systems, ensuring compatibility with legacy S-76B configurations.

We have also supported the implementation of AD 2024-02-51 by providing technical documentation, inspection tooling, and maintenance training modules to operators and certified repair stations. Our engineering teams have integrated predictive maintenance analytics into our customer support platform, enabling operators to monitor component health trends and schedule inspections based on actual usage rather than fixed intervals.

Looking forward, we propose several additional improvements to advance rotorcraft safety. First, we recommend the development of a next-generation avionics architecture that fuses terrain mapping, real-time meteorological data, and flight path prediction into a unified decision-support interface. Second, we advocate for expanded use of full-flight simulators with high-fidelity IMC and spatial disorientation scenarios, ensuring that pilots are trained to recognize and respond to degraded visual environments before they become critical. Third, we support the establishment of a centralized, anonymized safety data repository for Part 135 operators, enabling trend analysis and proactive risk mitigation. Finally, we will continue to work with the Safety Board, the FAA, and international regulatory bodies to align certification standards with emerging technologies, ensuring that rotorcraft operations benefit from the same safety advancements that have transformed commercial aviation.

The January 26, 2020, accident serves as a sobering reminder of the operational challenges inherent in low-altitude flight. Through rigorous engineering analysis, transparent safety management, and collaborative industry action, we can honor the memory of those lost by implementing systemic improvements that prevent similar tragedies in the future.
