## [sc-0_internal_memo_062] Internal Memo

> **Type:** internal_memo | **Reliability:** 0.572 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

TO: All Flight Operations, Maintenance Control, and Training Department Personnel
FROM: Director of Flight Safety & Standards / Chief Pilot
DATE: February 14, 2020
SUBJECT: URGENT: VFR-into-IMC Mitigation, Terrain Awareness, and Crew Resource Management Protocols
REF: SAF-BUL-2020-014, OPS-MEMO-2019-088, WO-TRN-4492

PURPOSE:
This Training Bulletin and Safety Communication is issued to mandate immediate updates to our VFR weather minimums, terrain avoidance procedures, and crew coordination protocols. The directive establishes revised training requirements and maintenance verification steps to prevent inadvertent flight into instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) and mitigate spatial disorientation risks. Compliance is mandatory for all flight crews, dispatchers, and maintenance personnel operating under Part 135 and Part 91K.

BACKGROUND:
On January 26, 2020, a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter crashed into terrain in Calabasas, California, during instrument meteorological conditions, resulting in the loss of all nine persons on board. Preliminary investigation data indicates the flight continued under visual flight rules into an area of rapidly deteriorating visibility and rising terrain. The Federal Aviation Administration has subsequently issued multiple safety alerts emphasizing the critical need for strict adherence to published weather minimums and proactive terrain avoidance strategies. 

While our fleet composition differs from the aircraft involved in the Calabasas event, the operational risk profile remains identical. Historical data and recent industry incidents demonstrate that degraded situational awareness, whether caused by environmental factors or overreliance on automated systems, consistently precedes loss-of-control events. The aviation community’s recent focus on the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) and similar flight control augmentation architectures underscores a broader industry lesson: pilots must maintain continuous manual awareness and cross-verify system behavior, particularly when environmental cues degrade. 

Furthermore, crew resource management (CRM) breakdowns frequently occur when the monitoring pilot fails to assertively challenge deviations. The second in command (SIC) must be empowered and trained to execute immediate intervention protocols when the pilot flying exhibits signs of spatial disorientation or continues flight into marginal weather without a verified escape route. The S-76B manufacturer has also released updated flight manual supplements reinforcing these exact principles, which we are now integrating into our standard operating procedures.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, the following procedural updates and technical verifications are in effect:

1. Weather Minimums & Go/No-Go Criteria
   • All VFR operations must maintain a minimum of 1,000 feet AGL and 3 statute miles visibility, regardless of local terrain familiarity.
   • If ceiling or visibility drops below 1,500 feet AGL or 5 SM, a mandatory weather diversion briefing must be completed prior to departure.
   • Dispatchers are required to log all marginal weather decisions in the Flight Operations Tracking System (FOTS) under code WX-DEC-04.

2. Terrain Awareness & Avionics Verification
   • All aircraft equipped with Class B TAWS must have the terrain database updated to Revision 2020.1 or later.
   • Maintenance Control will issue Work Order WO-AV-8821 to verify TAWS alert thresholds and cross-check against Part Number 450-992-001 software patches.
   • Pilots must verbally confirm TAWS functionality during the pre-flight checklist. Any discrepancy requires immediate grounding per MEL Item 34-45-01.

3. Crew Resource Management & Intervention Protocols
   • The SIC is designated as the primary terrain and weather monitor during all phases of flight.
   • If the pilot flying deviates from published routes or continues into deteriorating visibility, the second in command must issue a standardized callout: “TERRAIN/WEATHER AHEAD, DIVERT NOW.”
   • Failure to acknowledge the callout within five seconds requires the SIC to assume control and execute the published escape maneuver.
   • All crews will complete the updated CRM scenario module (TRN-CRM-2020-03) focusing on assertive intervention and automation dependency awareness.

4. Training Integration & Cross-Fleet Lessons
   • The Training Department will incorporate case studies on system awareness, including fixed-wing automation anomalies, to reinforce manual flying proficiency and continuous cross-checking.
   • Simulator sessions will now include unannounced IMC entry scenarios with mandatory diversion execution.
   • Line check airmen will evaluate SIC intervention authority during all recurrent proficiency checks.

ACTION REQUIRED:
1. Flight Operations Management: Distribute this bulletin to all active and reserve pilots by February 17, 2020. Ensure all crew members acknowledge receipt via the electronic training portal.
2. Training Department: Schedule and complete TRN-CRM-2020-03 for all flight crews by March 15, 2020. Update simulator profiles to reflect the new IMC diversion scenarios.
3. Maintenance Control: Execute WO-AV-8821 across the entire fleet by February 28, 2020. Verify TAWS software compliance and submit completion reports to the Quality Assurance office.
4. Chief Pilots / Line Check Airmen: Conduct focused line checks emphasizing terrain awareness, weather minimum adherence, and SIC intervention protocols. Submit evaluation summaries to Flight Safety by April 1, 2020.
5. All Personnel: Direct any procedural questions or system discrepancies to the Flight Safety Hotline (Ext. 4400) or via email to safety@ops.internal. Non-compliance will result in immediate suspension of flight duties pending review.

This directive supersedes all prior weather and CRM guidance. Strict adherence is required to maintain our safety management system standards and ensure continued operational integrity.

## [sc-0_preliminary_report_063] Preliminary Report

> **Type:** preliminary_report | **Reliability:** 0.857 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. SYNOPSIS
On January 26, 2020, at approximately 0945 Pacific Standard Time, a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, registered N72EX and operated by Island Express Helicopters, impacted mountainous terrain in Calabasas, California. The aircraft was conducting a visual flight rules (VFR) flight that inadvertently entered instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), resulting in the destruction of the airframe and the fatal injury of all nine persons on board. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has initiated a major accident investigation to document factual circumstances, secure evidence, and establish the investigative scope. All findings documented herein are preliminary and subject to revision as additional data is collected and analyzed.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary information gathered during the initial response phase indicates that the flight departed John Wayne Airport (SNA) in Orange County, California, with a planned destination of Camarillo Airport (CMA). Radar telemetry and automated dependent surveillance-broadcast (ADS-B) data suggest the aircraft maintained a generally northwesterly track before deviating from its expected route and descending into a localized area of reduced visibility. Initial witness accounts describe low cloud cover, restricted visibility, and the sound of an aircraft operating at a low altitude prior to impact. Several observers reported hearing engine noise consistent with a rotorcraft maneuvering in proximity to terrain, though these accounts remain unverified and are subject to corroboration through additional interviews and acoustic analysis.

Meteorological data obtained from nearby surface observation stations, satellite imagery, and pilot reports indicate that the accident area was experiencing a dense marine layer with ceilings below 1,000 feet above ground level and visibility restricted to less than one mile in fog. Preliminary examination of the flight path suggests the pilot may have continued VFR flight into deteriorating weather conditions while navigating rising terrain. The aircraft sustained catastrophic structural damage upon impact with a steep hillside, followed by a post-impact fire that consumed a significant portion of the airframe and interior components. Initial wreckage distribution patterns are consistent with a high-energy, near-vertical impact. No evidence of pre-impact mechanical failure, in-flight breakup, or controlled flight into terrain avoidance system activation has been identified at this stage, though this assessment remains preliminary and subject to detailed forensic analysis.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The NTSB has activated multiple investigative groups to conduct a comprehensive, methodical examination of the accident. The Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Human Performance, Weather, and Survival Factors groups have been formally established and dispatched to the accident site. The Board has designated the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation, Island Express Helicopters (IEH), and the Helicopter Association International as parties to the investigation. Additional parties may be added as the scope of the inquiry evolves and technical requirements are identified.

All recoverable wreckage has been secured, cataloged, and transported to a designated examination facility under strict chain-of-custody protocols. Initial documentation includes high-resolution photography, three-dimensional laser scanning of the impact site, and preliminary mapping of debris fields. Maintenance records, pilot training files, operational logs, and dispatch communications have been requested from the operating company and are currently under review. The aircraft’s flight data recording equipment, if present and recoverable, will undergo specialized data extraction, validation, and synchronization procedures.

Procedurally, the investigation will maintain strict adherence to established NTSB protocols for rotorcraft accidents. While the Systems group will conduct a thorough evaluation of the helicopter’s avionics, flight control interfaces, and engine management systems, it is noted that certain fixed-wing-specific augmentation architectures, such as the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), are not applicable to this rotorcraft design and will not be factored into the technical analysis. The investigation team will, however, coordinate with other active NTSB inquiries, including those involving commercial carriers such as Southwest Airlines (SWA), to share procedural best practices, cross-reference operational safety data, and align documentation standards where relevant. All group chairpersons have been instructed to document findings with appropriate caution, ensuring that preliminary observations are clearly distinguished from validated conclusions. No determination of probable cause has been made, and all technical assessments remain subject to peer review and additional testing.

4. NEXT STEPS
Over the coming weeks, investigative groups will proceed with component teardowns, metallurgical examinations, and systems bench testing. The Human Performance group will conduct structured interviews with air traffic control personnel, company dispatchers, and individuals familiar with the pilot’s recent flight operations, duty schedules, and training history. The Weather group will continue to reconstruct the meteorological environment using high-resolution numerical weather prediction models, localized sensor data, and atmospheric soundings. A detailed wreckage examination will be conducted to identify any potential anomalies in the flight control linkages, rotor system, or powerplant components, with all findings documented in the public docket.

The NTSB will issue a formal Preliminary Report within approximately 30 days of the accident date, which will summarize factual data collected to date without offering analytical conclusions or probable cause determinations. Subsequent updates will be published through the public docket system as group reports are finalized, peer-reviewed, and approved for release. All parties and stakeholders are reminded that early-stage findings are inherently subject to revision as additional evidence is recovered, analyzed, and validated. The Board will continue to prioritize a methodical, evidence-based approach to ensure the accuracy, transparency, and integrity of the final investigative record.

## [sc-0_investigation_report_064] Investigation Report

> **Type:** investigation_report | **Reliability:** 0.901 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On January 26, 2020, at approximately 0945 Pacific Standard Time (PST), a helicopter accident occurred in Calabasas, California. The geographic coordinates of the primary impact site were recorded as 34°08'12.5" North latitude and 118°41'28.1" West longitude. The accident site elevation was approximately 1,650 feet mean sea level (MSL). The event occurred during daylight hours, with sunrise recorded at 0658 PST and sunset at 1724 PST.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator Identification
The aircraft involved was a Sikorsky S-76B, bearing United States registration number N3644S. The aircraft was owned and operated by Island Express Helicopters, Inc., a Part 135 certificate holder. The operator's principal base of operations was located at John Wayne Airport (SNA), Orange County, California. The aircraft was configured for passenger transport operations and was equipped with standard S-76B instrumentation and flight control systems.

1.3 Nature of Flight and Regulatory Framework
The flight was conducted under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 135, operating as an on-demand charter flight. The planned route originated at John Wayne Airport (SNA), Orange County, California, with a destination of Camarillo Airport (CMA), Ventura County, California. The flight was conducted under visual flight rules (VFR) with a planned cruise altitude of 1,500 feet MSL. The flight departed SNA at approximately 0906 PST. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) initiated an investigation under its statutory authority, classifying the event as a major accident due to the total loss of the aircraft and the fatalities of all nine persons on board.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Pilot Certificates and Ratings
The pilot in command held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate with rotorcraft-helicopter and instrument helicopter ratings. The pilot also held commercial pilot certificates for airplane single-engine and multi-engine land, along with certified flight instructor (CFI) and CFI-instrument ratings. The pilot's medical certificate was a first-class medical, issued on October 14, 2019, with no limitations or waivers. The medical certificate remained valid through October 31, 2020.

2.2 Flight Experience and Currency
Review of the pilot's logbooks and operator training records indicated a total flight time of approximately 8,200 hours. Of this total, approximately 1,200 hours were accumulated in the Sikorsky S-76 series. The pilot's recent flight experience met the requirements of 14 CFR § 135.247, including three takeoffs and landings within the preceding 90 days in the same make and model. The pilot's instrument currency was current, with six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting/tracking courses completed within the preceding six calendar months. Duty and rest records indicated compliance with 14 CFR §§ 135.263 and 135.265, with the pilot reporting for duty at 0630 PST and accumulating approximately 3.25 hours of flight time prior to the accident.

2.3 Training and Proficiency Records
The pilot completed recurrent training and proficiency checks in accordance with 14 CFR § 135.351 and the operator's FAA-approved training program. The most recent recurrent training was completed on November 12, 2019, and included ground and flight instruction covering emergency procedures, instrument flight rules (IFR) operations, spatial disorientation recognition, and VFR flight into instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) avoidance. The training syllabus emphasized decision-making under deteriorating weather conditions, terrain awareness, and autopilot management. No discrepancies or deficiencies were noted in the pilot's training records. The operator's chief pilot and director of operations confirmed that the pilot's performance during recurrent evaluations met or exceeded established standards.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 Airframe and Engine Specifications
The accident aircraft was a Sikorsky S-76B, manufacturer serial number 760364, manufactured in 1988. The airframe total time was recorded at approximately 11,200 hours, with approximately 8,500 hours accumulated since the last major structural overhaul. The aircraft was powered by two Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6B-36A turboshaft engines. Engine serial numbers were documented in the maintenance logs, with time-since-overhaul values of approximately 2,100 hours for the left engine and 1,950 hours for the right engine. Both engines were within manufacturer-recommended service life limits and had no outstanding maintenance discrepancies.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
The aircraft was maintained in accordance with an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program. The most recent 100-hour inspection was completed on January 10, 2020, at 11,185 airframe hours. All applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) were reviewed and found to be in compliance per 14 CFR § 43.16. No deferred maintenance items were recorded in the aircraft maintenance logbook. The operator's maintenance control center confirmed that all scheduled inspections, component replacements, and service bulletins were current. The aircraft's weight and balance were within approved limits for the flight, with a calculated takeoff weight of approximately 10,850 pounds and a center of gravity within the forward and aft limits specified in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual.

3.3 Avionics and Flight Control Systems
The aircraft was equipped with a dual-axis autopilot system, attitude director indicators (ADI), horizontal situation indicators (HSI), a radar altimeter, and a Garmin GNS 430/530 navigation suite. The flight control system utilized conventional mechanical linkages with hydraulic boost for primary controls. The aircraft was not equipped with a terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS), as such equipment was not mandated for Part 135 rotorcraft operations at the time of the accident. The investigation reviewed the aircraft's flight control augmentation architecture and noted that, unlike certain fixed-wing transport category aircraft that utilize automated pitch trim systems such as the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), the S-76B relies on pilot-managed autopilot modes and manual control inputs for attitude and altitude management. All avionics and flight control components recovered from the wreckage were examined for pre-impact anomalies, with no evidence of system failure or degradation identified.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Weather Analysis
On January 26, 2020, a low-pressure system was situated over the eastern Pacific Ocean, advecting a dense marine layer into the Southern California coastal region. The synoptic pattern produced widespread stratus clouds, fog, and reduced visibility across the Los Angeles Basin and adjacent mountainous terrain. Surface pressure gradients were weak, resulting in calm to light winds. The marine layer depth was estimated at 1,200 to 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL), with a temperature inversion layer capping the moisture.

4.2 Surface Observations and Terminal Forecasts
Aviation routine weather reports (METAR) and terminal aerodrome forecasts (TAF) from surrounding airports indicated deteriorating conditions. At 0953 PST, the METAR for Burbank (KBUR) reported: 00000KT 1/4SM FG VV002 12/11 A3005. The METAR for Camarillo (KCMA) at 0953 PST reported: 00000KT 1/2SM FG VV003 11/10 A3006. Visibility was consistently reported at 1/4 to 1/2 statute mile, with vertical visibility between 200 and 300 feet AGL. The TAF for the region forecasted continued fog and low ceilings through 1200 PST, with gradual improvement expected by midday.

4.3 Pilot Weather Reports and En Route Conditions
Multiple pilot reports (PIREPs) were filed between 0830 and 0930 PST along the coastal and inland routes. Reports indicated ceilings at 200 to 400 feet AGL, visibility less than 1 statute mile, and widespread IMC. One PIREP at 0915 PST from a fixed-wing aircraft operating at 1,200 feet MSL reported complete loss of visual reference and immediate transition to instrument flight. The accident flight path traversed terrain that rose from approximately 800 feet MSL near the departure corridor to over 1,700 feet MSL in the Calabasas area. The combination of low ceilings, fog, and rising terrain created an environment where VFR flight was not sustainable. The pilot's last recorded radio transmission at 0942 PST indicated a request for a higher altitude due to weather, but no IFR clearance was obtained.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Impact Site and Terrain Profile
The primary impact site was located on a steep, south-facing hillside covered with dense chaparral vegetation. The terrain slope at the point of initial contact was approximately 35 degrees. The initial impact occurred with the upper canopy of mature oak and eucalyptus trees at an elevation of approximately 1,620 feet MSL. The aircraft's descent angle was calculated at approximately 45 degrees relative to the horizontal plane. The ground scar measured 120 feet in length and 15 feet in width, oriented on a magnetic heading of 210 degrees.

5.2 Wreckage Distribution and Fragmentation
The debris field extended approximately 300 feet in length and 200 feet in width, with the majority of wreckage concentrated within a 150-foot radius of the initial impact point. The main rotor blades were fragmented into multiple sections, with evidence of high-energy rotational forces. The tail boom was separated from the fuselage and located 85 feet downslope from the primary impact zone. The fuselage structure was heavily fragmented, with the cabin section compromised by impact forces. No evidence of pre-impact fire, explosion, or in-flight breakup was observed. The distribution pattern was consistent with a controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) scenario under low-visibility conditions.

5.3 Component Examination and Systems Analysis
Recovered flight control components, including cyclic, collective, and anti-torque pedals, were examined for continuity and mechanical integrity. All control linkages were intact, with no evidence of binding, separation, or pre-impact failure. The engine fuel control units, fuel pumps, and combustion chambers were disassembled and inspected. Rotational signatures on turbine blades and compressor stages indicated that both engines were producing power at the time of impact. The fuel system was intact, with no fuel leaks or contamination identified. The radar altimeter and attitude indicators were recovered and subjected to bench testing; all units functioned within manufacturer specifications. The investigation confirmed that the aircraft's systems were operational and that the flight path was consistent with continued VFR flight into deteriorating visibility and rising terrain.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Operator Policies and Operational Control
Island Express Helicopters maintained an operations manual approved by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in accordance with 14 CFR § 135.21. The manual established VFR weather minimums, IMC avoidance procedures, and pilot decision-making protocols. The operator's dispatch procedures required pilots to obtain current weather briefings prior to departure and to continuously monitor en route conditions. The operations manual explicitly prohibited flight into known or forecast IMC without an IFR clearance and appropriate equipment. The operator's safety management system included voluntary reporting mechanisms and recurrent training focused on weather-related risk mitigation. Records indicated that the pilot had previously declined flights due to adverse weather, demonstrating adherence to company policy.

6.2 Regulatory Oversight and Guidance Material
The FAA's oversight of the operator was conducted in accordance with FAA Order 8900.1, Flight Standards Information Management System, Volume 12, Chapter 4, Section 2, which outlines surveillance and inspection procedures for Part 135 operators. The Principal Operations Inspector (POI) and Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) conducted routine surveillance, including ramp inspections, training program audits, and operational control reviews. The most recent comprehensive surveillance was completed on September 18, 2019, with no significant findings or enforcement actions documented. The investigation reviewed the operator's compliance history and confirmed that all regulatory requirements were met at the time of the accident.

6.3 Industry Comparisons and Automation Considerations
The investigation examined industry-wide practices regarding flight control augmentation, automation dependency, and weather decision-making across different certificate holders. While the accident aircraft utilized conventional mechanical-hydraulic flight controls with pilot-managed autopilot functions, the investigation reviewed fixed-wing transport category systems, including the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), to evaluate training paradigms and regulatory oversight frameworks for automated flight control interventions. Additionally, operational procedures from Part 121 scheduled carriers, such as Southwest Airlines, were reviewed for comparative analysis of weather dispatch protocols, crew resource management, and IMC avoidance training. The review highlighted differences in operational control structures, with Part 121 operators typically utilizing centralized dispatch and mandatory IFR routing, whereas Part 135 on-demand operations rely more heavily on pilot-in-command discretion and real-time weather assessment. The NTSB noted that these structural differences influence risk exposure and decision-making timelines in deteriorating meteorological conditions.

6.4 Applicable Federal Aviation Regulations
The following 14 CFR provisions were identified as relevant to the operational context of the accident:
- 14 CFR § 91.155: Basic VFR weather minimums, requiring 3 statute miles visibility and 1,000-foot ceiling for Class E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL.
- 14 CFR § 135.215: VFR weather minimums for Part 135 operations, specifying visibility and distance from cloud requirements.
- 14 CFR § 135.223: IFR operations requirements, including equipment, pilot qualifications, and clearance procedures.
- 14 CFR § 135.247: Pilot qualifications and recent experience requirements for Part 135 operations.
- 14 CFR § 135.351: Training program requirements, including recurrent training and proficiency checks.
- 14 CFR § 135.263/265: Flight time limitations and rest requirements for Part 135 crewmembers.
All regulatory references were cross-referenced with the operator's approved operations specifications and training manuals. The investigation confirmed that the operator's policies aligned with applicable 14 CFR requirements at the time of the flight. No regulatory violations were identified in the pre-flight planning, aircraft airworthiness, or pilot qualification records. The factual data compiled in this report will be utilized by the NTSB investigative groups for further analysis and safety recommendations.

## [sc-0_technical_analysis_065] Technical Analysis

> **Type:** technical_analysis | **Reliability:** 0.852 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis performed by the NTSB Materials Laboratory and Flight Data Recorder Group in support of the investigation into the January 26, 2020, aviation accident involving a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, registration N72EX, which impacted terrain in Calabasas, California. The scope of this examination encompasses the recovery, preservation, and technical evaluation of the aircraft's solid-state flight data recorder (FDR) memory module, primary flight control linkage assemblies, and the main rotor hub spindle components. All examinations were conducted between February 10 and February 18, 2020, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory, Washington, D.C., and the NTSB Data Recovery Facility, Washington, D.C.

Items examined under this specialist's purview include:
- Flight Data Recorder (FDR) memory module, part number (P/N) 980-4700-001, serial number (S/N) 18472
- Main rotor hub forward spindle assembly, P/N 76100-00101-041, S/N 76B-0452-FWD
- Main rotor hub aft spindle assembly, P/N 76100-00101-042, S/N 76B-0452-AFT
- Collective pitch control rod assembly, P/N 76100-00315-008, S/N 76B-0452-COL
- Tail rotor drive shaft coupling, P/N 76100-00205-012, S/N 76B-0452-TRC

All components were received in a secured evidence chain, documented via high-resolution macro photography, and subjected to non-destructive testing (NDT) prior to destructive material sampling. The examination adhered to NTSB Laboratory Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) 4.12, "Recovery and Analysis of Flight Recorder Data," and ASTM E2375-18, "Standard Practice for Ultrasonic Testing of Wrought Products."

2. BACKGROUND

The Sikorsky S-76B is a twin-engine, medium-lift utility helicopter certified under 14 CFR Part 29, Amendment 29-23. The aircraft utilizes a fully articulated, four-blade main rotor system with elastomeric bearings and titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) spindles. The flight control system is mechanically actuated via push-pull tubes, bellcranks, and hydraulic servo actuators, supplemented by a three-axis Stability Augmentation System (SAS) that provides rate damping and attitude hold functions. The SAS architecture operates independently of the primary mechanical linkages, utilizing electro-hydraulic servovalves modulated by analog rate gyros and accelerometers. This design philosophy contrasts with modern fixed-wing flight control augmentation systems, such as the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), which rely on software-mediated pitch authority and single-sensor input validation. The S-76B's mechanical redundancy and analog SAS design preclude automated control surface authority that could override pilot inputs without direct hydraulic pressure modulation.

The accident aircraft, manufactured by Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation (SAC) in 1989, accumulated 12,450.3 airframe hours and 8,920 flight cycles at the time of the accident. Maintenance records indicate compliance with all Sikorsky Service Bulletins (SB) and Airworthiness Directives (AD) applicable to the main rotor hub and flight control systems. The most recent heavy inspection, conducted on November 14, 2019, included eddy current inspection of the main rotor spindles per SB 76-62-001, with no anomalies reported. The FDR was installed per 14 CFR § 135.152 and configured to record 28 mandatory parameters, including barometric altitude, indicated airspeed, collective position, cyclic longitudinal/lateral position, engine torque, main rotor RPM, and vertical acceleration.

For data validation and parameter correlation, the laboratory utilized cross-referencing protocols adapted from commercial aviation maintenance tracking frameworks, including those standardized by Southwest Airlines (SWA) for FDR parameter drift analysis and sensor calibration verification. These methodologies ensure that recorded analog voltages are accurately mapped to engineering units (EU) within ±1.5% tolerance, as specified in RTCA DO-178C and DO-254 guidelines for airborne equipment.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

Physical examination of the recovered components was conducted in a controlled cleanroom environment (ISO Class 7). The FDR memory module exhibited localized thermal discoloration on the aluminum housing, with surface temperatures estimated at 180–210°C based on oxide layer thickness and colorimetric analysis. The solid-state memory board (P/N 980-4700-001-PCB) was extracted using a JTAG interface adapter. No physical damage to the NAND flash memory chips (S/N 18472-01 through 04) was observed. The module was subjected to a low-voltage read cycle at 3.3V DC, yielding 98.7% data recovery.

The main rotor hub forward and aft spindles were sectioned at 120° intervals for metallurgical evaluation. Macroscopic examination revealed impact-induced plastic deformation consistent with high-energy terrain contact. The forward spindle exhibited a primary fracture surface originating at the 0.045-inch subsurface region, approximately 1.2 inches from the blade grip interface. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) at 500x magnification revealed fatigue striations with an average spacing of 0.0008 inches, indicating progressive crack propagation under cyclic loading. Beach marks were visible at 0.15-inch intervals, correlating with approximately 1,200 flight cycles of crack growth prior to final overload failure. The fracture surface morphology is consistent with post-impact dynamic loading rather than in-flight structural failure.

Material analysis was performed per ASTM E8/E8M-21 (tensile testing) and ASTM E18-21 (Rockwell hardness testing). Specimens were extracted from the non-fractured regions of the aft spindle. Chemical composition analysis via optical emission spectroscopy (OES) yielded: 6.12% Al, 4.05% V, 0.18% Fe, 0.012% C, 0.008% N, 0.001% H, balance Ti. These values fall within the AMS 4911 specification for Ti-6Al-4V annealed condition. Tensile testing at room temperature (22°C) resulted in an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 132.4 ksi, yield strength (0.2% offset) of 121.8 ksi, and elongation of 14.2%. Hardness testing across five locations averaged 34.2 HRC, consistent with the manufacturer's specified range of 33–37 HRC.

Non-destructive testing of the collective pitch control rod assembly utilized fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) per ASTM E1417-21. No linear indications were detected on the rod body or spherical bearing interfaces. The tail rotor drive shaft coupling exhibited torsional shear deformation, with a measured angular displacement of 18.5° relative to the neutral axis. Ultrasonic thickness measurements (per ASTM E2375-18) indicated wall thickness reduction of 0.003 inches at the impact zone, consistent with localized plastic yielding.

Photographic documentation includes:
- Photo 1: FDR memory module housing, thermal discoloration mapping
- Photo 2: Forward spindle fracture surface, SEM micrograph at 500x
- Photo 3: Collective control rod FPI results, UV illumination
- Photo 4: Tail rotor coupling torsional deformation, 3D laser scan overlay

All measurements were calibrated against NIST-traceable standards. Dimensional tolerances were verified using a coordinate measuring machine (CMM) with ±0.0005-inch accuracy.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

The recovered FDR data was decoded using the manufacturer's proprietary software suite (v4.2.1) and cross-validated against raw binary telemetry. The recording interval was 1.0 second per parameter, with a total of 28 channels active. Data integrity was confirmed via cyclic redundancy check (CRC) validation, with no bit-flip errors detected in the primary memory sectors.

Timeline reconstruction was synchronized with CVR audio timestamps and secondary surveillance radar (SSR) returns. The FDR recorded valid data from 14:38:00 PST to 14:42:11 PST. Key parameter trends are summarized below:

- Barometric Altitude: Decreased from 1,850 ft MSL to 420 ft MSL over 251 seconds. Descent rate increased from 500 fpm to 2,800 fpm at 14:41:45 PST.
- Indicated Airspeed (KIAS): Decayed from 115 KIAS to 42 KIAS between 14:40:10 and 14:41:50 PST.
- Collective Position: Maintained at 68–72% travel until 14:41:30 PST, followed by a rapid increase to 89% travel at 14:41:55 PST.
- Cyclic Longitudinal Position: Varied between 12° aft and 8° forward, with a sustained 15° aft input at 14:41:40 PST.
- Main Rotor RPM: Maintained at 100% (324 RPM ± 2 RPM) throughout the recording period.
- Engine Torque (Left/Right): Averaged 82% and 79% respectively, with transient spikes to 94% during collective input.
- Vertical Acceleration: Remained within ±0.3g until 14:42:08 PST, where a +4.2g spike was recorded, followed by immediate data termination.

Comparison with normal operational parameters per the Sikorsky S-76B Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) indicates that the aircraft remained within certified flight envelope limits until the final 15 seconds of flight. The RFM specifies a maximum descent rate of 1,500 fpm for autorotative approaches and a Vne of 155 KIAS. The recorded airspeed decay and collective input pattern are consistent with a controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) scenario under instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), where spatial disorientation and loss of visual reference likely contributed to delayed corrective action.

The SAS system data, though not directly recorded by the FDR, was inferred from cyclic position stability and rotor RPM consistency. The absence of oscillatory control inputs or servo actuator hunting indicates the SAS remained functional and did not introduce destabilizing feedback. This operational behavior contrasts with software-mediated augmentation systems like the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), which rely on single-sensor validation and automated pitch authority. The S-76B's analog SAS design requires continuous pilot input for attitude changes, and the recorded control positions reflect direct mechanical actuation without automated override.

Data validation utilized parameter correlation matrices adapted from commercial aviation maintenance protocols, including those implemented by Southwest Airlines (SWA) for FDR drift compensation. Cross-referencing barometric altitude with radar altimeter returns (where available) yielded a mean deviation of 12 ft, well within the ±25 ft tolerance specified in RTCA DO-160G Section 21. Engine torque and rotor RPM correlation confirmed proper powerplant response to collective inputs, with no evidence of compressor stall, fuel flow restriction, or governor malfunction.

5. SUMMARY

The technical examination and data analysis of the recovered flight data recorder, main rotor hub components, and flight control linkages yielded the following factual findings:

1. The FDR memory module (P/N 980-4700-001, S/N 18472) sustained localized thermal exposure but retained 98.7% of recorded data. All 28 mandatory parameters were successfully decoded and validated against NIST-traceable calibration standards.

2. The main rotor hub forward and aft spindles (P/N 76100-00101-041/042) exhibited impact-induced plastic deformation and post-impact fatigue crack propagation. Metallurgical analysis confirmed Ti-6Al-4V composition within AMS 4911 specifications, with UTS of 132.4 ksi and hardness of 34.2 HRC. No pre-impact structural anomalies or manufacturing defects were identified.

3. The collective pitch control rod and tail rotor drive shaft coupling showed no evidence of in-flight mechanical failure. Fracture surfaces and deformation patterns are consistent with high-energy terrain impact loading.

4. FDR data indicates the aircraft operated within certified flight envelope parameters until the final 15 seconds of flight. Main rotor RPM remained stable at 100% (324 RPM), engine torque responded appropriately to collective inputs, and control surface positions reflect direct mechanical actuation without automated system intervention.

5. The recorded descent rate, airspeed decay, and control input timeline are consistent with continued VFR flight into instrument meteorological conditions, with delayed terrain avoidance maneuvers. The Stability Augmentation System (SAS) functioned within design parameters, and no evidence of flight control system malfunction or software-mediated authority override was identified.

All findings are strictly factual and derived from physical examination, standardized testing procedures, and recorded flight data. No conclusions regarding probable cause or operational decision-making are presented in this report.

## [sc-0_witness_testimony_066] Witness Testimony

> **Type:** witness_testimony | **Reliability:** 0.891 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

INTERVIEW OF DAVID R. CHEN, PRIVATE PILOT & AVIATION SAFETY CONSULTANT
Date: March 18, 2020
Time: 14:30 PST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Los Angeles, California
Interviewer: NTSB Investigator (J. Miller)
Witness: David R. Chen

Q: Please state your full name and current occupation for the record.
A: David Robert Chen. I’m a private pilot, instrument rated, and I work as an independent aviation safety consultant. I also do some part-time advisory work for a few regional charter operators, mostly on risk management and training compliance.

Q: What is your relationship to the January 26, 2020, helicopter accident in Calabasas?
A: I wasn’t on the aircraft, obviously. I was... I was actually flying a Piper Archer out of Whiteman that morning, doing some local instrument approaches. I was roughly four miles east-southeast of the impact site when I observed the helicopter. I later submitted my flight data, a written account, and I’ve been cooperating with the NTSB since the initial notification.

Q: Walk us through your observations that morning. Start with approximate time and your position.
A: Okay. It was... I’d say around 9:35, maybe 9:37 AM. I was cruising at about two thousand eight hundred feet, just skirting the base of the marine layer. The ceiling was dropping. I remember checking my altimeter and thinking, “This is getting tight.” I had my transponder on, listening to SoCal Approach. I heard a helicopter call sign—didn’t catch the full tail number, but it sounded like a commercial charter. They were squawking VFR, I think, or maybe just maintaining flight following. Then, about two minutes later, I saw it. It was a Sikorsky S-76B. I recognized the profile, the twin-engine nacelles, the way the tail boom angles. It was heading northwest, climbing slightly, but it was already in the soup. Not heavy rain, just that thick, uniform gray that swallows contrast.

Q: Describe the aircraft’s flight path and your sensory observations.
A: Right. So, I’m looking out the left window, and I see this dark shape against the fog. It’s banking left, maybe twenty, twenty-five degrees. The rotor sound was... it was a steady, rhythmic thump, but then it changed. It got higher pitched, almost strained, like the pilot was pulling collective or trying to climb out of a sink. I couldn’t see the ground, obviously, but I knew the terrain was rising fast out there. I remember thinking, “He’s too low for that ridge.” Then, maybe ten, fifteen seconds later, the sound just... cut out. Not an explosion, not at first. Just a sudden stop, like a heavy object hitting dirt and chaparral. Then a dull thud, and a few seconds later, a muffled pop. I didn’t see flames immediately because of the fog, but I saw a dark plume of smoke start to rise. I immediately turned away, keyed the emergency frequency, and started heading back to Whiteman.

Q: You mentioned the pilot was in reduced visibility. What was your assessment of the weather conditions?
A: It was classic coastal IMC. Visibility was probably under a mile, maybe half a mile in the thicker patches. The ceiling was around eight hundred feet, but it was uneven. I was flying VFR, but I was on the edge. I had my instruments cross-checked, but I was still looking outside. The pilot of that helicopter... I don’t know his exact training, but continuing VFR into that kind of weather, especially with rising terrain, it’s... it’s a known trap. Spatial disorientation sets in fast. You lose the horizon, your inner ear lies to you, and before you know it, you’re descending into a hillside.

Q: You’ve worked in aviation safety. How do you view the operational and regulatory context surrounding this type of flight?
A: Well, it’s... it’s complicated. I mean, the NTSB has been looking at VFR-into-IMC for decades. It’s not a new problem. But when you look at how operators manage risk, it really comes down to training and oversight. I’ve reviewed a lot of FAA guidance, like Order 8900.1, which lays out how inspectors are supposed to evaluate operator safety programs. But in practice, there’s a lot of pressure to complete the mission. I’ve seen it in corporate aviation, in charter, even in some airline environments. You know, Southwest Airlines has a really robust safety culture, right? They’ve got strict SOPs, crew resource management, and they don’t mess around with weather minimums. But not every operator has that kind of institutional discipline. When you’re flying a high-performance machine like a Sikorsky, the aircraft will do what you tell it to, but it won’t save you from bad decisions.

Q: You mentioned automation and training. Some have drawn comparisons to other aircraft systems. What’s your perspective?
A: Yeah, I’ve heard people bring up the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System, or MCAS, from the 737 MAX incidents. And I get why. It’s about automation dependency, right? When pilots aren’t trained to handle the raw aircraft, or when systems mask underlying problems, you get into trouble. But in this case, it’s not an automated system pushing the nose down. It’s a human decision to keep going when the weather closed in. Still, the principle is similar: you can’t out-train a lack of discipline, and you can’t out-automate poor judgment. The IIC on this case, he asked me a lot about pilot decision-making and how operators track weather trends. I told him what I’ve always said: you need hard stops. If the ceiling drops below a certain threshold, you divert. Period.

Q: Have you followed any recent regulatory actions that might impact helicopter operations or maintenance standards?
A: I keep up with the ADs, yeah. There’s been a lot of focus on rotorcraft systems lately. I mean, Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-51, for example, that’s a newer one, but it shows how the FAA is tightening up on certain inspection intervals and component tracking. It’s not directly related to the S-76B, obviously, but it reflects a broader shift toward proactive maintenance and data-driven oversight. In the past, a lot of operators ran things until something broke. Now, there’s more emphasis on predictive maintenance, vibration analysis, that kind of thing. But again, it doesn’t matter how well you maintain the airframe if the pilot pushes into weather they can’t handle.

Q: Let’s return to the timeline. After you reported the incident, what did you do?
A: I landed at Whiteman around 9:55. I shut down, pulled the SD card from my Garmin, and called the tower. They patched me through to the local FSDO, and then the NTSB got involved pretty quickly. I stayed on the phone for about twenty minutes, gave them my coordinates, my heading, the time I lost audio contact. I didn’t want to speculate, just stick to what I saw and heard. I remember feeling... I don’t know, heavy. You hear about these things, but when you’re that close, it’s different. The silence after the impact, it just hangs in the air.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add for the record?
A: Just that... I hope the investigation focuses on the human factors side. The weather, the terrain, the decision to continue. I know the Board will do a thorough job. They always do. But I think we need to look at how charter operators are incentivized, how pilots are trained for IMC escape, and how we can make sure that when the fog rolls in, the right call is the easy call. That’s all I’ve got.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Chen. We’ll follow up if we need clarification.
A: Yeah, of course. I’m available. Just let me know.

## [sc-0_regulatory_filing_067] Regulatory Filing

> **Type:** regulatory_filing | **Reliability:** 0.87 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION
FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
FLIGHT STANDARDS SERVICE
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20591

INTERAGENCY REGULATORY OVERSIGHT REPORT
DOCKET NO. FAA-2021-0452 | NTSB ACCIDENT NO. DCA20MA028
DATE OF ISSUANCE: October 14, 2024

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This document constitutes the Federal Aviation Administration’s formal regulatory response to National Transportation Safety Board Safety Recommendation A-21-014 through A-21-018, issued in conjunction with the investigation of the January 26, 2020, aviation accident involving a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter (Registration N72EX) operating under 14 CFR Part 135. The referenced accident occurred in Calabasas, California, under instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), resulting in the fatal destruction of the rotorcraft and the loss of all nine occupants. This correspondence addresses compliance obligations, airworthiness directives, and systemic regulatory oversight deficiencies pertaining to visual flight rules (VFR) operations in deteriorating meteorological conditions, terrain awareness system mandates, and flight crew training standards. All actions herein are executed pursuant to 14 CFR Chapter I, Subchapter F, and are coordinated with the NTSB Office of Aviation Safety.

2. BACKGROUND
The regulatory framework governing rotorcraft operations under Part 135 establishes baseline requirements for weather minimums, flight planning, and crew resource management. Specifically, 14 CFR § 91.155 prescribes VFR weather minimums, while 14 CFR § 135.215 governs IFR operations and the mandatory transition to instrument flight rules when meteorological conditions fall below established minima. The operator in question held a valid Part 135 certificate and operated under an approved Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) and Operations Specifications (OpSpecs) that did not mandate terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS) installation for the subject rotorcraft type.

Historically, the Agency has addressed VFR-into-IMC accidents through targeted surveillance and advisory circulars. However, the Lead Investigator’s preliminary analysis of the accident sequence identified critical deficiencies in pilot decision-making, inadequate real-time meteorological data integration, and the absence of mandatory terrain proximity alerting for Part 135 rotorcraft. These findings align with longstanding NTSB recommendations regarding the expansion of TAWS requirements and enhanced VFR/IFR transition training.

For comparative regulatory context, the Agency has evaluated certification and operational oversight paradigms applied to transport-category aircraft. The certification history of the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) on Boeing 737 MAX aircraft, governed under 14 CFR § 25.783 and § 25.1309, demonstrated systemic vulnerabilities in automated flight control augmentation, crew interface design, and supplemental type certificate (STC) validation processes. Similarly, operational oversight reviews of Southwest Airlines Co. under 14 CFR Part 121.344 highlighted the necessity of standardized crew resource management (CRM) protocols, fatigue risk management, and mandatory terrain avoidance training for multi-crew environments. While rotorcraft operations under Part 135 differ structurally from Part 121 transport operations, the regulatory principles governing automated system integration, crew coordination, and terrain avoidance remain directly applicable to the Sikorsky S-76B operational profile.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
The Agency’s compliance review, conducted in accordance with FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 3, Chapter 18, Section 4, indicates that the operator maintained nominal compliance with existing Part 135 airworthiness and operational requirements at the time of the accident. However, the regulatory framework itself exhibits material gaps that contributed to the accident sequence.

First, 14 CFR § 135.181 and § 135.215 do not currently mandate real-time terrain proximity alerting or automated flight path monitoring for rotorcraft operating under VFR in mountainous or rapidly rising terrain environments. The absence of a regulatory requirement for TAWS-B or equivalent systems in Part 135 rotorcraft operations represents a critical oversight deficiency. Second, the Second in Command (SIC) role in Part 135 helicopter operations lacks standardized CRM and instrument transition training requirements comparable to those mandated under 14 CFR § 121.344 for transport-category aircraft. The Lead Investigator’s operational analysis confirmed that inadequate crew coordination and delayed recognition of deteriorating visibility directly compromised the flight crew’s ability to execute a timely diversion or instrument transition.

Third, the Agency’s oversight procedures, as documented in FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 12, Chapter 1, Section 3, rely heavily on Principal Operations Inspector (POI) discretion for surveillance frequency and training program validation. This decentralized approach has resulted in inconsistent enforcement of VFR-into-IMC mitigation strategies across regional operators. Furthermore, the certification pathway for flight control augmentation systems in rotorcraft, including STC approvals for stability augmentation and autopilot integration, lacks harmonized human factors validation standards. The regulatory lessons derived from the MCAS certification review underscore the necessity of rigorous failure mode analysis, pilot interface standardization, and mandatory simulator-based upset recovery training prior to operational deployment.

The Agency concludes that while Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation’s type certificate design met all applicable 14 CFR Part 27 airworthiness standards at the time of manufacture, the operational environment and regulatory oversight framework failed to account for the compounding risks of VFR flight into IMC, rising terrain, and inadequate crew resource management. The current MMEL provisions do not adequately address terrain awareness system degradation, and the absence of mandatory instrument transition training for Part 135 helicopter crews creates an unacceptable safety margin deficiency.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
Pursuant to the findings detailed herein, the Federal Aviation Administration hereby mandates the following corrective actions and regulatory amendments:

a. Equipment Mandate: Within 365 calendar days of this directive, all Part 135 rotorcraft operators shall install and maintain a TAWS-B or equivalent terrain awareness and warning system compliant with TSO-C151b. Operators must submit revised MMELs and OpSpecs amendments to their respective Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) for approval within 90 days.

b. Training Program Revision: Within 180 calendar days, all Part 135 helicopter operators shall revise their approved training programs to include mandatory VFR-into-IMC recognition, instrument transition procedures, and CRM modules aligned with 14 CFR § 135.331 and § 135.335. Training curricula must incorporate scenario-based simulator exercises addressing rapid visibility degradation and terrain avoidance.

c. Regulatory Oversight Enhancement: The Agency shall issue a revision to FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 3, Chapter 18, within 120 calendar days to standardize POI surveillance protocols for VFR/IFR transition compliance, terrain awareness system validation, and crew training record audits. The revised guidance will mandate quarterly compliance reviews for operators conducting mountainous or coastal VFR operations.

d. Certification Process Harmonization: The Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) shall initiate a rulemaking action to align rotorcraft flight control augmentation system certification standards with the human factors and failure mode analysis requirements established under 14 CFR § 25.783 and § 25.1309. This action will include mandatory pilot interface validation and upset recovery training requirements for all STC and type certificate amendments involving automated flight control systems.

e. Follow-Up Inspection Schedule: The NTSB and FAA shall establish a joint oversight committee to conduct biannual compliance audits of Part 135 rotorcraft operators. Initial compliance verification shall occur 180 days post-implementation, with subsequent reviews scheduled at 12-month intervals until full regulatory integration is confirmed.

All affected certificate holders shall acknowledge receipt of this directive and submit a compliance implementation plan to the appropriate FSDO within 30 calendar days. Failure to comply with the mandated timelines will result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR § 13.11 and may include suspension of operating authority. This document serves as the official regulatory response to the referenced NTSB safety recommendations and shall be incorporated into the Federal Register docket for public comment and final rulemaking proceedings.

AUTHORIZED BY:
Office of Flight Standards
Regulatory Compliance Division
Federal Aviation Administration
Docket No. FAA-2021-0452

HEADLINE: Nine Dead After Helicopter Crashes in California Hills; Pilot Flew Into Low Visibility, Investigators Say

BYLINE: [Reporter Name], [News Outlet]
DATELINE: CALABASAS, Calif. —

A charter helicopter carrying nine people crashed into a steep, brush-covered hillside in Calabasas on Sunday, killing everyone on board, authorities confirmed. The aircraft went down in dense fog and low clouds, prompting an immediate federal investigation into the circumstances that led to the fatal accident.

Investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board determined the pilot continued flying under visual flight rules into deteriorating weather conditions, a scenario known in aviation as VFR into IMC. Visual flight rules require pilots to maintain clear sight of the ground and other aircraft, while instrument meteorological conditions describe weather that obscures visibility and requires reliance on cockpit instruments. The decision to press forward into the fog led to spatial disorientation and a high-speed impact with rising terrain, officials said. The crash has devastated families, halted local charter operations, and reignited a national conversation about aviation safety in adverse weather.

“The preliminary data indicates the pilot was operating in conditions that exceeded the minimums for visual flight,” said a spokesperson for the Safety Board during a Monday press briefing. “We are examining all aspects of the flight, including weather briefings, pilot decision-making, and operational pressures. Our focus remains on determining the exact sequence of events and issuing recommendations to prevent future tragedies.”

Federal aviation regulators echoed the call for caution. “The FAA is cooperating fully with the investigation and reviewing all applicable guidance, including Order 8900.1, which outlines inspector protocols for charter operator oversight,” said an FAA regional director. “We are committed to ensuring that commercial helicopter operators adhere to the strictest safety standards, particularly when navigating complex coastal weather patterns.”

The aircraft, a Sikorsky S-76B, was operated by Island Express Helicopters, a Southern California-based charter service. It had departed from John Wayne Airport in Orange County and was en route to Camarillo Airport when it encountered a thick marine layer that blanketed the Santa Monica Mountains. The S-76 is a widely used twin-engine helicopter known for its reliability and frequent use in corporate transport, emergency medical services, and VIP travel.

Aviation safety experts note that flying into low visibility without proper instrument training or clearance remains one of the leading causes of fatal helicopter accidents. “When a pilot loses visual reference to the horizon, the inner ear can send false signals to the brain, creating a dangerous illusion of level flight while the aircraft is actually banking or descending,” said Dr. Marcus Lin, an aviation human factors specialist at the University of Southern California. “This is why strict adherence to weather minimums is critical. Unlike fixed-wing aircraft that rely on complex automation like the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System to prevent stalls, helicopters in this class depend heavily on pilot judgment and real-time weather assessment.”

The Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System, or MCAS, is an automated flight control feature designed to adjust aircraft pitch in specific conditions, most notably discussed in recent years following commercial jet incidents. While not present in the Sikorsky S-76B, experts point to the broader industry debate over how much reliance should be placed on automated systems versus pilot training and decision-making in unpredictable environments.

Grief has rippled through the community as families of the victims process the sudden loss. “They were just trying to get home,” said Maria Gonzalez, whose brother was a passenger on the flight. “He loved flying, but he always said safety came first. We just want answers so no other family has to go through this.” Vigils have been held near the crash site, with flowers, photographs, and handwritten notes left at a makeshift memorial overlooking the canyon.

The incident echoes a troubling pattern in general aviation. According to NTSB data, controlled flight into terrain during poor weather accounts for a significant percentage of fatal helicopter crashes over the past two decades. While the S-76B has a strong overall safety record, charter operators face unique pressures, including tight schedules, client expectations, and the financial implications of canceled flights. Industry advocates stress that no schedule should ever override weather minimums.

Southwest Airlines, which operates one of the largest commercial fleets in the country, released a statement expressing condolences and highlighting the importance of standardized weather protocols across all aviation sectors. “Our thoughts are with the families and friends affected by this tragedy,” said a Southwest Airlines spokesperson. “While our operations differ significantly from charter helicopter services, we share a fundamental commitment to prioritizing passenger safety above all else. Every flight, regardless of size or mission, must be grounded when conditions fall below safe thresholds.”

The investigation remains active. Federal investigators have recovered the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, both of which are undergoing forensic analysis at a specialized laboratory in Washington, D.C. Wreckage mapping, weather radar reconstruction, and pilot training records are currently being reviewed. The Safety Board expects to release a preliminary report within 30 days, with a final determination likely taking up to two years.

Until then, the aviation community and grieving families await clarity. For now, the quiet hills of Calabasas stand as a somber reminder of the unforgiving nature of flight and the critical importance of respecting the sky’s limits.

## [sc-0_expert_deposition_069] Expert Deposition

> **Type:** expert_deposition | **Reliability:** 0.946 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. INTRODUCTION
Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation submits this technical analysis as a designated party to the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigative hearing regarding the January 26, 2020, accident involving a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, registration N72EX. As the original equipment manufacturer, Sikorsky provides engineering, systems performance, and human factors expertise to support the Safety Board’s fact-finding process. This submission addresses the aircraft’s design compliance, systems functionality, operational context, and the intersection of pilot decision-making with environmental conditions. The scope encompasses a comprehensive review of flight data recorder (FDR) telemetry, maintenance documentation, weather reconstruction, and industry-standard operational practices. Our objective is to present a technically rigorous, evidence-based assessment of the factors that contributed to the loss of the aircraft and to advance actionable safety recommendations that align with contemporary aviation risk management principles.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND
On the morning of January 26, 2020, the subject S-76B departed John Wayne Airport (KSNA) en route to Camarillo Airport (KCMA) under visual flight rules (VFR). The aircraft was operated by Island Express under Title 14 CFR Part 135. As documented in the Safety Board’s docket materials, including the Weather Reconstruction Report (Docket Exhibit 12A) and the FDR Data Package (Docket Exhibit 14B), the flight encountered rapidly deteriorating meteorological conditions characterized by low ceilings, reduced visibility, and rising terrain in the Calabasas area. The pilot elected to continue VFR flight into instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), resulting in spatial disorientation and controlled flight into terrain (CFIT). All nine occupants perished.

The aircraft’s maintenance records, reviewed in Docket Exhibit 8C, confirm full compliance with all applicable airworthiness directives, service bulletins, and manufacturer-recommended inspection intervals. No mechanical anomalies, system failures, or deferred maintenance items were identified that would have degraded flight control authority, engine performance, or avionics functionality. The aircraft was equipped with a standard S-76B avionics suite, including dual attitude and heading reference systems (AHRS), a primary flight display (PFD), and a multi-function display (MFD). The MCAS equipment, a multi-channel attitude stabilization and navigation augmentation system integrated into the aircraft’s flight control architecture, was operational and recorded nominal parameters throughout the flight. The Board’s preliminary systems analysis confirms that all recorded telemetry aligns with expected performance envelopes for the S-76B under the prevailing flight conditions.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS
The technical assessment of this accident centers on three interrelated domains: aircraft systems performance, environmental and operational context, and human factors in VFR-to-IMC transitions. Engineering data extracted from the FDR indicates that the helicopter remained within certified structural and aerodynamic limits until the final moments of flight. Engine torque, rotor RPM, and control input telemetry show no evidence of power loss, control surface binding, or flight control system degradation. The MCAS equipment maintained stable attitude reference outputs, with no fault codes or degradation in sensor fusion algorithms. This confirms that the aircraft’s design and maintenance posture did not contribute to the loss of control.

The primary technical challenge in this scenario is the physiological and cognitive impact of inadvertent IMC entry. When visual references are lost, the human vestibular system rapidly generates conflicting sensory inputs, leading to spatial disorientation. The FDR data reveals a gradual, uncommanded descent accompanied by increasing bank angles and pitch oscillations consistent with vestibular illusion and loss of horizon reference. This pattern is well-documented in aviation human factors literature and aligns with the Safety Board’s historical findings on VFR-into-IMC accidents. The aircraft’s standard avionics, while fully functional, do not provide automated terrain avoidance or synthetic vision capabilities that could mitigate the effects of disorientation in the absence of an instrument flight rules (IFR) clearance.

From an operational standpoint, the decision to continue VFR flight into deteriorating weather reflects a breakdown in operational risk management. Industry best practices, as outlined in FAA Advisory Circular 120-12A and ICAO Annex 6, emphasize proactive weather diversion, strict adherence to VFR minimums, and the implementation of formalized go/no-go decision matrices. The operator’s flight following procedures, while compliant with Part 135 requirements at the time, lacked real-time terrain proximity alerts and automated weather escalation protocols. The MCAS equipment, though designed to enhance attitude stability and navigation accuracy, does not override pilot authority or substitute for IFR certification. Its performance in this event underscores a broader industry limitation: flight control augmentation systems cannot compensate for the loss of visual reference or the absence of terrain awareness in VFR operations.

Comparative analysis with contemporary rotorcraft operations reveals that the integration of Helicopter Terrain Awareness and Warning Systems (HTAWS), synthetic vision, and automated weather decision-support tools significantly reduces CFIT risk. The S-76B platform, as originally certified, was not mandated to include these systems for VFR Part 135 operations. However, engineering evaluations demonstrate that retrofitting such capabilities is technically feasible and aligns with modern safety management system (SMS) frameworks. The absence of these systems, combined with the physiological inevitability of spatial disorientation in IMC, created a high-risk operational environment that exceeded the protective capacity of standard VFR procedures.

4. CONCLUSIONS
Based on a comprehensive review of flight data, maintenance documentation, weather reconstruction, and human factors research, Sikorsky concludes that the accident was primarily caused by the pilot’s continuation of VFR flight into deteriorating IMC, resulting in spatial disorientation and controlled flight into terrain. The aircraft’s airframe, propulsion, flight controls, and avionics systems, including the MCAS equipment, performed within design specifications and did not contribute to the loss of control. No maintenance deficiencies, manufacturing anomalies, or system failures were identified.

The Safety Board’s investigation has appropriately highlighted the complex interplay between environmental conditions, operational decision-making, and human physiological limitations. While the aircraft was fully airworthy and compliant with all regulatory requirements, the operational context exposed critical gaps in VFR risk mitigation, particularly regarding terrain awareness, weather escalation protocols, and pilot training for inadvertent IMC recovery. The manufacturer’s position is that the accident underscores the necessity of evolving regulatory and operational standards to address the inherent vulnerabilities of VFR flight in complex terrain and dynamic weather environments.

To prevent recurrence, Sikorsky recommends the following safety improvements: (1) mandatory installation of HTAWS or equivalent terrain awareness systems for all Part 135 rotorcraft operating in mountainous or high-terrain regions; (2) enhanced pilot training programs focused on spatial disorientation recognition, automated instrument scan techniques, and standardized IMC recovery procedures; (3) implementation of real-time weather decision-support tools integrated with flight following and dispatch operations; and (4) industry-wide adoption of formalized operational risk management frameworks that prioritize conservative weather diversion over mission completion.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS
In response to this accident and broader industry safety trends, Sikorsky has already implemented several corrective measures. The manufacturer has issued Service Bulletin S76B-2021-04, which provides updated guidance on inadvertent IMC recovery, enhanced pilot training curricula, and recommended avionics upgrade pathways. Sikorsky has also collaborated with training organizations to develop simulator-based modules that replicate VFR-to-IMC transitions, emphasizing vestibular illusion recognition and instrument cross-check discipline. Additionally, the company has made available retrofit kits for synthetic vision and terrain awareness systems, ensuring operators can integrate modern safety technologies into legacy S-76B fleets.

Looking forward, Sikorsky proposes the following improvements to advance rotorcraft safety: (1) development of an integrated flight deck decision-support system that combines real-time weather data, terrain mapping, and automated risk scoring to assist pilots in go/no-go decisions; (2) advocacy for regulatory updates that align Part 135 VFR operations with contemporary SMS requirements, including mandatory terrain awareness and enhanced weather monitoring; (3) expansion of manufacturer-operator partnerships to establish standardized operational risk assessment protocols for high-terrain, high-traffic corridors; and (4) continued research into human-machine interface design to reduce cognitive workload during high-stress, low-visibility scenarios.

Sikorsky remains fully committed to supporting the Safety Board’s investigative process and to advancing the safety of rotorcraft operations worldwide. The manufacturer will continue to provide technical expertise, engineering data, and safety recommendations to ensure that lessons learned from this tragedy translate into measurable, industry-wide improvements. By integrating advanced avionics, strengthening pilot training, and fostering a culture of proactive risk management, the aviation community can significantly reduce the likelihood of VFR-into-IMC accidents and protect the lives of those who rely on helicopter transportation.
