## [sc-0_internal_memo_070] Internal Memo

> **Type:** internal_memo | **Reliability:** 0.605 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

TO: All Flight Operations Personnel, Chief Pilots, Training Department, SMS Coordinators
FROM: Director of Flight Standards & Training, Corporate Aviation Safety Division
DATE: February 14, 2020
SUBJECT: MANDATORY TRAINING UPDATE: VFR INTO IMC PREVENTION & TERRAIN AWARENESS PROTOCOLS
REF: SMS-2020-014, FSTD-TRN-8892, Prior Bulletin TRN-2019-041

PURPOSE:
This Training Bulletin mandates immediate updates to all recurrent and initial pilot training curricula. The directive establishes standardized decision-making frameworks, terrain avoidance procedures, and instrument transition protocols to mitigate the risk of continued visual flight into instrument meteorological conditions (VFR into IMC). Compliance is required for all line pilots, check airmen, and simulator instructors effective immediately.

BACKGROUND:
On January 26, 2020, a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter crashed into terrain in Calabasas, California, during instrument meteorological conditions, killing all nine persons on board. Preliminary investigation data indicates the pilot continued VFR flight into an area of rapidly deteriorating visibility and rising terrain, leading to spatial disorientation and loss of control. While our operational fleet and mission profiles differ, the underlying human factors—pressure to complete a mission, degraded visual references, and delayed transition to instrument flight—are universal across rotorcraft and fixed-wing operations.

Internal Safety Management System (SMS) audits conducted in Q4 2019 identified a 14% increase in pilot-reported marginal weather encounters and a corresponding gap in standardized IMC escape training. Our current syllabus lacks explicit, scenario-based modules addressing rapid terrain closure during visual flight. Furthermore, industry-wide analysis of recent automation-related incidents highlights a recurring vulnerability: over-reliance on system alerts without proactive pilot intervention. The Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) failures on commercial transport aircraft serve as a stark reminder that automated safeguards cannot compensate for delayed pilot recognition or inadequate procedural training. Similarly, Southwest Airlines Co (SWA) recently published internal safety data demonstrating that standardized terrain awareness callouts and strict VFR/IFR decision gates reduced weather-related deviations by 32% across their regional operations.

Regulatory guidance remains clear. The FAA Flight Standards Order (FSO) 8900.1, Volume 3, Chapter 18, explicitly requires operators to train pilots on recognizing deteriorating weather, executing immediate 180-degree turns, and utilizing terrain awareness systems as primary decision aids. Our current procedures do not fully align with these updated FSO directives.

DETAILS:
Effective March 1, 2020, the following updates will be integrated into all training cycles. All referenced materials are available on the internal training portal under Document Control ID: TRN-2020-088.

1. Curriculum Revisions:
   - Add Module 4.2: “VFR to IMC Transition & Terrain Avoidance” to all recurrent training blocks.
   - Integrate mandatory simulator scenarios featuring rapid visibility degradation, rising terrain, and partial panel instrument failures.
   - Update the Pilot Operating Handbook (POH) supplement P/N 76B-TRN-441 to include the new “IMC Decision Matrix” (Form SMS-DEC-09).

2. Procedural Updates:
   - Implement the “Three-Point Weather Check” prior to departure and at all enroute waypoints.
   - Require explicit verbal callouts when visibility drops below 3 SM or ceiling falls below 1,000 ft AGL.
   - Mandate immediate 180-degree turn execution upon encountering unforecast IMC, regardless of mission priority.
   - Cross-reference terrain awareness system (TAWS/EGPMS) alerts with visual references. Do not suppress or ignore terrain warnings.

3. Automation & System Awareness:
   - Review limitations of automated flight control and terrain warning systems. Pilots must maintain manual instrument proficiency and not defer to system logic when visual cues conflict with instrument indications.
   - Reference the MCAS incident analysis (Report SAF-2019-112) during classroom briefings to illustrate the dangers of automation complacency and delayed manual intervention.
   - Verify all TAWS/EGPMS databases are current per Work Order WO-MAINT-2020-033. Outdated terrain databases will be flagged during pre-flight checks.

4. Instructor & Evaluator Requirements:
   - All check airmen must complete the updated “Weather Decision-Making” instructor course (Course ID: CPT-884) by February 28, 2020.
   - Simulator grading rubrics will be revised to penalize delayed IMC recognition and failure to execute immediate escape maneuvers.

ACTION REQUIRED:
All personnel must complete the following actions by the specified deadlines. Non-compliance will result in temporary suspension of flight status until training requirements are satisfied.

1. Line Pilots & First Officers:
   - Complete the online VFR/IMC Decision-Making e-learning module (Module ID: EL-2020-04) by February 25, 2020.
   - Schedule and complete the updated simulator scenario (Scenario ID: SIM-IMC-07) during your next recurrent training cycle.
   - Acknowledge receipt of this bulletin via the internal compliance portal (Ref: ACK-TRN-2020-014) by February 18, 2020.

2. Chief Pilots & Training Managers:
   - Distribute updated POH supplements and decision matrices to all flight crews by February 20, 2020.
   - Verify completion of instructor course CPT-884 for all assigned check airmen. Submit completion roster to Flight Standards by February 28, 2020.
   - Audit pre-flight weather planning logs weekly and report deviations to the SMS Coordinator.

3. Maintenance & Avionics Support:
   - Execute Work Order WO-MAINT-2020-033 to verify TAWS/EGPMS database currency across all fleet aircraft. Complete by March 5, 2020.
   - Log all terrain system discrepancies in the maintenance tracking system under Category: AVIONICS-WEATHER.

4. Safety Management System (SMS) Office:
   - Monitor training completion rates and generate weekly compliance dashboards.
   - Conduct unannounced line checks focusing on weather decision-making and terrain awareness callouts starting March 10, 2020.

This directive supersedes all prior training bulletins regarding weather avoidance and terrain awareness. Questions regarding syllabus integration or simulator scheduling should be directed to the Training Standards Office at ext. 4402 or via email to training.standards@company.internal.

Flight safety is non-negotiable. Adherence to these protocols is mandatory.

## [sc-0_preliminary_report_071] Preliminary Report

> **Type:** preliminary_report | **Reliability:** 0.866 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION SAFETY BOARD
PRELIMINARY ACCIDENT REPORT
AVIATION DIVISION
REPORT ID: WPR20FA088-PRELIM

1. SYNOPSIS
On January 26, 2020, at approximately 0945 Pacific Standard Time, a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, registered N72EX, impacted terrain in Calabasas, California, resulting in the fatal injury of all nine persons on board. The aircraft was operating under visual flight rules (VFR) when it encountered instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) and continued into an area of reduced visibility and rising terrain. This preliminary document summarizes initial factual information, establishes the investigative scope, and outlines procedural decisions for the ongoing inquiry. All information contained herein is subject to revision as the investigation progresses.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information has been compiled from on-scene observations, radar data, and initial witness interviews. The helicopter departed John Wayne Airport (SNA) in Santa Ana, California, en route to Camarillo Airport (CMA) in Ventura County. Initial radar track analysis indicates the aircraft maintained a generally northwesterly course before deviating from its planned route and entering a localized area of low cloud cover and fog. Witness accounts collected during the initial site survey describe hearing the sound of a helicopter engine operating at high power, followed by a brief period of silence prior to impact. Several observers noted the aircraft appeared to be flying at a low altitude relative to the surrounding hillsides, though these observations remain uncorroborated by independent telemetry at this stage.

Meteorological data obtained from nearby surface observation stations and satellite imagery suggest that the region was experiencing a marine layer with ceilings below 1,000 feet above ground level and visibility reduced to less than one mile in localized pockets. The pilot had been operating under VFR, and preliminary information indicates the flight may have inadvertently entered instrument meteorological conditions. The NTSB is currently evaluating all available weather products, pilot communications, and air traffic control recordings to reconstruct the environmental conditions at the time of the event.

Damage assessment conducted by the initial response team indicates the aircraft sustained catastrophic structural failure upon impact with a steep, brush-covered hillside. The main wreckage was located within a concentrated debris field, with fragmentation consistent with high-energy terrain impact. Preliminary examination of the recovered components revealed no evidence of pre-impact fire or in-flight breakup. The airframe, manufactured by Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation, will undergo detailed forensic analysis to determine the sequence of structural loading and failure modes. Investigators are also cataloging all recovered flight control components, avionics, and engine assemblies for subsequent laboratory evaluation.

As part of the systems review, the investigation team will examine all installed flight control and stability augmentation equipment. It should be noted that the Sikorsky S-76B does not incorporate a Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) or similar automated pitch-trim architecture; however, all relevant flight control linkages, hydraulic actuators, and autopilot interfaces will be thoroughly inspected to rule out any anomalous system behavior. The crew complement included a pilot in command and a First Officer (FO), whose roles, qualifications, and recent flight experience are currently under review. Initial records indicate the First Officer was seated in the right-hand position, and both crew members’ duty times, rest periods, and medical certifications are being compiled for the human performance analysis.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The NTSB has activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical and operational aspects of this accident. The following groups have been established and are currently conducting field and laboratory activities: Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Human Performance, Weather, Survival Factors, and Air Traffic Control. Each group is led by an NTSB investigator-in-charge and includes technical advisors from relevant industry and regulatory organizations.

Parties to the investigation have been formally designated in accordance with NTSB regulations. Participating entities include the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the operator of the aircraft, Sikorsky (as the airframe manufacturer), the engine manufacturer, the pilot’s professional association, and the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE) for initial response coordination. All parties have been briefed on the scope of the investigation, the requirement for factual data collection, and the prohibition against public speculation or release of unverified information.

Evidence secured to date includes the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR), both of which have been recovered and transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C. Initial readout of the CVR is underway, while the FDR is undergoing data extraction and validation. Additional physical evidence, including control cables, engine components, and avionics modules, has been cataloged, photographed, and secured for transport to specialized testing facilities. The NTSB has also obtained all available air traffic control communications, radar tracks, and weather observation logs for the relevant timeframe.

Planned examinations include a detailed teardown of the main and tail rotor systems, metallurgical analysis of critical structural components, and a comprehensive review of the aircraft’s maintenance records. The human performance group will conduct interviews with dispatch personnel, maintenance technicians, and individuals familiar with the crew’s recent operations. Weather specialists are reconstructing the meteorological environment using numerical weather prediction models, satellite data, and surface observations to determine the spatial and temporal evolution of the low-visibility conditions.

4. NEXT STEPS
The investigation will proceed through a structured sequence of data collection, analysis, and peer review. In the immediate term, the NTSB will complete the readout of the flight recorders, finalize the wreckage mapping, and conduct initial laboratory examinations of the recovered systems components. The operations group will continue to compile the pilot’s flight history, training records, and recent operational experience, while the weather group will refine the meteorological reconstruction to better characterize the visibility and ceiling conditions along the flight path.

A public hearing is anticipated once the factual record has been sufficiently developed, though no date has been established at this time. Interim updates will be issued as significant factual milestones are reached, and all findings will be subject to rigorous technical review before inclusion in the final report. The NTSB emphasizes that the information presented in this preliminary document is strictly factual, incomplete, and subject to change as additional data becomes available. No conclusions regarding operational decisions, system performance, or probable cause have been reached, and all investigative activities will continue in accordance with established NTSB protocols.

Further procedural directives will be issued to all participating parties regarding data submission deadlines, laboratory access schedules, and coordination meetings. The investigation team will maintain strict adherence to the factual record, ensuring that all analyses are grounded in verified evidence and peer-reviewed methodologies. Updates will be provided through official NTSB channels as the inquiry advances toward the development of a comprehensive factual report.

## [sc-0_investigation_report_072] Investigation Report

> **Type:** investigation_report | **Reliability:** 0.919 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 On January 26, 2020, at approximately 0945 Pacific Standard Time (PST), a helicopter impacted rising terrain in a hilly, residential area of Calabasas, California. The accident site was located at geographic coordinates 34°08′12″N, 118°41′36″W, at an elevation of approximately 1,200 feet mean sea level (MSL). The impact occurred during daylight hours under instrument meteorological conditions (IMC). The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) was notified of the event at 1012 PST by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Air Traffic Control System Command Center. The Board initiated an investigation in accordance with 49 CFR Part 831, establishing a command post at the accident site and deploying specialized investigative groups.

1.2 The aircraft involved was a Sikorsky S-76B, bearing United States registration number N72EX, manufacturer serial number 760352. The aircraft was operated by Island Express Holding Corp., conducting a commercial passenger flight under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 135. The flight originated from John Wayne Airport (SNA), Orange County, California, at 0906 PST, with a planned destination of Camarillo Airport (CMA), Ventura County, California. The flight was operating under visual flight rules (VFR) at the time of departure.

1.3 The operation was conducted as an on-demand charter flight carrying eight passengers and one pilot-in-command. The flight was authorized under the operator’s operations specifications (OpSpecs) for rotorcraft operations. The Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) coordinated with local law enforcement, fire departments, and FAA representatives to secure the accident site, preserve evidence, and initiate the recovery of human remains and aircraft components. All investigative activities were conducted in compliance with NTSB Group Chairman protocols and 49 CFR § 831.10.

1.4 Radar data obtained from the FAA’s Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON) facility indicated the aircraft departed SNA on a northwesterly heading, maintaining an altitude of approximately 1,500 feet MSL. The last recorded radar return occurred at 0944:32 PST, at an altitude of 1,150 feet MSL, with a ground speed of 142 knots. The track terminated approximately 0.8 nautical miles from the initial impact point. No emergency radio transmissions were recorded on the assigned frequency of 124.35 MHz.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 The pilot-in-command held an airline transport pilot certificate with a rotorcraft-helicopter rating, a commercial pilot certificate with airplane single-engine and multi-engine land ratings, and a certified flight instructor certificate. The pilot possessed a type rating for the Sikorsky S-76 series. Medical certification was current, with a first-class airman medical certificate issued on November 14, 2019, with no limitations, waivers, or special issuances. The pilot’s medical history, as documented in FAA records, indicated no disqualifying conditions.

2.2 Review of the pilot’s logbooks and operator records indicated a total flight time of approximately 8,200 hours, with 6,700 hours in rotorcraft and 1,200 hours in the S-76B. Within the 90 days preceding the accident, the pilot had accumulated 145 flight hours, including 32 hours in the accident aircraft. The pilot’s most recent flight review was completed on October 12, 2019, and the most recent instrument proficiency check was conducted on December 5, 2019, in accordance with 14 CFR § 135.297. The pilot’s recent experience included 18 hours of simulated instrument flight and 12 hours of actual instrument flight within the preceding 60 days.

2.3 Training records maintained by the operator indicated completion of recurrent training on December 10, 2019, which included simulator sessions covering instrument flight rules (IFR) procedures, emergency operations, and spatial disorientation awareness. The training curriculum was developed in accordance with 14 CFR § 135.341 and approved by the FAA Principal Operations Inspector. The pilot’s duty time on the day of the accident began at 0630 PST, with a scheduled flight time of approximately 1 hour and 15 minutes. The pilot’s rest period prior to the duty day was documented as 10 hours, compliant with 14 CFR § 135.263.

2.4 The pilot’s personnel file contained no record of enforcement actions, certificate suspensions, or operational deviations. Performance evaluations from the preceding 24 months indicated satisfactory proficiency in all required maneuvers and emergency procedures. The pilot’s training records were cross-referenced with the operator’s approved training program and found to be complete and current.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 The accident aircraft was a Sikorsky S-76B, manufactured in 1988. The airframe was equipped with two Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6B-36A turboshaft engines, each rated at 650 shaft horsepower. At the time of the accident, the airframe had accumulated 11,450 total flight hours and 18,200 total cycles. The left engine had 2,100 hours since overhaul, and the right engine had 1,850 hours since overhaul. The main rotor system utilized a four-blade, fully articulated design with elastomeric bearings. The tail rotor was a two-blade, semi-rigid configuration.

3.2 Maintenance records were reviewed and found to be current. The aircraft was maintained under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program approved by the FAA. The most recent 100-hour inspection was completed on January 10, 2020, with no deferred maintenance items. All applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) were complied with, including AD 2018-15-09 regarding main rotor blade tracking and AD 2019-02-12 concerning fuel control unit inspections. Component life limits were tracked using the operator’s maintenance tracking software, and no components were found to be operating beyond their approved service intervals.

3.3 The aircraft was equipped with a standard analog flight instrument panel, supplemented by a Garmin GNS 430W GPS/NAV/COM unit and a King KX 165A navigation/communication radio. The aircraft did not have a flight data recorder (FDR) or cockpit voice recorder (CVR) installed, as these are not required for rotorcraft operating under 14 CFR Part 135 with fewer than 10 passenger seats. The flight control system utilized conventional mechanical linkages with hydraulic boost for primary controls. Notably, the aircraft did not incorporate automated flight envelope protection systems such as the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), which is a fixed-wing transport category feature designed to modify pitch authority and is not applicable to rotary-wing aircraft. The autopilot system, a S-76B standard three-axis system, was functional per maintenance logs but was not engaged during the flight.

3.4 Fuel system examination revealed that the aircraft was equipped with two main fuel tanks, each with a capacity of 115 gallons. Post-accident fuel sampling indicated the presence of Jet A fuel with no evidence of contamination or water separation. The fuel quantity at departure was documented as 180 gallons, providing an estimated endurance of 2 hours and 15 minutes at cruise power settings. The fuel management system operated within normal parameters, and no fuel starvation or imbalance conditions were identified.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 On January 26, 2020, a low-pressure system was moving through Southern California, producing widespread low ceilings and reduced visibility. The synoptic weather pattern featured a marine layer advecting inland, resulting in dense fog and stratus clouds. Surface observations indicated temperatures between 52°F and 55°F, with dew points near 50°F, creating relative humidity levels exceeding 90%. The National Weather Service (NWS) issued a dense fog advisory for the Los Angeles Basin and surrounding mountain corridors at 0600 PST, valid through 1200 PST.

4.2 Aviation routine weather reports (METAR) from nearby airports documented deteriorating conditions. At 0935 PST, the METAR for Van Nuys Airport (KVNY) reported wind 270° at 5 knots, visibility 1/2 statute mile in fog, ceiling 200 feet overcast, temperature 53°F, dew point 51°F. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) for KVNY, issued at 0500 PST, predicted visibility 1/2 to 1 statute mile in fog through 1200 PST. Pilot reports (PIREPs) filed between 0800 and 0930 PST indicated ceilings between 300 and 500 feet AGL, with visibility frequently below 1 statute mile in the Santa Monica Mountains corridor. Automated weather observing system (AWOS) data from Camarillo Airport (CMA) at 0940 PST reported visibility 1/4 statute mile, ceiling 100 feet overcast.

4.3 The accident flight route traversed a terrain corridor with elevations rising from approximately 500 feet MSL near the departure point to over 1,500 feet MSL in the Calabasas area. The pilot was operating under VFR, which requires a minimum visibility of 3 statute miles and a distance from clouds of 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 2,000 feet horizontal, per 14 CFR § 91.155. The observed meteorological conditions were below these minimums. The pilot’s last known position, derived from radar data, indicated a descent into a valley with terrain rising to 1,200 feet MSL while visibility was estimated at less than 1/4 statute mile.

4.4 Post-accident meteorological reconstruction utilized data from the FAA’s Aviation Weather Center, NWS surface analysis charts, and satellite imagery. The analysis confirmed that the marine layer had thickened and lowered throughout the morning, with a temperature inversion layer capping the fog at approximately 1,800 feet MSL. Wind shear was minimal, with surface winds remaining below 10 knots. The meteorological conditions were consistent with a classic coastal advection fog event, which is known to rapidly reduce visibility and ceiling heights in the region.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 The wreckage was distributed across a steep, brush-covered hillside with a slope gradient of approximately 35 degrees. The initial impact point was identified by a 12-foot-long scar in the chaparral, oriented on a magnetic heading of 045°. The debris field extended approximately 180 feet downslope, with major components concentrated within a 60-foot radius. No evidence of in-flight breakup or fire prior to impact was observed. The impact angle was estimated at 25 degrees nose-down, with a right-wing-low attitude.

5.2 Examination of the airframe revealed severe crushing and fragmentation consistent with high-energy terrain impact. The main rotor blades were separated at the root fittings, with fracture surfaces exhibiting ductile overload characteristics. The tail rotor assembly remained attached to the tail boom, which was fractured at the aft fuselage attachment point. The landing gear was retracted at impact, and the skid tubes were bent inward. Engine examination revealed that both PT6B-36A engines were rotating at impact, with compressor blades exhibiting rotational scoring and turbine blades showing thermal distress consistent with power application. The fuel control units were intact, and the fuel lines showed no evidence of pre-impact rupture.

5.3 The aircraft’s navigation and communication radios were recovered and sent to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for data extraction. The Garmin GNS 430W unit was severely damaged, but partial memory retention was confirmed. No flight data recording system was installed, limiting post-impact data recovery to radar track analysis, wreckage examination, and meteorological reconstruction. The Federal Aviation Administration’s Flight Standards Service provided technical support for the wreckage documentation and component preservation. All recovered components were cataloged, photographed, and stored in accordance with NTSB evidence handling procedures.

5.4 Structural analysis of the main transmission and drive shafts indicated no evidence of mechanical failure prior to impact. The elastomeric bearings in the main rotor hub were intact, with no signs of fatigue cracking or delamination. The hydraulic boost actuators for the cyclic and collective controls were functional, with fluid reservoirs at normal levels. The examination concluded that the aircraft’s flight control systems were operating within design parameters at the time of impact.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 The operator maintained a safety management system (SMS) in accordance with 14 CFR § 135.601, which included policies for weather minimums, flight following, and pilot decision-making. Company operations specifications (OpSpecs) authorized VFR operations only, with specific guidance requiring pilots to divert or land when visibility dropped below 3 statute miles or ceilings fell below 1,000 feet AGL. Internal audit records from the preceding 12 months indicated no findings related to weather-related deviations. The operator’s dispatch procedures required pilots to obtain updated weather briefings prior to departure and at 30-minute intervals during flight.

6.2 The FAA’s Flight Standards Order 8900.1, Volume 3, Chapter 18, Section 4, provides guidance for inspectors evaluating Part 135 operators’ compliance with weather minimums and VFR flight into IMC. The document emphasizes the importance of pilot training in spatial disorientation recognition and the use of terrain awareness systems. The Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) coordinated with the FAA’s Western-Pacific Region Flight Standards District Office to review the operator’s training curriculum and dispatch procedures. The review confirmed that the operator’s manuals were current and aligned with regulatory requirements.

6.3 Comparative operational data from other Part 135 and Part 121 operators, including Southwest Airlines Co, highlight industry-wide efforts to mitigate controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) and VFR-into-IMC accidents. While Southwest Airlines Co operates under a different regulatory framework (14 CFR Part 121) with mandatory FDR/CVR requirements and advanced terrain awareness and warning systems (TAWS), the underlying principles of weather decision-making and pilot situational awareness remain consistent across commercial aviation sectors. The NTSB has previously investigated similar rotorcraft accidents where continued VFR flight into deteriorating weather resulted in terrain impact. Industry safety bulletins and FAA advisory circulars (AC 91-79A) continue to emphasize the risks of VFR flight into IMC and the necessity of strict adherence to published minimums.

6.4 The IIC established a multi-disciplinary investigation team comprising specialists in operations, maintenance, meteorology, and human performance. All evidence was cataloged in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols, and chain-of-custody documentation was maintained for all recovered components. The factual data presented in this report was compiled from operator records, FAA databases, meteorological archives, and on-site wreckage examination. No operational or maintenance deficiencies were identified that would have precluded the aircraft from being airworthy at the time of departure. The investigation remains ongoing, with additional analysis of radar data, pilot communications, and training records pending. All findings will be documented in subsequent factual reports and incorporated into the final accident report.

## [sc-0_technical_analysis_073] Technical Analysis

> **Type:** technical_analysis | **Reliability:** 0.801 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

1. INTRODUCTION
This Specialist’s Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis of the flight data recorder (FDR), cockpit voice recorder (CVR), associated avionics wiring harnesses, and selected primary structural mounting components recovered from the January 26, 2020, accident involving a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter, registration N72EX, operated by Island Express. The examination was conducted at the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Materials Laboratory and Flight Recorder Readout Facility in Washington, D.C., between February 3 and February 28, 2020. The scope of this investigation encompassed the physical inspection of the recorder crash-survivable memory units (CSMUs), verification of data integrity, extraction and decoding of recorded flight parameters, metallurgical evaluation of the FDR/CVR mounting brackets, and correlation of recorded data with maintenance tracking systems. All procedures were performed in accordance with NTSB Investigator’s Manual Chapter 12, RTCA/DO-160G environmental qualification standards, and manufacturer technical manuals. The examination was coordinated with representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation, and the operator’s maintenance organization. Reference is made to FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 6, Chapter 2, Section 3, regarding operator maintenance program compliance and record retention requirements. The Modular Component Analysis System (MCAS) test bench was utilized for signal conditioning, parameter validation, and cross-referencing of analog-to-digital conversion linearity during the data extraction phase.

2. BACKGROUND
The accident helicopter was equipped with a dual-channel solid-state flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder system manufactured by L3Harris Technologies, model 2100-0000 series. The FDR (Part Number 2100-0000-00, Serial Number 18-0452) and CVR (Part Number 2100-0000-01, Serial Number 18-0453) were installed in the aft equipment bay, forward of the tail rotor pylon, per Sikorsky Service Bulletin 76B-31-0042. The system is certified under Technical Standard Order (TSO) C124a (FDR) and TSO-C123b (CVR), with crash survivability meeting 14 CFR § 29.1457 and § 29.1459 requirements. The CSMU housing is constructed from titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V (AMS 4911), rated to withstand 3,400 g impact loads, 1,100 °C for 60 minutes, and hydrostatic pressure equivalent to 20,000 feet of seawater. The system records 28 mandatory parameters plus 14 optional parameters at a sampling rate of 1 Hz for low-frequency data and 4 Hz for high-frequency control surface and engine parameters, formatted per ARINC 717/767 standards.

The operator, Island Express, maintained the aircraft under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program approved by the FAA. Maintenance records indicate the FDR/CVR system underwent its most recent functional check and calibration on November 14, 2019, at 1,842.3 airframe hours. The inspection was documented in accordance with the manufacturer’s Component Maintenance Manual (CMM) 2100-0000-00, Rev. 12, and tracked via the operator’s maintenance control software. Compliance with FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 6, Chapter 2, Section 3, was verified through audit of the operator’s maintenance tracking logs, which confirmed all life-limited components, calibration intervals, and software version controls were within prescribed limits. The MCAS equipment, utilized by the operator for predictive maintenance and component health monitoring, logged no fault codes or parameter deviations for the FDR/CVR system in the 90 days preceding the accident. The system’s underwater locator beacon (ULB) was a Dukane Model 173-001, operating at 37.5 kHz ± 1 kHz, with a certified battery life of 30 days. The helicopter’s operational history included 2,104.7 total airframe hours and 1,892.3 total cycles, with no recorded discrepancies related to the avionics or data recording systems.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS
The FDR and CVR were recovered from the accident site on January 27, 2020, and transported to the NTSB laboratory under chain-of-custody protocol NTSB-20-001. Visual inspection revealed the titanium CSMU housings remained structurally intact, with localized abrasion and minor denting on the forward-facing surfaces. The FDR housing exhibited a maximum deformation of 2.3 mm on the upper left quadrant, while the CVR housing showed no measurable deformation. The ULB on the FDR was activated, with the acoustic transducer intact and the battery terminal voltage measured at 8.4 VDC, consistent with post-activation discharge. The CVR ULB was not recovered; however, the mounting bracket was located 14.2 meters from the primary wreckage cluster.

The mounting hardware for both recorders consisted of four AN3-5A bolts per unit, torqued to 45 ± 5 in-lbs per Sikorsky Standard Practices Manual (SPM) 76B-20-00. Post-impact inspection revealed all eight bolts remained engaged, with thread engagement exceeding 90% of nominal length. The aluminum alloy 7075-T6 mounting brackets (Sikorsky P/N 76B-31-0042-001) exhibited ductile overload fracture at the primary load-bearing lugs. Fracture surface analysis via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed microvoid coalescence and dimpled rupture morphology, consistent with rapid tensile failure under high-G loading. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) confirmed base alloy composition within AMS 4045 specifications, with no evidence of intergranular corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, or fatigue striations. Hardness testing yielded an average Rockwell B value of 87.2, within the 85–90 range for 7075-T6 temper.

Data extraction was performed using the manufacturer’s proprietary readout software (Version 4.2.1) interfaced with the MCAS test bench for signal validation. The solid-state memory modules were accessed via JTAG interface, with no error correction codes (ECC) triggered. All 42 recorded parameters were successfully decoded, with data continuity verified across the entire 15-minute pre-impact recording window. Parameter synchronization was confirmed via the aircraft’s 28 VDC power bus timestamp, with a maximum clock drift of 0.08 seconds relative to GPS time. The CVR audio was extracted from the four-channel solid-state memory, with channel 1 (Captain), channel 2 (Co-pilot), channel 3 (Cockpit Area Microphone), and channel 4 (Radio) all exhibiting clear signal-to-noise ratios exceeding 22 dB. No evidence of thermal degradation, water intrusion, or electromagnetic interference was observed in the memory arrays.

Photographic documentation (NTSB-20-002 through NTSB-20-0045) includes macro and micro imaging of the CSMU housings, mounting bracket fracture surfaces, bolt thread engagement, and ULB activation status. All measurements were recorded using calibrated digital calipers (Mitutoyo 500-196-30, ±0.01 mm) and torque verification tools (Snap-on TQFR300, ±2% accuracy). The examination confirmed the FDR/CVR system met all TSO crashworthiness requirements and retained full data integrity through the impact sequence.

4. DATA ANALYSIS
The decoded FDR data was analyzed using NTSB-standardized parameter mapping software, with all values cross-referenced against the Sikorsky S-76B Flight Manual (FM) limitations and normal operating envelopes. The recording commenced at 09:42:11 PST and terminated at 09:57:03 PST, capturing the final 14 minutes and 52 seconds of flight. Altitude data was derived from both the static pressure system (corrected to 29.92 inHg) and GPS-derived geometric altitude, with a maximum differential of 42 ft during the final descent phase.

At 09:48:33 PST, the helicopter was established in level cruise at 2,100 ft MSL, with an indicated airspeed of 118 knots, heading 245° magnetic, and a collective position of 62%. Engine torque values for both Pratt & Whitney Canada PW210A engines were stable at 84% ± 2%, with main rotor RPM (NR) maintained at 100.2% ± 0.3%. At 09:51:17 PST, the aircraft initiated a gradual descent, with vertical speed increasing from -200 ft/min to -850 ft/min over a 45-second interval. Radio altitude decreased from 1,850 ft AGL to 1,120 ft AGL, with terrain proximity alerts not recorded, consistent with the absence of a terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS) on this configuration.

Between 09:53:42 and 09:55:18 PST, the flight profile exhibited increasing control inputs. Pitch attitude oscillated between -4° and -12°, while roll attitude varied between +14° and -18°. Lateral acceleration peaked at +0.6 g and -0.5 g, with vertical acceleration reaching +2.8 g and -0.4 g during a series of corrective maneuvers. Indicated airspeed fluctuated between 92 and 124 knots, with collective position varying between 58% and 71%. The data indicates the pilot was actively managing aircraft attitude and energy state in response to deteriorating visibility and rising terrain. At 09:56:01 PST, radio altitude dropped below 500 ft AGL, with a descent rate of -1,240 ft/min. The final 12 seconds of data show a rapid pitch-down to -18°, roll excursion to -22°, and vertical acceleration spike to +3.1 g, followed by immediate data termination at 09:57:03 PST.

CVR audio analysis corroborated the FDR timeline. The cockpit area microphone captured continuous engine noise, rotor blade passage frequency, and intermittent radio communications with Los Angeles Center. At 09:54:12 PST, the pilot acknowledged a clearance to maintain VFR conditions, followed by a 23-second period of reduced verbal communication. Background audio at 09:55:48 PST revealed increased rotor blade slap and aerodynamic buffeting, consistent with flight in marginal visibility and proximity to terrain. No automated warning tones (e.g., stall, overspeed, or ground proximity) were recorded, aligning with the aircraft’s avionics configuration.

All recorded parameters remained within the S-76B FM operational limits until the final impact sequence. No parameter dropouts, sensor failures, or data corruption were identified. The MCAS validation suite confirmed linear response across all analog inputs, with maximum deviation of ±0.3% from calibrated reference values. The data integrity was further verified through checksum validation and ARINC 717 frame synchronization, with zero bit errors detected across the entire recording.

5. SUMMARY
The examination of the flight data recorder, cockpit voice recorder, and associated structural components recovered from the January 26, 2020, accident yielded the following factual findings:
- The FDR (P/N 2100-0000-00, S/N 18-0452) and CVR (P/N 2100-0000-01, S/N 18-0453) were recovered with intact titanium CSMU housings, meeting TSO-C124a and TSO-C123b crash survivability requirements.
- The FDR ULB was activated, with battery voltage measured at 8.4 VDC and acoustic output confirmed at 37.5 kHz.
- Mounting brackets fabricated from 7075-T6 aluminum alloy exhibited ductile overload fracture consistent with high-G impact loading. Metallurgical analysis confirmed compliance with AMS 4045 specifications, with no evidence of pre-existing fatigue, corrosion, or material degradation.
- All 42 recorded flight parameters were successfully extracted with 100% data continuity. Parameter synchronization, clock drift, and signal linearity were verified using the MCAS test bench, with maximum deviation within ±0.3% of reference standards.
- FDR data indicates the helicopter was operating within normal performance envelopes until the final descent phase, with active control inputs recorded in response to deteriorating visibility and terrain proximity.
- CVR audio captured continuous engine and rotor noise, intermittent ATC communications, and aerodynamic buffeting consistent with flight in reduced visibility. No automated warning systems were activated.
- Maintenance records reviewed in accordance with FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 6, Chapter 2, Section 3, confirmed the FDR/CVR system was within calibration intervals, with no outstanding discrepancies or deferred maintenance items.
- The data recording system functioned as designed throughout the flight, with no evidence of pre-impact system malfunction, data corruption, or structural failure of the recorder assembly.

This report contains factual findings derived from physical examination, materials testing, and data analysis. No conclusions regarding probable cause are presented herein. All referenced measurements, test procedures, and engineering standards are documented in the NTSB laboratory case file and supporting photographic exhibits.

## [sc-0_witness_testimony_074] Witness Testimony

> **Type:** witness_testimony | **Reliability:** 0.709 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

INTERVIEW OF MARCUS T. VEGA, AVIATION SAFETY CONSULTANT / FORMER FAA INSPECTOR
Date: February 14, 2020
Time: 14:30 PST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Los Angeles, California
Interviewer: Investigator J. Lin, National Transportation Safety Board

[Recording begins]

Q: Mr. Vega, thank you for coming in today. For the record, please state your full name and your current professional role.

A: Marcus Thomas Vega. I’m an independent aviation safety consultant now, but I spent twenty-two years with the FAA, mostly in Flight Standards. I was an inspector, then a program manager. I still do contract work for a couple of Part 135 operators, mostly safety audits, SOP reviews, that kind of thing.

Q: And what was your relationship to the flight that crashed on January 26th?

A: I wasn’t on board. I wasn’t in the cockpit. I was actually at the Van Nuys FBO that morning, doing a pre-audit walkthrough for a client that shares the same maintenance facility. I knew the operator, I knew the pilot, and I was tracking the flight on my tablet just out of habit. It’s something I do when I’m on-site. I like to see how the day’s weather is playing out against actual operations.

Q: Can you walk me through what you observed that morning, starting from when you first became aware of the flight?

A: Yeah. I got there around eight-thirty, maybe eight-forty-five. The marine layer was already sitting heavy over the valley. You could see it from the ramp, just this flat, gray ceiling. I remember checking the METARs for Burbank and Van Nuys. Visibility was dropping, ceiling was maybe a thousand feet, but it was trending down. I pulled up the flight tracker around nine-oh-five. The Sikorsky S-76B had just departed, heading northwest toward Camarillo, I think. Standard routing. I watched the track for a few minutes, then I went inside to grab coffee. When I came back out, maybe nine-twenty, nine-twenty-five, the fog had really thickened. It wasn’t just low clouds anymore. It was rolling down the canyons. You could feel the dampness in the air, smell the wet dirt and chaparral. The hills were completely socked in.

Q: Did you attempt to contact the pilot or the operator?

A: I did. I called the company’s dispatch line first, left a message. Then I tried the pilot on the company frequency. He answered. I told him what I was seeing from the ramp, that the layer was pushing inland fast, and that the terrain up toward Calabasas was already obscured. He acknowledged. He said he was still VFR, still had the ground in sight, but… I don’t know. There was a pause. A hesitation. He said something like, “Yeah, I’m watching it, Marcus. I’ll turn back if it closes in.” I told him to be careful. That’s about it. I didn’t want to overstep. I’m not his dispatcher, I’m just a consultant.

Q: At what point did you lose visual or radar contact with the aircraft?

A: I didn’t have radar, obviously. Just ADS-B on my tablet. The track was moving northwest, then it started to… it curved slightly south, following the 101 corridor, I think. Around nine-thirty, nine-thirty-two, the icon just stopped updating. I refreshed it. Nothing. I looked out toward the hills. The cloud base was maybe eight hundred feet, but the terrain up there is twelve, fifteen hundred. It’s a classic trap. You’re flying along, you think you’re clear, then the fog drops, the ground rises, and suddenly you’re in a box. I lost sight of any aircraft within seconds. The rotor beat was there for a moment—steady, twin-engine rhythm—but then it just… faded into the mist. I couldn’t tell if it was the S-76 or something else, but the timing matched.

Q: You mentioned the terrain and visibility. From your experience, how does a pilot typically handle deteriorating conditions in that corridor?

A: Well, the textbook answer is you turn around, you climb, or you divert to an alternate. But the real world is messier. You’ve got schedule pressure, passenger expectations, sometimes just the human tendency to think, “I can make it through this patch.” I’ve seen it a hundred times. The FAA’s guidance is clear—Order 8900.1, Volume 4, Chapter 1, Section 3, basically spells out the prohibition on VFR flight into IMC. It’s not a suggestion. But manuals don’t fly the airplane. People do. And when you’re in a cockpit, looking out at a gray wall, your brain starts playing tricks. You lean on what you think you see. You trust your gut instead of your instruments. It’s not a failure of the machine. It’s a failure of the decision loop.

Q: You’ve mentioned automation in past safety seminars. Do you see parallels here?

A: I do, but I want to be careful not to conflate systems. The Sikorsky has a capable flight director, a decent autopilot, but it’s not a full-envelope protection system. It’s not like the MCAS on the 737 MAX, where the software actively trims the stabilizer based on a single sensor. That’s a completely different architecture. But the human factors side? Absolutely. When you’re relying on partial automation, or when you’re trying to maintain a visual reference that’s just… gone… the workload spikes. You get tunnel vision. You stop scanning. You fixate on one thing, and the rest of the picture disappears. I’ve briefed crews on this. I’ve run sim sessions on spatial disorientation. It’s insidious. You don’t realize you’re turning until the ground is right there.

Q: Did you witness the impact or hear anything unusual?

A: No. I didn’t see it. Nobody did, really. The fog was too thick. I heard sirens maybe twenty, twenty-five minutes later. First responders were already rolling. I stayed on the ramp, called the operator again, then I started pulling up weather archives, saving screenshots, logging my notes. I knew the NTSB would want everything. I didn’t want to lose the timeline.

Q: When did you first interact with the Board’s investigators?

A: Later that afternoon. A team from the agency arrived at the FBO around three. I handed over my tablet, my call logs, the weather printouts. They were thorough, as you’d expect. I gave them my statement, answered their questions. I know how the process works. I’ve sat on the other side of the table. I just… I wish I’d pushed harder. Maybe if I’d called SoCal Approach directly, filed a PIREP, made it official. But hindsight’s a luxury. You can’t unmake a decision once it’s made.

Q: To clarify the timeline, you’re estimating the last visual contact around nine-thirty, and the crash occurred approximately nine-forty-five?

A: Yeah. Roughly. I’d say nine-thirty-two for the track freeze. The actual impact, I think, was around nine-forty-five, maybe nine-forty-six. I’m going off the news reports and the later NTSB preliminary, but I don’t want to guess. I’ll stick to what I personally observed. I was on the ramp, I saw the weather close in, I heard the rotors, I lost the track. That’s it.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add for the record?

A: Just that… the S-76B is a solid machine. Sikorsky built it well. It’s not a maintenance issue, not a mechanical failure. It’s a weather and decision-making scenario. I’ve reviewed the operator’s training records, their SOPs, their checklists. They’re compliant. But compliance doesn’t equal immunity. You can follow every line in the manual and still get caught in a microburst, a sudden inversion, a fog bank that moves faster than the forecast said. I hope the investigation looks at the whole chain. The weather, the terrain, the human factors, the pressure. All of it. I’ll review the transcript before it’s finalized. I want to make sure I’m clear on the times, the sequence. I don’t want to overstate anything.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Vega. We’ll be in touch if we need clarification.

A: Appreciate it. I’ll be available. Just… do right by them. All nine. They didn’t deserve to be in that fog.

[Recording ends]

## [sc-0_regulatory_filing_075] Regulatory Filing

> **Type:** regulatory_filing | **Reliability:** 0.915 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION
FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
FLIGHT STANDARDS SERVICE
WASHINGTON, D.C.

DOCKET NO. FAA-2020-0852
NTSB ACCIDENT NUMBER: ERA20MA085
DATE OF OCCURRENCE: JANUARY 26, 2020
REFERENCE: NTSB SAFETY RECOMMENDATION A-21-012; FAA ORDER 8900.1, VOLUME 3, CHAPTER 18; 14 CFR PARTS 91, 121, AND 135

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This document constitutes the Federal Aviation Administration’s formal regulatory response and compliance directive regarding the January 26, 2020, controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) accident involving a Sikorsky S-76B helicopter (N72EX) operating under 14 CFR Part 135 in Calabasas, California. The referenced regulatory framework addresses visual flight rules (VFR) flight into instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), automated flight control system oversight, crew complement requirements, and terrain awareness system mandates. This correspondence is issued pursuant to NTSB Safety Recommendation A-21-012, FAA Docket No. FAA-2020-0852, and applicable provisions of 14 CFR Parts 91, 121, and 135.

2. BACKGROUND
The January 26, 2020, accident occurred when the pilot-in-command continued VFR flight into an area of rapidly deteriorating visibility and rising terrain, resulting in spatial disorientation and fatal impact. The National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation identified critical deficiencies in operational control, weather minimums compliance, and risk mitigation protocols. The applicable regulatory baseline is established under 14 CFR 91.155 (Basic VFR Weather Minimums), 14 CFR 135.181 (Second in Command Required), and 14 CFR 135.183 (Pilot Qualifications). While Part 135 operational specifications permit single-pilot operations under defined conditions, the absence of a mandated second in command during marginal VFR operations has been identified as a systemic vulnerability in high-workload, degraded-visibility environments.

Concurrently, the Agency has conducted a cross-cutting regulatory review of automated flight control system certification and operational oversight, informed by recent airworthiness actions concerning the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) on Boeing 737 MAX series aircraft. The MCAS certification and subsequent Airworthiness Directive (AD) processes necessitated comprehensive revisions to FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 11, Chapter 2, Section 4, which governs the validation of automated flight control functionality, pilot interface requirements, and failure mode analysis. These revisions established a precedent for enhanced human-machine interface scrutiny applicable to both fixed-wing and rotorcraft type certificates (TC) and supplemental type certificates (STC).

Historical safety recommendations, including NTSB A-19-008 and A-20-015, have consistently emphasized the necessity of enhanced terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS) installations, mandatory IMC escape training, and standardized crew resource management (CRM) protocols. Operational compliance data from Southwest Airlines Co has been utilized as a comparative baseline to evaluate adherence to 14 CFR 121.344 (Flight Crewmember Duties) and the efficacy of dual-pilot procedural redundancy during rapid meteorological deterioration. The integration of these findings has directly informed the current regulatory posture regarding minimum equipment list (MMEL) restrictions, automated system reliance, and crew complement requirements for operations in complex terrain.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
The Agency’s analysis of the ERA20MA085 accident, in conjunction with broader regulatory oversight activities, reveals several critical deficiencies in the existing compliance and surveillance framework. First, the operator’s failure to maintain 14 CFR 91.155 VFR weather minimums was compounded by an inadequate risk assessment matrix that did not account for rapid meteorological deterioration in mountainous terrain. Surveillance conducted pursuant to FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 3, Chapter 18, Section 2, identified that the operator’s operational control procedures lacked explicit protocols for mandatory diversion or IMC escape maneuvers when visibility fell below prescribed thresholds.

Second, the regulatory allowance for single-pilot operations under 14 CFR 135.181, while operationally efficient, presents an unacceptable risk profile during high-workload, degraded-visibility flight phases. The absence of a qualified second in command eliminates critical cross-checking capabilities, CRM redundancy, and shared situational awareness, all of which are essential for mitigating spatial disorientation. Comparative analysis of Part 121 operations, including those conducted by Southwest Airlines Co, demonstrates that dual-pilot configurations significantly reduce the probability of CFIT and VFR-into-IMC incidents through standardized callouts, task sharing, and automated system monitoring.

Third, the certification and oversight framework for automated flight control systems, as previously examined in the context of the MCAS type certificate amendment, reveals a persistent gap in human-machine interface validation. While MCAS was developed for transport category fixed-wing aircraft, the underlying regulatory principles governing automated system reliance, pilot override authority, and failure mode analysis are directly applicable to rotorcraft flight control augmentations. The current airworthiness standards under 14 CFR Part 27 and Part 29 do not sufficiently mandate real-time pilot feedback mechanisms or explicit training requirements for automated system degradation.

Finally, the Agency has identified inconsistencies in the application of MMEL provisions and STC approvals for terrain awareness and warning systems. Operators have historically been permitted to dispatch with inoperative TAWS components under MMEL relief, despite operating in terrain where such systems are critical to flight safety. This regulatory gap, coupled with insufficient Principal Operations Inspector (POI) oversight per FAA Order 8900.1, has permitted a degradation of safety margins in high-risk operational environments.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
In response to the identified deficiencies, the Federal Aviation Administration hereby issues the following regulatory directives and compliance requirements:

a. MANDATORY TAWS INSTALLATION AND MMEL REVISION: All Part 135 rotorcraft operators conducting flights in mountainous or complex terrain shall install and maintain Class A or Class B TAWS in accordance with 14 CFR 135.154. The FAA shall issue an Airworthiness Directive within 90 days to restrict MMEL dispatch relief for TAWS components when operating in designated high-terrain zones. Operators must submit revised MMEL documentation for POI approval within 60 days of AD issuance.

b. CREW COMPLEMENT AND CRM ENHANCEMENT: The FAA shall initiate rulemaking to amend 14 CFR 135.181, requiring a qualified second in command (SIC) for all Part 135 operations conducted under marginal VFR conditions or in designated high-terrain corridors. Pending final rule publication, operators shall implement enhanced CRM training modules specifically addressing single-pilot decision-making, spatial disorientation recognition, and IMC escape procedures. Compliance with revised training curricula shall be verified during the next scheduled operational surveillance cycle, not to exceed 180 days from the date of this directive.

c. AUTOMATED FLIGHT CONTROL SYSTEM OVERSIGHT: Drawing upon lessons learned from the MCAS certification process, the FAA shall revise FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 11, Chapter 2, to mandate comprehensive human factors validation for all supplemental type certificates involving automated flight control augmentations. Manufacturers and STC holders shall submit updated pilot interface documentation, failure mode analysis, and training requirements for Agency review within 120 days. The FAA will conduct targeted certification audits to ensure compliance with 14 CFR 25.783 and 14 CFR 27.1309 equivalent standards.

d. SURVEILLANCE AND COMPLIANCE VERIFICATION: Principal Operations Inspectors shall conduct quarterly surveillance of affected operators in accordance with FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 3, Chapter 18, Section 2. Surveillance shall include unannounced line checks, weather minimums compliance verification, and crew resource management evaluation. Operators failing to demonstrate corrective action within prescribed timelines shall be subject to operational specification amendments, including the imposition of additional crew requirements or route restrictions.

e. INTERAGENCY COORDINATION AND FOLLOW-UP: The FAA shall coordinate with the NTSB to establish a joint oversight working group to monitor the efficacy of implemented corrective actions. A comprehensive regulatory effectiveness review shall be published within 365 days, incorporating operational data, incident reporting trends, and compliance audit results. All findings shall be docketed under FAA-2020-0852 and made available for public comment in accordance with the Administrative Procedure Act.

This directive is effective immediately upon publication in the Federal Register. Operators are required to acknowledge receipt and submit a preliminary compliance plan to the appropriate Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) within 30 days. Failure to comply with the provisions outlined herein may result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR 13.19 and 14 CFR 13.21.

## [sc-0_press_coverage_076] Press Coverage

> **Type:** press_coverage | **Reliability:** 0.685 | **Subcorpus:** sc-0

HEADLINE: Nine Dead After Helicopter Crashes in Southern California Hills Amid Dense Fog

BYLINE: Marcus Thorne, The Metropolitan Herald
DATELINE: CALABASAS, Calif. —

Nine people died on Jan. 26, 2020, when a charter helicopter slammed into a steep, brush-covered hillside in Calabasas, California, amid heavy fog and low visibility. The aircraft, a Sikorsky S-76B, went down at approximately 9:45 a.m. local time, killing all eight passengers and the pilot aboard.

Preliminary radar data and weather reports indicate the pilot was operating under visual flight rules when the helicopter entered a bank of thick clouds and rising terrain. Emergency responders arrived to find the wreckage scattered across a rugged canyon, with no survivors. The crash has devastated families, halted local air traffic, and triggered an immediate federal probe into the circumstances surrounding the flight.

“Our top priority is determining exactly what happened in those final minutes,” said the Lead Investigator from the National Transportation Safety Board during a Sunday evening briefing. “We are treating this as a complex accident involving weather, terrain, and operational decision-making. The recovery of the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder will be critical.”

The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it is cooperating fully with the NTSB. “We are deeply saddened by this tragic loss of life,” an FAA spokesperson said. “Our inspectors are assisting with the on-site investigation and will review all maintenance and operational records associated with the aircraft and its operator.”

While the incident involves a private charter flight rather than commercial passenger service, industry leaders have expressed solidarity and renewed focus on aviation safety protocols. “Though our operations differ significantly from rotorcraft charters, the principles of risk management and weather avoidance remain universal,” said a Southwest Airlines spokesperson. “We extend our deepest condolences to the grieving families and stand with the broader aviation community in supporting a thorough, transparent investigation.”

The helicopter was operated by a regional charter service and was en route from Orange County to the Calabasas area when it encountered deteriorating conditions. The S-76B, manufactured by Sikorsky Aircraft, is a twin-engine medium helicopter widely used for corporate transport, emergency medical services, and VIP travel. It is known for its reliability and advanced avionics, but like all rotorcraft, it requires strict adherence to weather minimums.

The pilot had filed a visual flight plan, meaning the flight was intended to be conducted with clear visibility and visual reference to the ground. However, meteorological data shows the region was experiencing instrument meteorological conditions, or IMC, where cloud cover and fog reduce visibility to near zero. When pilots continue flying visually into IMC, they risk spatial disorientation—a phenomenon where the inner ear and eyes send conflicting signals to the brain, making it nearly impossible to maintain level flight without relying on cockpit instruments.

Aviation safety experts note that continuing visual flight into deteriorating weather remains one of the leading causes of fatal helicopter accidents. “The transition from visual to instrument conditions can happen in seconds, especially in coastal and mountainous regions,” said Dr. Elena Rostova, a former commercial pilot and aviation safety consultant. “Without proper instrument training and a disciplined decision to divert or land, pilots can quickly lose control.”

While recent aviation tragedies have drawn attention to automated flight control systems—such as the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System, commonly known as MCAS, which was implicated in two fatal Boeing 737 MAX crashes—experts emphasize that this incident appears rooted in environmental and human factors rather than mechanical automation. “Helicopters don’t rely on the same kind of pitch-trim automation as large commercial jets,” Dr. Rostova explained. “This is fundamentally about weather assessment, terrain awareness, and the decision to turn back when conditions deteriorate.”

The crash has left a community in mourning. Several of the passengers were traveling to a youth basketball tournament, and their families have gathered near the crash site, leaving flowers, jerseys, and handwritten notes. “They were just trying to get to a game,” said David Chen, whose nephew was among the passengers. “The fog rolled in so fast. We’re just heartbroken. All we want is answers and to know they didn’t suffer.”

Local residents described hearing a sudden, deafening roar followed by a plume of black smoke rising above the hills. “It sounded like a jet engine, then a massive thud,” said Maria Gonzalez, who lives near the canyon. “Within minutes, the sky was filled with emergency helicopters. It’s a nightmare we never thought would happen in our backyard.”

The Calabasas hills have long posed a challenge to low-flying aircraft. According to NTSB data, more than a dozen fatal helicopter crashes have occurred in Southern California over the past two decades, with a significant portion linked to pilots inadvertently entering clouds or fog. The agency has repeatedly warned about the dangers of “get-there-itis,” a psychological pressure that can lead pilots to press on despite worsening conditions.

Sikorsky Aircraft has maintained a strong safety record for the S-76 series, which has been in production since the late 1970s. The model is equipped with terrain awareness and warning systems, but these tools are only effective when pilots actively monitor them and adhere to instrument flight procedures.

The NTSB has deployed a full investigative team to the site, including specialists in weather, human performance, and aircraft systems. Investigators are currently mapping the debris field, interviewing air traffic controllers, and reviewing the pilot’s training and flight history. The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered and are being transported to NTSB laboratories in Washington, D.C., for analysis.

“We will leave no stone unturned,” the NTSB's top investigator reiterated. “This process takes time, but we owe it to the victims and their families to deliver a definitive, evidence-based report.”

The FAA has temporarily restricted low-altitude helicopter flights in the immediate area while the investigation proceeds. A preliminary report is expected within 30 days, with a final determination likely taking up to two years. Until then, the aviation community and a grieving public await answers from the wreckage of a flight that never reached its destination.
